GENERAL INTRODUCTION
SAINT AUGUSTINE AND MANICHEISM *
AUGUSTINE AT THE THRESHOLD OF MANICHEISM

At nineteen years old, at a moment that cannot be better specified, Augustine embraced Manichaeism. The event was not pure coincidence. Behind him is the reading of Cicero's Hortensius with the new internal situation that it created in the young man; There is also the disappointment that came from contact with the Bible; What remains, above all, is the skillful and profuse Manichean propaganda, which Augustine had to assume as the response to the longings that reading Ciceron's work had awakened within him; propaganda that in turn, most likely, had been partly responsible for both the positive effects that reading the aforementioned work had on him, and the disappointment that followed his encounter with the Bible. This propaganda was not the result of the actions of individuals, but rather an important chapter in the life of the Manichean sect, of every Manichean even.' programmed principles, be it of praxis alone, the Augustinian pages present us with a well-defined type of propaganda in terms of the recipient, in terms of the attitude of the propagandist and in terms of the method and content of the propaganda itself. Manichaeism, as a universal religion, was open to all people. In North Africa, his action was aimed at both pagans and Christians. We know several Manichaeans who came from paganism. The first of them, Bishop Faust, who even boasted about it (Faust XIII 1); Honoratus, Augustine's friend, passed directly from paganism to Manichaeism (Util 1,2), as did Nebridius (Conf IX 3,6). Augustine himself also tells us that certain Manichaeans had previously been Catholics, others never (Faust IX 2). But above all it was addressed to Christians, whether they were simple catechumens, even baptized, Catholics or Donatists 2. In this sense Augustine applies to the Manichaeans the text of Jeremiah: Partridge that hatches eggs that it has not laid (Faust XIII 17). On the other hand, the works of Manichaeans that we know, that of Adeimantus and that of Faust, are "anti-Christian" or rather anti-Catholic works. The Augustinian pages want us to see that they were trying to sell their religious merchandise not to any Christian, but particularly to those lacking training, although sometimes with great enthusiasm, this type of Christian being precisely the best ally of the sect's propagandists. In fact, by accepting the debate he soon fell into the networks of his opponents who were better prepared than him. When mentioning the usual recipients of Manichean propaganda, the Bishop of Hippo constantly speaks of the unlearned, of ignorant and poorly educated Christians, of slow-witted and "imbeciles", of the lazy and negligent people who constitute the great mass (Util 2,4), and above all of the imperiti. This is the most frequently repeated term, either referring to a specific incompetence (Almas 8; Adiman 14,2), or to an indeterminate one (passim). This inexperience of the Christians becomes a guarantee of hunting for the Manichaeans. It is them who usually

these harass and introduce into the networks of their fallacies (Faust XIV 8). We cannot doubt the truth of these statements 3. This is testified on the one hand by the Ability of Augustinian testimony in general; This is also witnessed by what he personally testifies about his own behavior in his Manichean period (Util 2,4); and once he has become an apologist for the Catholic cause, he must compose a commentary on Genesis in simple language so that it can be understood precisely by those who suffered the most from the attacks of the Manichaeans. The information acquires greater force when it is known that it was a request made by others (Genes I 1,1). But this is only part of the truth, since the complete truth is another. The Manichaeans also addressed the cultivators of intelligence. Agustín leaves this information in the shadows, but he does not silence it. It expressly says that they also addressed cultured men (Genes I 1,1). Although he had not stated it explicitly, he let us see it in what he told about his personal story. Augustine was not really one of those imperiti. He fell into the traps that were laid out for him precisely during his university period, we would say today. He himself campaigned among friends and fellow students, university students like him. Furthermore, the reasons that he will give as the cause of his fall into the sect are not exactly reasons for imperiti; rather, for people who were paid for their intellectual capacity, and who were not content with Monica's faith, which was equivalent to pure superstition for him and all who thought like him, but who demanded reasons or, in his words, the clear and naked truth (Faust XV 5). But Augustine, already a Catholic propagandist, puts into practice the wise pedagogy that his former coreligionists had taught him, to "reconvert" the Manichaeans, which is rather difficult, or, at least, to prevent other Catholics from falling. The resource consists of presenting those seduced as uneducated people, without preparation, without sufficient personal enlightenment, and who let themselves be carried away by others. In this sense he does not mind throwing stones on his own roof. Referring, no doubt, to those of unquestionable intellectual quality who succumbed to the claims of such propaganda, Augustine speaks of the "dupes" (Adiman 15,2; Costum I 12), among whom he himself is counted, since he would never have fallen

There is not much data on the relations of the Manichaeans with the Donatists and it is understandable given that the Manichaean sources from North Africa all come to us from Catholic sources. However, the information that Possidius gives us is very significant that it was the Donatists, along with the Catholics, who asked Augustine to confront Fortunatus in public debate (Life of Augustine 6). A sure sign that the Manichaeans were achieving success in both places.

Of the opposite opinion is L. J. R. Ort, who writes: «Manicheism had then and there the form of a Christian sect to which intellectuals only where admitted» (Mani. A religio-historical Vescription of his Personality [Leiden 1967] p.41). The "then" and "there" refer to the end of the 4th century in North Africa.

if his thoughts had been guided by piety and caution (Almas 3,24). In his own defense, he even resorts to the mitigating factor of age: he was seduced when he was still very young (Libre alb I 2,4). That it was not only or even preferably the unlearned and the imperiti who focused the attention of the Manichaean propagandists is also proven by Augustine's repeated statement that men full of curiosity for knowledge were easy prey; These were easily captured with the promise of showing them great discoveries (Genes II 26.40; Fund 21.23). Perhaps the most accurate thing is to reverse the order of priorities offered by Augustine. The Manichaean addressed itself primarily to the learned and to the most demanding spirits, and only secondarily to men without excessive intellectual pretensions. Augustine presents us with the Manichean propagandist with the favorite image of the hunter, who uses sweet baits to capture his prey (Faust XXII 13). Their language usually refers to that image. Thus he speaks of taking prey, of capturing (Faust XVII 2; Util 1,2), of surrounding without leaving a way out (Faust I 2; Adiman 14,2) or of harassing (Genes I 1,1). This image obviously carries a negative judgment, as it is associated with cruelty, the search for personal interest and the use of deception and trickery (Useful 1,2). The same negative judgment is evidenced by systematically presenting them as seducers (Util 9,21; Faust XVI 10, etc.), and obviously with harmful seduction (Costum I 17,20). Augustine also tells us how to prey and seduce they had no better weapon than the word. There is no evidence that they offered their books, although they did boast about them and show them. They were great debaters, and this gave them abundant success, especially when they chose their interlocutors among the imperiti we talked about before. They were even prepared for it. In the years of his Manichean fervor, Augustine experienced how he became more inflamed every day with the firewood of those triumphs (Util 1,2; Almas 11; Conf IV 1,1). The writing against Fausto has left us wonderful evidence of the method they used. The dialectic used to be vigorous, often based on dilemmas that left the inexperienced with no way out (Faust XVIII 3; XXII 5). The questionnaire-guide of the discussion was already established in advance in its general lines both by praxis and by the "Manuals", such as the one written by Faustus, which Augustine transmitted to us when refuting it.

who always took the initiative, which worked in his favor by catching the opponent off guard, while he had the answer prepared for the possible counter-question of the interlocutor. In these discussions, which were sometimes formal and solemn, but almost always street-based *, they tended to become great doctors, despite the fact that—according to Augustine's criticism—they were usually more ignorant than the person being questioned and only had the advantage of having first asked what they themselves did not know (Almas 10). Always according to Augustine's criticism, they confuse questioning with knowledge, clearly different realities, because, otherwise, no one would be wiser than him (ibid.). Propaganda sought first to destroy opposing positions, to then present and defend its own. This reality is beautifully expressed by Augustine himself by resorting to the image of the hunter to which we previously referred. "And so they did with us the same thing that bird hunters usually do: they stick reeds smeared with garter next to the water to catch those who go there thirsty, but first they hide and in a certain way cover the remaining waters in the vicinity, or they scare the birds away from them so that they will fall into their trap, not by free choice, but for lack of anything else" (Useful 1,2). Such was, always according to Augustine, the tactic: close all other possibilities and then set the trap in one's own. The image, then, tells us that they worked in two directions: one consisted of destroying other possibilities, specifically the Catholic and Donatist possibilities 5, and the other was offering their own. They are two sides of the same coin. There were two main resources that the Manichaeans used to deceive the unwary and to be considered teachers: one, to censor the Scriptures, and another, to pretend to live a chaste life of admirable continence (Costum I 1,2). They are undoubtedly two very important ones, but not the only ones. The first tried to undermine faith in the Church, the second to offer itself as an alternative. Let's see the first thing. His exacerbated criticism of Scripture, particularly the Old Testament, was the weapon most used to combat the Church. In this field victory was easy for them. We will see the criticisms in detail later. Of the formal and solemn debates, with notaries included, we know two: those with Fortunato and with Félix, whose minutes are found in this volume.

Regarding street debates, it is enough to remember Conf V 11,21; Costum II 8,11; Useful 6.13). Also note Agustín's information about his triumphs, which were undoubtedly street triumphs (Almas 11). Do not forget that the Donatists form common cause with the Catholics against the Manichaeans. See note 2,

so we do not stop here. There are two aspects that must be distinguished: first, the content of the Old Testament itself and then its acceptance by Catholics (and Donatists). Although both aspects cannot be separated in Manichaean criticism, we are going to do so and pay particular attention to the second. They used that reality to deny Catholics their being Christians. Contrary to what was established by Christ, Catholics pour the new wine of the New Testament into the old wineskins of the Old Testament (Faust XV 1), thus converting the Christian faith into something similar to the mythological figure of the hippocentaur, half horse and half man (Faust XV 1). They easily argued ad hominem against them: if they accept that the Christian, in imitation of Christ who did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it (Mt 5:17), must fulfill the law, since they do not fulfill it literally, they are showing that they are not Christians (Faust XIX 6). At the same time they used a misleading interpretation of Paul (Genes I 2,3; II 13,19; Util 3,8). In short, they considered Catholicism a Christian heresy (Faust XVI 7). Anti-Catholic criticism had other favorite targets: the reality of faith and the moral life of Christians. The first aspect acquires notable relevance and importance particularly for higher education levels. Above all, the Church was reproached for requiring reckless faith from those who came to it (Util 9,21; Faust XX 9). The Catholic Christian is a reckless credulous who, in practice, condemns in man the natural gift of reason, to which it corresponds as a religious duty to judge between what is true and what is false (Faust XVIII 3). The demands of the Catholic Church lead to creating people incapable of behaving rationally, who in disputes have no other arguments than recourse to faith. To such an extent - say the Manichaeans - they are unaccustomed to the use of reason, that they are not even capable of defending their faith. Faust, in particular, takes pleasure in highlighting what he considers the weakness of the Catholic defense (Faust XXI 1; XXVII 1). This explains why their number is mainly made up of women (Secund 4). Criticism of Catholic customs was also very effective for select spirits hungry for greater moral perfection.

The strength of the continuous wear and tear of the opponent through propaganda about his incoherent behavior cannot be overlooked, especially among the masses. This is what Augustine refers to when he writes: "Prego-

"to be before men who are blind and incapable of discerning our tares" (Costum I 31,68; I 34,75), Those who married and were in possession of fields, houses or money, were denied the title of Christians (Costum I 35,78), or, at most, they were considered as semi-Christians, while in this context they considered ascetics as christianiores, more Christian (Faust I 2.3). In order to present themselves as the authentic and only Christians, they even went so far as to relate Catholicism to paganism. In fact, as Faustus expresses himself, the law of Moses is not far from him (Faust XVI 10; XVIII 5). Furthermore, since there are only two religions: paganism and Manichaeism, that is, monotheism and "dualism", Jews and Catholics are a schism of paganism; The differences with respect to him are minimal (Faust XX 4), since they have maintained the pagan faith and customs in their entirety with minimal changes. In fact, the Catholics, consciously separating themselves from the pagans, took with them their idea of ​​principled monarchy to the point of believing that everything comes from God; they changed sacrifices into agapes; Instead of venerating idols, they worship martyrs with the same vows; They appease the shadows of the dead with wine and food and celebrate the same dates with the pagans, like New Year and the solstices. In short, nothing changed in customs; They are, in truth, a schism that is only distinguished from its parent by the different place of meeting (Faust XX 4). This moral life with high theoretical ideals, but with hardly any practical demands, explains why the masses go after the Catholics and not after the Manichaeans (Faust V 2). As in any proselytizing campaign, it is not always played with nobility and resorting to means that we could call immoral is not uncommon. Thus Augustine denounces that they, the Manichaeans, have no qualms about falsifying or simplifying Catholic doctrine (Faust XXII 8.22). In turn, they presented themselves as the valid alternative. On the one hand, they have the authentic Scriptures, not the corrupted ones *; On the other hand, they give a comprehensive explanation of reality 7 and, in particular, about the pressing problems for each man who has to live them daily, which is that of evil (Almas 10; Util 18,36; Conf III 7,12). And they do it in a way appropriate to the rational nature of man, that is,

eliminating blind faith and giving reasons. Agustín saw in them the sponsors, the guarantors of reason. The promise to give reason, and reason for the most obscure things (Util 7,17; 9,21), was a good "slogan" for cultured people or those who considered themselves so, since, as Augustine notes, these are promises that by their very nature cause joy to the soul (Util 9,21). They resort to that promise, according to Augustine, with the desire to conquer the masses in the name of reason (ibid.). Compared to the Catholic who places his happiness in believing without having seen, so he judges that it must be believed without first applying judgment and reason, the Manichaean prefers to renounce that happiness to remain joyful with his reason, if both things are at odds (Faust XVI 9). The reason offered by the Manichean propagandists was not just any reason, but precisely a certissima watt (Faust XXXIII 9). With the right method, the one that passes through reason, they can reach the truth. They promised it so much (Genes I 1,1) that Augustine can present them as deceivers in the name of truth (Faust XV 2). It is like a veil with which any errors can be covered to enter the souls of the imperiti through a beautiful door, without them noticing (Futid 11). Truth and reason: two great offers of Manichean propaganda. Final objective and method. A full and total truth about before, now and after, and about the existing totality. Truth that is reached after having penetrated into great mysteries (Phutid 21.23; Genes II 27.41). The result will be the elimination of all enigmas, since everyone will become clearer than the sun (Faust XV 6). The praise they give to Manes is based precisely on the fact that he has eliminated the shell of the figures and symbols and has offered the naked and authentic truth (Faust XV 5). The very title of the books of Manes is intended to seduce the miserable (Felix I 14; II 5). We said previously that the main recipients of Manichean propaganda were Christians. They accommodate that audience to the maximum. For this purpose, they dress all their propaganda in Christian clothing. They quote little from Manes and his writings and a lot from Christ and his Scripture. In the words of Augustine, they try to cover their foolish and sacrilegious fables with the pallium of the Christian name (Faust XXII 16).

When they present the points of their doctrine, they try to make them coincide with Christian truths (Faust XX 12) and present elements that coincide with that same Christian faith, like very sweet bait with which

to capture those dedicated to Christ (Faust XXII 13). This is one of the reasons most repeated by Agustín. Referring to Manes, he affirms that he sought to enter the minds of the imperiti by using the name of Christ, to the point of wanting to be worshiped instead of Christ himself (Phutid 8), or that he seduces with the holy name of the Paraclete (Faust the poisoned edges of his glass (Faust XIII 17). Likewise they accept the Scripture, better yet, the New Testament, to more easily deceive under the appearance of Christianity (Faust XIII 5; XXII 13; Felix I 5). The recourse to the authority of Christ is no less frequent in their mouth and they gladly accept learning from him where salvation comes to man (Faust V 3). It is not in vain that the category to which Augustine belonged within Manichaeism was called that of "listeners." To designate the period of his affiliation to the sect he usually uses the phrase "when I heard you", that is, when he was your listener (Costum II 8,11; II 12,25; Fortun 37; Futid 8; Util 1,3, etc.). The Manichaean worshiped the word. We already talked about its use in the advertising campaign and in street and non-street discussions. Now we have to refer to the process of internal catechization to which the new conquests were subjected. They called it “enlightenment” (Futid 5). Agustín makes frequent references to it, even if indirectly, and to the contents. The solebatis dicere turn is not exactly a "hapax" in the anti-Manichean work of the bishop of Hippo (Costum I 29,61; II 13,28; II 18,60; Phutid 6; 10; 21; Genes I 11,17). His memory is so vivid that he can complete what Faust indicates in his writing with what is stored in his memory (Faust XXII 92). "You are not little known to me," he will tell them in the heat of the controversy (Costum I 17,30), although he does not refer directly to doctrines, but rather indirectly. Augustine can later confront and refute the Manichaeans from a privileged position: that of having known the system "from within." Not only the books of the sect, but also the exegesis of those books. It is true that his condition as a simple listener closed the doors to certain aspects of her life (Fortun 3), but not at a doctrinal level, regarding which, if anything remained unclear, they promised him that Fausto would explain it to him with absolute clarity. That is why he can argue with the force of a novi (Costum II 2,4; Contra Secund 20). A novi that comes from an audire atiente et studiose, magna cura et diligentia (Costum II 12,25; II 19,68; Útil 1,3), which shows us the initial eagerness of the young man. In this regard, Agustín will feel like he has perfectly fulfilled his obligations as a listener. So much so that later, and in the midst of the controversy, he would ask the Manichaeans to have the same attitude toward Catholic doctors that he had toward them; that they listen to him with such great peace of soul and with the same desires with which he listened to them, and thus "the nine years during which they mocked him will not be necessary" (Costum I 18,34). It was an instruction for personal use, we would say,

and also with a view to controversy and public disputes. The Manichean doctors were particularly interested in providing answers to the objections that they would encounter in the debates with the Catholics26. To give this instruction, they did not have schools or institutions as such, but instead gave it in private homes 27. If the first was practically impossible in Africa due to the illegal situation of the sect, the second favored the climate of familiarity and friendship that Augustine so frequently praises in them. In this "Manichean school" Augustine learned or increased his wealth of knowledge regarding Manes, his writings, his dogmatic and moral system. He also met other Manichaeans. But don't fool yourself. The term Scripture or, better, Christian Scripture has in their mouths and in their pens a different, more restricted meaning than it has in the mouth of a Catholic. In fact, at the same time that they accept the New Testament globally, within the limits that we will later analyze, they reject the Old Testament in its entirety in the most absolute way. There are few data more abundant than this and with more variety of expressions in all of Augustine's anti-Manichean polemical work. For them, the Old Testament must be called Jewish Scripture, never Christian Scripture, a term that fits only the New. Furthermore, the Old Testament is the Scripture of Catholics54, while the New belongs to them. The importance that the Manichaeans themselves assigned to this point, as well as that which Augustine himself attributed to it, undoubtedly seeing the effectiveness it brought to them, can be shown both by the two works of Manichaeans that have been left to us thanks to Augustine, that of Adeimantus and that of Faustus 55, and by the effort that Augustine put into refuting them. To which must be added a third book specifically dedicated to the subject: Commentary on Genesis in Reply to the Manichaeans. The acceptance or rejection of the Old Testament constitutes a decisive criterion to distinguish the Manichaean from the Catholic56, to know true Christianity. The Manichean opposition to the Old Testament takes two directions: one is global and the other is particular, that is, referring to each of the groups or parts that compose it: history of the patriarchs, the prophets and Moses and the law. In his writing, Faust considers the question he puts in the mouth of a Catholic about whether they accept the Old Testament almost superfluous, since the obvious fact that they do not comply with its precepts already anticipates the answer; the practical position is already an indication and proof of what the theoretical one is (Faust VI 1;

He claims to accept the Old Testament and then rejects it in practice58. A text from Faust himself explains the reasons why they do not accept him; The first formulates it conditionally, and then denies the condition: «If he offers me any inheritance, I accept it; If you don't offer it to me, no, because it is a sign of great improbity to accept a will in which one appears as disinherited. In fact, since he promises the land of the Canaanites to the Jews who follow his rules, dignity requires that, once the inheritance is rejected, the will is also rejected. A second reason is based on the poverty of what it promises, compared to what is promised in the New: the kingdom of God and eternal life. What he promises is something such that even if it were given to him, it would annoy him (Faust IV 1). This recourse to the New Testament to reject the Old is one of the typical features of the Manichean position, always more attentive to disqualifying the Catholic adversary than to exposing the doctrine itself. It is precisely out of fidelity to the New Testament that the Manichean refuses to accept the Old 59. Mt 9:16 lends them a hand by prohibiting mixing Christian novelty with Hebrew obsolescence (Faust VIII 1). And, in case there was any doubt about the interpretation that should be given to this evangelical text, there is apostolic praxis. If the apostles, who were born in the Old Testament, abandoned it, it would be incongruous for those who, on the one hand, were born outside of it and, on the other hand, venerate them, to accept it. These are the words of Faustus, who relies on Paul: "If what was bitter became sweet, must what was naturally sweet become bitter?" (Faust IX 1). Other New Testament precepts force the Manichaean to walk in the same direction. Rom 7,7 prohibits desiring what belongs to others; Consequently, starting from the irreducibility between the Jewish and the Gentile, the born Gentile is prohibited from desiring the Jewish, that is, the Old Testament (Faust X 1). They referred to this "everything" to the knowledge of the three stages of reality: the beginning, the middle and the end (Felix I 6; II 7; Faust XIII 6); a "science" of which they were proud and which was what they transmitted in their catechism to the followers of the sect. Thanks to the explanations of his doctors and his own readings, Agustín learned about this "rational" explanation of reality, although progressively (Almas 16) and he has transmitted it to us, just as he understood it. Relying on the data provided by their works, we are going to present it following each of the stages, with the certainty that overall its data are worthy of faith 7S. The beginning.—Manicheism is presented, we have said, as an explanation of reality. This explanation is not disinterested, that is, from merely philosophical-speculative positions. The explanation of reality is the result of the desire to explain another, more concrete and more pressing reality, the problem of evil, the starting point in their missionary work and terrain in which it was easier for them to reap triumphs (Costum II 2,2). How can we explain evil? Obviously it is difficult to explain from a theological monism, and even more difficult from the idea of ​​a creation carried out by a good God, which is the Catholic proposal. Whatever step in the degrees of evil one begins with, it will always end up ultimately at the author of everything, the sole creator, who is responsible for evil (Fortun 15.16.19.20), with the logical consequence of being deprived of his fundamental attribute: goodness (Fortun 14; Conf III 7,5; Secund 19), unless to safeguard his goodness one intends to present him as ignorant of the consequences of their actions, which would not improve the response in any way, since it would also destroy the image of God. Manes believed he found an easy solution by resorting to initial and radical dualism, the pillar on which his entire system is based. Since there are contrary things - Fortunatus tells Augustine - there cannot be a single substance (Fortun 14). There are, then, two principles (Faust XXI 1), or two natures (Costum II 3,5; Felix II 2); two kingdoms (Costum II 2,5; Fund 13; Felix I 17); two lands (Felix I 17), two substances (Fortun 14.18; Fund 13). One is the substance of the body, another is the

eternal presence, that of the almighty Father (Fortun 14), or, as Faustus calls them: God and Hyle; the first, the beginning of all good, and the second, of all evil (Faust XXI 1). They are the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness, respectively (passim). They are, therefore, radically, as roots (Fortun 14), not only different, but also opposite. The existence of these two substances or principles is a postulate of the undeniable existence of evil in the world. But the Manichean propagandists and catechists put all their effort into showing that it is evangelical and apostolic doctrine. It is precisely Fortunato and Félix who insist most on this aspect, before a largely Catholic audience. Fortunato sees dualism indicated in Mt 7:17: the good tree and the bad tree (Fortun 14) and Felix increases the repertoire of scriptural proofs. In addition to Mt 7:17, he presents Mt 13:27-28: the enemy who sows tares; Mt 25,31-41: sheep and goats in the final judgment; From the Pauline texts he turns to Rom 8:7; 2 Cor 4,4; 12.7-9; Proof also of this dualism is the crucifixion of Christ and his apostles (Felix II 2). Nor is there any lack of the argument drawn from the theology of redemption: If God sends his Son to liberate, it is because what needed liberation was in the power of someone or something other than him (Fortun 9.11; Felix I 19; II 20). This dualism is what distinguishes it from paganism and, therefore, what constitutes authentic Christianity (Faust XX 3). The kingdom of light.—Texts from the Letter called the Fundament, which Augustine has preserved for us, allow us to know the description of the kingdom of light (Fund 13). But it is not the only source we have. The disputes with Fortunato and Félix, as well as the works Reply to Faust, The Nature of Good and The Heresies also provide us with data, although some are repeated. The aforementioned Letter describes the kingdom of light with these words: "In him the Father occupies the empire of light, eternal by his holy origin, magnificent by his power, true by his very nature, always exultant by his very eternity, containing within himself the wisdom and the meanings of life" (Fund 13). The text distinguishes, therefore, the Father and the empire of light. That is to say, although one can and should speak of unity, the kingdom does not constitute a single reality.

The unity results from the same and unique substance, incorporeal and spiritual (Fund 21), in which the Father and his peaceful kingdoms participate in absolute equality and coeternity, that is, the luminous earth (Fund 13; Nature 42), the ungenerated earth and air

According to the Manichean doctor Felix, there are three realities that participate in the same divine substance: the Father, what is generated by him, and the places where he has placed what is generated by him, which would correspond to a triple category in the light itself in which the divine substance consists: the inaccessible light where the Father dwells, the uncreated and ungenerated light of the luminous earth, and the uncreated, but generated, light of the sun and the moon, the abode of Power and Wisdom of the Son (Faust XX 2). But, although everything that exists in the kingdom of light has the same substance, it does not have the same nature, which is different. Thus God has a nature that is his own and exclusive, different from that of the rest of the beings that participate in his substance. Fortunato's profession of faith describes God in the following way: «... he is incorruptible, luminous, inaccessible, ungraspable, impassible, inhabitant of an eternal light that is his own; He does not produce anything corruptible from himself, and in his kingdom nothing can be discovered that is contrary to him: neither darkness, nor demon, nor Satan" (Fortun 3). Augustine also reminds us how they conceive it: "the supreme good, immutable, impenetrable and inviolable... inaccessible to all harm" (Costum II 3,5; 11,20). Faust explicitly recognizes him as finite, limited by the presence of evil (Faust XXV 1), while describing him with features that have the flavor of Manes's original text: "The great king who rules with an eternal scepter, with his head crowned with flowers and his face resplendent with light;... twelve 'centuries' dressed in flowers and full of melodies, throw their flowers at the face of the Father" (Faust XV 5); twelve 'centuries' that must be identified with the twelve members of its light spoken of in the Letter of the Foundation (13). The principle of evil.—Also with reference to the principle of evil, it is the Letter called the Fundament that allows us to know directly how Manes understood this second original principle. In contrast to the sobriety used by the polemicists Fortunato and Félix, who try to present it to a Catholic audience with Catholic terminology, relying on texts from the New Testament, here the language is flowery. Augustine himself will find himself proclaiming to the four winds, in his writings, if not in his public discussions, the fruits of such exuberant imagination in the description of the principle of evil.
The kingdom of evil, the stirps or gens tenebrarum, an expression preferred by Augustine, or the terra pestifera, as Manes calls it, was composed of

ta of five provinces with their corresponding inhabitants. The provinces are the following: that of darkness, that of muddy and murky waters, that of impetuous winds, that of fire and that of smoke, ordered in such a way that each one includes the next within it. Each one also has its specific inhabitants: darkness, snakes; the waters, the native animals, which are the fish; the winds, the volatiles, which are the birds; fire, quadrupeds, such as horses, lions, etc.; the smoke, the bipeds, from which men come (Costum II 9,14; Fund 28; Conf III 6,11; Heresies 46, etc.). Each of these provinces produced a species of tree that gave rise to the princes who fathered the other inhabitants (Faust VI 8). The inhabitants of each of these provinces were subject to that prince, father of all, and all these princes, in turn, were subject to a single superior leader, to the king of the bipeds, inhabitants of smoke (Faust XXI 14). This prince is sometimes called God - Faust acknowledges - but it is in inappropriate language, since there is only one God (Faust XXI 1). Just as the kingdom of light lacked all evil, the kingdom of darkness lacks all good (Costum II 5,7). While the substance of the kingdom of light is spiritual and incorporeal, that of the kingdom of darkness is corporeal (Fund 21). Of both principles they offered, as if it were the revelation of a great mystery (Fund 21), a graphic representation: that of a loaf of bread divided into four equal parts, three of which were white and one black; The white ones forming a unit correspond to the kingdom of light, the black one to that of darkness. The latter is infinite in the longitudinal direction and in depth, while upwards there is emptiness; the other, on the other hand, is infinite in all its directions, except in that where it borders on evil (Fund 21). It is the theory or image of the cuneus (Fund 22-25; Faust IV 2; XXII 98). The middle time.—At a certain moment a combat takes place between the two kingdoms (Adiman 20,3; Fund 12; Secund 6; Heresies 46, etc.). The initiative comes from the prince of darkness, as a consequence of the perception, after one of his internal convulsions, of the light beyond the borders of his own kingdom, by the animals that lived in it (Costum II 9,17; Faust XXI 10; X 3).

In a speech addressed to the inhabitants of his kingdom, the prince of darkness invited them to go to war against God and thus capture the light of which they were deprived (Faust XXI 10; Costum II 9,14).

For combat, he came out armed with the elements that compose it and that were mentioned before. According to Augustine, God the Father only realized this when he perceived a great tumult on the borders of his kingdom (Faust V 4). According to Fortunatus (Fortun 15.16.33; Secund 6), on the contrary, God's foreknowledge acted to deal with the rebellion and contain the enemy within his own limits. The concrete means consisted of sending a part of oneself, a virtus or sermo (Fortun 20), a part of the divine substance, of the luminous earth (Secund 6), frequently called by Augustine as the first man (Faust V 4.5; VI 8; To face the enemy he dresses in a kind of armor made up of his own five elements: light, air, wind, water and fire (Faust II 3; XI 3). He was defeated and fell prisoner of matter; The five elements are devoured by demons, which gives rise to the mixture of light and darkness, which still persists today (Fortun 7; Faust II 5; VI 3.4). Augustine presents the result of the combat as a clear defeat of God; the Manichaeans, on the other hand, as a sample of their wisdom who used that trick to defeat the enemy. In fact, where he thought he had triumphed, he found his own defeat. Although it is true that the first man and the part of the divine substance devoured by the demons remained lethargic, forgetful of their own being, the situation is temporary and, furthermore, it becomes the destructive principle of those who devoured it (Fortun 22), like a poison that corrupts it (Faust XXII 13), which will force them to return it. But the definitive triumph will only be at the end. The continuation of middle time is dominated by God's attempt to recover the part of his substance that was imprisoned in the kingdom of darkness, and by the actions he undertakes to that end. Indeed, the God that Augustine shows as cruel by sending a part of his substance to certain defeat is not insensitive to its fate, a lamb sent among the wolves to defend the kingdom of light (Fortun 22), and to avoid seeing the unfortunate situation he covers his face with a veil (Faust XVIII 7; XX 17). The Father's initial action will consist of freeing the First Man, who, returned to consciousness, shouts at him, repeated seven times.
To do this, he evokes the powerful Spirit who descends into the darkness, reaches out to the First Man, frees him and makes him return to the kingdom of light. but

The divine elements he carried with him remained to be released. To this end, the same Spirit will proceed to the fabrication—not creation—of the world (Faust XX 9.10; XV 5). In fact, it was not made from nothing, but from the substance of evil or matter to which the light part had been mixed, or as a consequence of the initial combat (Faust II 5; Fortun 1). In Augustine's expression, of the bodies of the race of darkness and the members of God who had been defeated (Faust XX 9). Such fabrication consisted of nothing other than putting order in the orderless kingdom of darkness. With this material the Spirit formed the world that consists of eight earths and ten heavens (Faust XXXII 19), each one occupying a more or less elevated place according to the amount of light they possessed (Faust VI 8). The first, from above, is occupied by the sun and the moon, both composed of luminous substance (not stained with matter), fire and water, respectively (Heresies 46); "ships" that God uses to carry out the transfer of the purified divine substance to the kingdom of light. Then come the other celestial beings, in which the Spirit places most of the princes of demons, males and females, some of whom were pregnant (Faust VI 8); others were placed in lower strata, depending on the amount of light (Faust VI 8). The earth, in turn, contains the remains of the demons who died in combat. The rocks are his bones, the wine his gall (Faust XV 4; Heresies 46). The Manichean cosmological myth introduces a notable variety of agents who are united by belonging to the kingdom of light. In addition to the First Man and the powerful Spirit, already mentioned, Augustine speaks of the Lightbringer, the Atlas and the King of honor (Faust XX 10.11.12), adding that they are innumerable, with various names and offices. The first of them, the Light Bearer (Splenditenens), with six faces, resplendent with light, holds the world suspended and weeps for the defiled and captured members of God (Faust XV 5.6; XX 9.10). Atlas, in turn, resting on one knee, supports the mass of the world on his powerful backs. Another agent, the glorious King, is in charge of moving the wheels of the winds, the fires and the waters from below, and another agent travels through the sky with his rays and collects the particles of God (Faust XX 10) 76.

In the myth the sun and the moon occupy a prominent place. Other "characters" are the King of Honor, surrounded by armies of angels; Adamante, warrior hero who has the staff on the right and the shield on the left (Faust XV $).

It consisted of being means of transport - that is why they are called "ships" - of the divine substance, already freed from matter, to the kingdom of light. More specifically, the moon takes it to the sun and the sun passes it to the kingdom of God (Nature 44; Heresies 46; Letter 55,4,6). But its function in the service of the work of liberation is not reduced to being a means of transportation, but includes another aspect. The sun is also the place where a third messenger77 will reside, sent to serve the same cause, accompanied by several collaborators or androgynous virtutes, that is, with the ability to transform into males or females, as appropriate. Specifically, before the females of the race of darkness they present themselves as beautiful young men and before the males as also beautiful maidens, with the purpose of exciting the concupiscence of each, and in this way the vital substance, which is part of the divine substance, can escape from its members weakened by the same concupiscence and, collected and purified, achieve liberation. The theme is repeatedly exploited by Augustine to show the ridiculous and shameless nature of the Manichaean fable (Faust XX 6.8.9; But such liberation is not always automatic or total. In fact, the divine substance released from the bodies of demons, if it comes out with a sufficient degree of purity, mixes with the pure air, is completely purified and ascends to the luminous ships that take it to the homeland. But it may also be the case that it carries with it too many impurities, a result of the previous situation; In this case, it descends to the earth to mix with the trees, other plants and seeds, where it is already subject to a very different fate, since either it can be eaten by an animal, once again remaining a prisoner of flesh and matter, or it can be eaten by a chosen one, thus achieving definitive liberation (Nature 44; Costum II 15,36). Only thanks to that part of the divine substance do both plants and animals have some good. Neither of the two categories of beings come from God (Fund 24). The Manichean myth, however, takes longer to explain the origin

of animals. The smallest ones (fleas, lice, bedbugs) are born by spontaneous generation from the squalor of our bodies (Costum II 17,63). The rest are born from the abortions that the females of the demon princes suffered when the stars to which they were chained began to rotate. Having been conceived before the mixture of good and evil, they had no part of any good, being totally evil (Costum II 17,61; Faust VI 8; XXI 12), until the moment when they ate the herb that already contained part of the divine substance fallen from the princes of demons. The categories reproduce those of the different departments of the kingdom of darkness. A particular case is man, who also comes, as far as his body is concerned, from abortions from the prince of the kingdom of smoke, that is, from the prince of the bipeds. He dominated over all the inhabitants and leaders of the other dens, until he became prince of darkness. His name was Sacias (Heresies 46). Contemplating the light of the rising sun, he addresses his subordinates to ask them for the light that they have imprisoned in themselves, to make a replica of that sun and to be free from the darkness in which they live. They gave their consent as a means also to preserve it (Nature 46). The transmission took place in an original way: they united with their females and they conceived; The creatures, similar to their parents, received, as firstborn, the maximum amount of strength. The prince devoured them. Full of strength, after this delicacy, he had carnal intercourse with his wife, the result of which was the birth of Adam, who contained within himself a large amount of light-strength that he had received from his father. Thus Adam's soul was almost all light, with hardly any mixture of darkness (Costum II 19,73). Unfortunately, the prince of darkness once again joined his companion, a union from which Eve was born, with very little substance in her soul (Heresies 46). She caused the minimal part of evil that he possessed to rebel in Adam against the much more abundant good, so that it defeated him and he sinned. Thus through reproduction the chaining of divine light in the kingdom of darkness is perpetuated. Consequently, every man who is born receives a part of the divine substance in his being, one of his souls. But the Manichaeans did not formulate this reality positively, but rather in a negative way: man becomes God's prison.
Procreation is the way devised by the prince of evil to contain part of the divine substance under his dominion. The woman, as a place

The myth about the origin of man explains two things: the division that he experiences within himself, which is referred to in Rom 7 Saint Paul. Man is not a unitary being, but a compound of two substances, not only different, but also opposite and enemies. They are the two types of souls, one born of God and which is the same as him by nature, and the other born from the kingdom of darkness, the origin of indecision, since one tends towards good and the other towards evil. These are not two rational souls, but two vital principles, one intellectual and the other not. One is related to the mind and the other to the animating principle of the body at the level of flesh and blood 78. This also explains the existence of evil in man: one soul, the bad one, tries to overcome the other, the good one. Their radically opposite natures make them be in continuous opposition, and sin would be the submission of the good to the will or whim of the evil. According to Secundino it is a "fight of spirits." This mixture of good and evil present in man is what leads him to sin, which occurs when the good soul, already awakened from its sleep and its ignorance, already knowing its origin and its being, gladly surrenders and submits to the nature of evil, to the bad soul (Fortun 21). The starting point for sin is, therefore, the mixture of good and evil, for which the soul is not responsible, since at that level it is subject to necessity. At the other level, the soul already sins by voluntarily granting its consent (Secund 3; Contra Secund 14). Soteriology.—Such is the situation of the world and that of the beings that are in it. The world is a great structure built with the precise purpose of releasing a part of the divine substance, imprisoned in darkness and currently mixed in different proportions in each of the beings that compose it. How is liberation carried out specifically? It goes without saying that it is a plan and decision of God the Father and that he carries it out through "divine beings." The second appellatio of the only numen that Faustus speaks of is the Son. In the words of Saint Paul (1 Cor 1:24) it is designated as the Power and Wisdom of God, always in relation to the saving work. It is related to the secondary and visible light and its abode is placed in the sun and the moon, with reference to its condition of Power and Wisdom. From here comes the importance that both stars had in Manichaeism both at the level of "dogma" and of cult. Augustine repeatedly accuses the Manichaeans of worshiping the sun (Costum II 8,13; Fund 2; Genes I 3,5; II 25,38; Faust V 11; VIII 2; XIV 11; XV 15; XX 9). In the Confessions he affirms that it was the food they offered to his soul hungry for God, instead of him (Conf I I I 6,10). The Saint explicitly states that the Manicheans consider this visible and, therefore, corporeal sun, as God and part of God (Contra Secund 16.20; Faust V il), who do not consider it as a creature, but as prolatio or missio of God (Faust XXI 3). Prolatio as part of God and missio as his presence in the world is due to the fact that he was sent by the Father to fulfill a specific mission. But other texts by Augustine himself allow us to note that the previous statements were the result of controversy and that the Manichaeans did not identify this visible sun with the Son. Firstly, in the same Confessions he affirms that this visible sun is more excellent than the resplendent ghosts that were offered to him (Conf III 6,10). And in his Reply to Faust he writes that instead of worshiping the visible sun in a spherical shape, they worship a certain ship, the fruit of their imagination, from which light escapes through a triangular window (Faust XX 6) 83. That is, the sun that they worship is not this visible sun, but something else that is hidden behind it, or that is symbolized in it. The Son, therefore, is not identified with the sun. We have already made reference to the Trinitarian formula that appears in the Letter called the Foundation.

His work with Adam and Eve was not harmful, but beneficial. The words he addressed to Eve were intended nothing more than to open their eyes so that they would not be deceived by the God of the Old Testament, who is none other than the prince of demons, afraid that they would discover his true being, his own divine being (Faust XXII 49; Genes II 26,39; Heresies 46).

That visible presence was rather occasional. Another more lasting one took place in a known historical moment: in the time of Pontius Pilate. But the great difference in the faith in Christ, compared to the Catholic faith, is in the Docetism professed by the Manichaeans. It is a fundamental consequence of his dogmatic faith, with notable derivations in other aspects. Perhaps the most notable is his attitude toward the New Testament. Such Docetism forces them to consider as interpolated any texts that refer to the human aspect of Christ. A concrete consequence of this Docetism is the total disconnection of Jesus from David and, at the same time, from the Old Testament. Jesus is not the Son of David, as we already pointed out85. All texts that include any link must be eliminated as interpolations carried out by the Jews who wanted to corrupt the New Testament precisely with Jewish mystifications (Faust XXII 2). Davidic filiation cannot be maintained either in the figurative sense or in the proper sense. In the first case, because there is no connection between the two Testaments, but rather an unbridgeable break or fissure as an expression of the radical dualism of the beginning. Any effort to link Jesus with David amounts to trying to link light with darkness, good with evil, spirit with matter. It is an attempt doomed to failure in advance. This shows us why it is not possible to maintain the Davidic sonship in the proper sense. Christ could not have flesh taken from anyone, least of all from David. The seal of the mouth. The seal of the mouth regulates the two activities related to it: what should be said or, better yet, what should not be said or eaten. In the first order it prohibits blasphemy (Costum II 11,20), lying (Faust VI 1), perjury and even swearing (Faust XIX 3). In the second, it prohibits eating any kind of meat (Costum II 14,36ff; Heresies 46). The reason that supports the prohibition is provided, logically, by dogmatics; but they opportunely support it with scriptural texts94. In fact, the flesh is nothing more than a mass of sordidness (Costum II 15,37; 16,49; Faust XXXI 4), in that it belongs to the kingdom of darkness and, therefore, defiles those who take it. The flesh of a dead animal is totally impure, since the part of divine substance that it contained within has abandoned it and it no longer has anything that can be purified by the elect (Heresies 46). Along with meat, it is prohibited to drink wine, considered by them as the bile of demons (Costum II 16,44; Heresies 46). Drinking it constitutes sacrilege (Faust XX 13). His only drink is water (Faust XX 23). Fish receive the same treatment: the good Manichean must prefer to die rather than eat them (Faust XVI 9). They should not eat eggs either because when the shell is broken the vital or divine substance escapes. Milk is also avoided, even freshly milked or sucked from a live animal, because it loses the divine part with the violence of the milker (Heresies 46).

Consequently, keeping the seal of the mouth implied a completely vegetarian diet (Costum II 13,29.30; 16,33-44). Unlike meats, plant foods, particularly seeds, had a large amount of divine substance, which they collected when it fell from the heavenly spaces. The rest were allowed to eat them, although this was a concession to the lower grade of listeners; but it was always a sin that could be atoned for by good works. The elect, on the other hand, in addition to not eating meat, were obliged to eat all the food that the listeners brought them, which on some occasions was a cause of scandal due to the consequences that derived from the fact (Costum II 16,52). On the other hand, they practiced frequent fasts to mortify the body and reduce it to servitude (Letter 36,27 and 236,2), particularly on Sundays. The hand seal. If the previous seal and the following one tried to free man from matter, the present one aims to respect the divine substance enclosed in it. The foundation of the seal is the belief that in all reality, particularly in living beings, a particle of the divine substance exists mixed, as we have seen. From this derives the demand not to harm him and to limit any activity to the maximum, since this necessarily entails violating the divine substance. Consequently, it is prohibited to kill not only man, but all living beings, animals and

They believe that plants not only live but even experience sensations and pain when they are damaged, which is why they cannot be uprooted or picked up without causing them great torment. This is the case of the figs spoken of in the Confessions (III 10,18). The consequence is that even he who pulls up weeds from the field commits a crime. As Augustine will tell you, it is preferable to be a usurer than to be a farmer (Commentary on Psalm 140:12). It is aimed at undoing the device that the princes of evil use to keep the light prisoner in the flesh (Faust XIX 26.29; Heresies 46). It prohibits in the most absolute way all carnal commerce (Faust XIX 3; Felix I 7.8) and, consequently, marriage, which is the institutionalization of that reality (Costum I 35,80; Contra Secund 21; Faust XV 7). In effect, each procreation of a new child means creating one more prison in which God will be imprisoned. It is necessary to avoid ergastules for God (Contra Secund 21).. From this it follows that all carnal intercourse, even that which is had with one's own woman, is a sin, a fornication (Felix I 7.8.12). The Manichean does God a great favor if he avoids uniting himself with a woman and thus saves him from having his substance become prisoner and becoming more intensely defiled (Faust VI 3; XV 7; XXII 30). From all of the above it follows that our parents have been our worst enemies (Faust XV 7), which is why we must abandon them and not even return to bury them (Faust V 1). But the ideal of celibacy cannot be supported by everyone. They only demanded it from the chosen ones; the listeners, on the other hand, were allowed or tolerated to marry (Costum I 35,80; Heresies 46), as a concession to their weakness. But, at the same time, they had to limit its negative effects as much as possible, avoiding conception as much as possible (Faust XV 7; XXII 30; Contra Secund 21; Heresies 46). For this purpose, they exhorted them to be attentive to the woman's fertile cycles, so as not to use them during such periods (Costum II 18,65). The Manichean listener marries, not to have children, but to satisfy his concupiscence (Faust XIX 26). And he sins more seriously if he approaches his wife to seek offspring than if he does so to seek only pleasure. Every child is unwanted, although when he arrives he must be loved (Faust XV 7; Conf IV 2,2), because the seal of the hand prevents him from being killed. It is preferable to have carnal union with a prostitute than to have it with one's own woman, since the former personally provides the means to prevent procreation (Faust XXII 80; Contra Secund 21). According to what has been said, the Manichaean is more opposed

The Manichean bishop Faustus considers himself the perfect Christian, among other reasons, because his worship is spiritual, the rational worship that Saint Paul speaks of. He has no material temples, since the faithful Manichean considers himself to be the spiritual temple of God, carrying within himself the living image of the living Majesty, Christ his Son; the altar is none other than one's own mind imbued with good arts and disciplines; The only sacrifices he offers to God and the only honor he pays Him are pure and simple prayers (Faust XX 3.15-18). It is possible to suspect, therefore, that the Eucharist consisted of the reception by the chosen ones of the vegetarian food offered to them by the listeners. In fact, according to Faust, the Manichaeans believe in every tree the same as Catholics believe in only bread and wine, that is, they believe in the presence of Christ in them (Faust XX 2) 105. Penance is much better attested. The invitation to it by the Manichaeans is a fact that appears repeatedly in the Augustinian pages (Almas 22; Fortun 17.20.21; Félix II 8) and is eloquent even with respect to Secundino's Letter to Augustine. It consists of a washing in the divine source, thanks to which the soul can return to the kingdom of God from which it came, free from the stains and vices of both the entire world and the bodies in which they are found (Fortun 21). It takes place in the soul that, after having been "enlightened", becomes attached to matter again, but then repents (Secund 2). The listeners confessed their sins to the elect and the elect to each other according to forms that included the possible transgressions of each category of faithful. The great date for penance was the annual festival of Bern, but not only then. The Tunes used to be the penitential days,0é.

Puech considers that there was no baptism in Manichaeism unless it is understood as the laying on of hands that adds to the sect or introduces it to a higher degree (Le mankháisme... p.87, with abundance of data in note 364). The following text from the Kephalaia may be instructive in this regard: «Der Geist des Kónigs der Archonten des Wassers íst derjenige, der heutzutage herrscht in den Sekten des Irrglaubens, welche taufen in der Wasser-Taufe, in den ihren Hoffnung (und) ihr Vertrauen (gesetzt ist) auf die Wasser-Taufe» (Kephalaia 6, p.33,29-32). O. Widengren, on the other hand, is of the opposite opinion. His are these words: «It is a connection of ideas that is found in both the Manichaeans and the Mandaeans, Gnostics and Christians: the ascent of the soul, the bath of purification and the nuptial entry are organically united between them. Pre-Christian conceptual elements converge in this vision... The fact that this vision is also found in the Manichaean texts indicates with certainty that in Manichaeism there were corresponding baptismal rites, of whose nature, however, the vagueness of the allusions does not allow us to form a precise picture... And since Baur has already convinced us of the possibility that there was a baptism of consecration of the elect, there are two cases: either there has been an erroneous interpretation of the data available or there were two types of baptism, the first at the moment of becoming elected, corresponding to Christian baptism, and the other at the point of death, corresponding to the Christian anointing and comparable from the ritual point of view to a true and proper baptism, but on a reduced scale. And he concludes: "If it is true that before venturing a certain conclusion one must wait for new data, the existing material seems to indicate that the Manichaeans knew a kind of baptism" (II Mankheism... p.120-121). See also P. AtFARic, Vévolution...137-161, and F. DÉCRET, Aspects... p.295. A text from the commentary on Psalm 36 informs us that the Donatists doubted Augustine's Catholic baptism, suggesting that he was a baptized Manichaean. This forces Augustine to defend himself by proclaiming the celebrity of the Church in which he was 103 baptized (Commentary on Psalm 36 III 19). Toribius of Astorga informs us that, according to the acts of Thomas, this apostle baptized not with water, but with oil, and adds: "as the Manichaeans do" (PL 54,694C).

In this regard, do not forget that the Manichaeans, as we have already pointed out (p.45), made use of the Acts of Thomas (Adiman 11,25; Faust XXII 79) and that they considered oil as a good substance (Costum II 16,39). However, see note 364 of H. CH. PUECH in Le mankhéisme... p.181-182.

discoveries of Manichean texts, of which the psalms form a notable part, imbued with authentic piety 107. Augustine does not tell us their frequency either, but from other documents we know that they were daily. They made them oriented towards the sun and the moon: during the day, towards the sun, wherever it was along its route; during the night, towards the moon, if it appeared; Otherwise, they headed north, and, once the sun had risen, towards the east (Heresies 46; Faust XIV 11; Fortun 3, etc.). They did them standing (Heresies 46), although they genuflected in the sun (Costun II 8,13). The only feature that Augustine detected in the Manichean prayer contrary to the Catholic faith was its direction towards the sun. Otherwise, there was nothing new (Fortun 3). The Manichaeans also had their holidays. First of all, they celebrated the day of the Sun, or Sunday (Faust XVIII 5), a day on which they used to gather to pray and when fasting was obligatory (Letter 36,12,27), but the most important festival was that of Berna. As a result of their Christological Docetism, they did not celebrate the feast of the passion, death and resurrection of the Lord, although some did, but not with excessive enthusiasm, as it was stripped of everything that showed the solemnity of the Catholic Easter celebration: vigils, longer fasts and all external festive manifestations. On the other hand, they celebrated with the utmost solemnity the day on which Manes had died, which they called Berne day or tribunal. For this reason, they built a stage as a chair and a tribunal at the same time, with five steps and decorated with beautiful carpets, in a place that was accessible and visible to the worshipers. Manes was the one who had truly suffered, not Christ, whose flesh was only apparent. This was the reason why the death of the former and not the latter was solemnly celebrated. This contrast made the party more pleasant: celebrating one instead of the other, which was also very sweet (Futid 8). In fact, the festival fell in the month of March, around the time of Catholic Easter (Faust XVIII 5) 109. As we already remember, it was also a penitential day.

Augustine adhered to Manichaeism as if driven by a need to the offer presented to him (Util 1,2). And this offer was fundamentally one: the promise of a rational Christian religion, removed from all credulity. That's how, at least, he received it. The other elements that Manichaean propaganda included were - let's say it this way - decorations of that central offer, to make it more striking: both the covering with Christian terminology "3, and the confirmation through moral means, through the supposedly irreproachable conduct of those chosen, without forgetting the previous demolishing action of both the dogmatic and moral positions of the Catholics. It was obvious that Augustine, an intelligent and restless young man, became a Manichean for very specific reasons, not by routine or social accommodation, it was going to take its toll very soon. Once inside and knowing the Manichean myth that he was forced to believe 114, the first thing he sought, in full logic and with absolute coherence, was to avoid falling into what he had rejected in Catholicism: credulity, and, therefore, to ensure that the new faith that he would have embraced became rational in him. that he, an intelligent man like no one, has accepted such a creed. Not even Augustine himself escapes this astonishment, although with a retrospective view (Almas 3; Conf III 6,11). himself or else they would reveal it to him (The Happy Life 1,4). This was his non-assent (ibid.). He believed that all this was like a kind of dressing up of the truth that he was going to know. In fact, despite all the enthusiasm with which he embraced religion, deep down he always had a kind of doubt, expressed with the terms pedetentim et caute with which he designates the way of his adherence to the sect (Almas 11). His proselytism was sincere, not a kind of self-justification " 5. His acceptance was total, although conditional on the fulfillment of the promises of truth, about which he had no doubts. In this sense it must be taken into account that he does not enter as chosen, but as a listener 116, and this must not only be due to not wanting to do without the woman. On the other hand, when in the eighth book of the Confessions he refers to the reading of the Hortensius and the desires for chastity that it awakened In it, he continues to affirm that he had begun to walk along the crooked paths of sacrilegious superstition, although not because he was sure of it, but simply because he preferred it to the others, towards which he behaved not as a pious researcher, but as a hostile persecutor (Conf VIII 7,17). In this sense, Augustine saw the difference between Catholics and Manichaeans in the following way: Catholics offered faith at the beginning and at the end. Manichaeans only at the beginning because, later, after the study and the pertinent clarifications of the doctors of the sect, the faith would cease to exist forever, like a stage that must be left behind, as happens with childhood. A text from the Contra Vaustum (XX 21) tells us about the three channels of information available to it. Referring to the shadows of the deceased, it says: "We never hear in your conversations.

that such shadows existed, we never read it in your writings; Furthermore, you tend to refute those who defend such opinions. Here are the three channels: the internal catechesis of the sect, personal reading, contact with those who defend other opinions, which are then refuted in the internal circles. Each of these three channels had its part in the development of Augustine's later attitude towards Manichaeism. Augustine dedicated himself with enthusiasm to the task of overcoming that stage of believing Manichean to move on to that of understanding Manichean. As we have already seen, he attends the internal catechesis with diligence and attention, honoring his status as a “listener.” But in that catechesis he did not find what he was looking for. The result was not understanding, but faith. In his desire to understand, he becomes a young questioner. The problem resulted from their teachers not being competent enough to answer their questions and solve their problems. They had no other recourse than to invite him to be patient while waiting for the arrival of Fausto, who, as the ultimate doctor, would solve everything for him. The Augustinian pages have transmitted to us some of those questions that he asked. Let's see them. In the work The Customs of the Church he states that when he listened to them attentively he was oppressed with great anguish as he asked himself, without finding an answer, what the race of darkness could have done to God, if he had not wanted to engage in combat. For if it could do nothing to harm him in his rest, there was reason to complain that he had acted so cruelly towards us, by putting us in such calamities. It is the famous argument of Nebridius (Conf VII 2,3). Someone then answered him that God did not want to avoid evil or prevent it from happening to him, but rather, moved by his natural goodness, he had wanted to put that kingdom of darkness in order. The solution, however, created more problems than it solved (Cos tum II 12,25). Linked to the previous one is the following question: "If the substance of evil could not harm God, why did he send a part of himself against it?" He confesses to the priest Fortunato that he never found an answer to this question during the time in which he listened to them and that from there God took the lead to admonish him to abandon his error and return to the Catholic faith (Fortun 37). Logically, when it came to putting the hand seal into practice, it was another reason for confusion (Costum II 17,64). Furthermore, as a keen observer, it was not lost on him that they were much more skillful in refuting others (particularly Catholics) than in maintaining their own assertions. According to him, this was one of the reasons why he did not completely surrender to them, remaining in the category of listeners, and why he did not renounce worldly hopes and categories (Util 1,2.3). One of the weapons that the Manichaeans had to oppose the reasons of the Catholics was the theory of interpolations. Well, during the time of his Manichean militancy it always seemed unfounded to him. And not only to him, but also to the group that moved around him, since they strove to be more critical than the majority. To maintain such a position the Manichaeans should have presented other authentic copies, something they never did (Util 3,7). Augustine's doubts found no solution; On the contrary, they increased over time. The rational explanation that he wanted and that he had deduced from the sect's propaganda was not forthcoming. The Manichean doctors were incapable of offering it to them. He was promised the arrival of Faust, but no date was given. There can be no doubt that Augustine maintained the hope of finding in him the desired answers. But the delay worked against the Manichaeans themselves. To the difficulties that Augustine faced from the simple internal exposition of the doctrine, were added those created by his own readings. He had given himself to them out of scientific desire and also seeking an explanation of what the Manichaeans promised him. Perhaps with some surprise he discovered that scientific and philosophical books offered him another vision of reality that was more rational than theirs. What these books offered him was more understandable and acceptable than what they presented. The theories of the philosophers had more overtones of probability; The scientists' approaches, especially regarding astronomy, were completely transparent and open to anyone who wanted to study them. Little by little he establishes the comparison, which is negative for Manichaeism (Conf V 3,6). But Agustín does not abandon him, nor does the hope that his doubts will find a solution after the meeting with Faust. The greater number of difficulties present will lead to a fuller understanding. He continues to believe the words of the Manichaeans.
They are honest and honest people, he thinks, and they cannot

deceive him; just be patient. But the doubts continued to increase. Doubts that arise not only from an insufficient explanation within the sect, nor from the readings themselves. An important role is played by the street. Agustín is an ardent proselytizer and is present where there is something to say or something to hear to refute him. In those street meetings he hears everything. In polemics with Catholics he sees how they too, at least some, know how to defend their positions; how his reasons are of a certain weight, although fanaticism or the blindness of the moment does not allow him to grasp them in all their force. But such reasons remain inside, ready to emerge and revive at the opportune moment (Conf V 11,21). But what undermines the young Manichean's faith the most is seeing the weak response of the sect's doctors. On the one hand, they do not give it to the public, to the enemy, undoubtedly to avoid being refuted. On the other hand, the answers lack consistency, in that they are based on assumptions that are not demonstrated. Let's take a specific case. For example, a Catholic denied that evil was a substance. The "listeners", impressed, turned to one of the leaders of the sect to whom they were united by friendship and assiduous dealings. He answers them: «I wish I could place a scorpion in that man's hand and see if he would remove it or not; If he did, that very fact, not my words, would convince him that evil is a substance. And Augustine notes: «But he did not say this in the presence of the Catholic, but in our presence...; He responded in a childish way to children” (Costum II 8,11). From the street he also received information about the morality of the chosen ones, particularly with regard to the seal on the belly. He was not only scandalized by their behavior, but also and even more so by the behavior of the authorities of the sect who found easy excuses not to act against them (Costum II 19,67ff). It can be said that until the arrival of Faustus, Augustine's problems and doubts were numerous, objectively weighty, but not overwhelming his spirit. This statement, which seems to contradict others by Augustine (Conf V 6,10), is based on the fact that he hoped that a solution would be obtained. The effect of hunger is different on those who are certain of being able to quench it, even if they have to wait for something, than on those who lack all hope. It is true that Augustine

He spent many years waiting for Faust n 7. But we must assume that the reasons for waiting were not always the same and that they changed over time. It is fair to think that at the beginning, in full fervor and enthusiasm, it was more of a desire to meet a famous person in the sect; Then he began to wait for him as the only one who could bring light to his mind, and rekindle his desire to progress within the same sect. Faust's arrival was received, for the moment, with joy by Augustine; so we must assume it. But very soon he must have felt disappointed. Agustín had dreamed of having a personal meeting with him, in which they could discuss the problems face to face. In other words, Augustine did not intend to place himself before the Manichean doctor and bishop as a docile student who accepts everything based on the principle of authority, but rather in a situation of parity, so that only the weight of reasons would have value, as was consistent with Manichean logic, or at least with its propaganda. That dream faded immediately, because at first he could only see and hear it in general meetings with groups of the sect's faithful. Presumably, Augustine's insistence and his own personal courage, which the Manichaeans were not willing to do without,118 obtained the desired interview, which was then multiplied. But, when it arrived, Agustín's enthusiasm had already suffered another disappointment. The disappointment had already arisen from the first contact, although not direct, with him. The effects of the meeting with Fausto were various. Augustine tells us that, after learning of his ignorance, he began to lose hope (Conf V 7,12), that is, he began to get used to the idea that no one could solve his doubts. If the oracle of the sect had disappointed him, he could expect nothing from the other doctors of the sect, to whom he had previously resorted and in vain (Conf V 7,13). The immediate consequences were twofold: intellectual and moral. In the intellectual order, the enthusiasm for Manes' writings cracked, and in the moral order, the same thing happened with the effort he had made to progress in the sect; everything fell apart. It did not effectively mean the complete separation of Manichaeism, but its permanence in it was conditioned on the discovery or not of something better (Conf V 7,13). Agustín begins to live in a provisional regime. In the eyes of the sect, he is still a listener, but in his intelligence and in his heart Augustine is no longer a Manichean 121. Shortly afterwards he leaves Carthage. The reasons that others attributed to him are different from those he gives. The Donatist Petiliano accuses him of having fled in the face of the intensifying anti-Manichean persecution,22; He affirms that he changed the headquarters of his teaching, from Carthage to Rome, fundamentally in search of more serious and responsible students (Conf V 8,14). There are no reasons not to give him credit, but perhaps others should be added, in addition to those he suggests of earning more and aspiring to greater honors: disconnected, at least to a certain extent, from Manichaeism, he could not continue with his same tenor of life within the sect or alongside his usual companions. The proselytism, to which he had devoted himself with ardour, gave way and it was going to be difficult for him to live in its scenario,23. In fact, although in Rome he is still in relationship and contact with the Manichaeans, linked to them more for reasons of friendship than of any other order, and staying in their house, his proselytizing activity takes the opposite bias: he suggests to those who host him not to be too fond of the young professor of rhetoric, P. Brown (Augustine p.45) considers that under the guidance of Augustine he will apply himself to the more serious study of the classics, given that such a study would have meant for him the passport to enter among the people. cultured and influential people who could support their cause.
