credulous (Conf V 10,19). His state of mind is well reflected in this text addressed to his friend and former companion in faith, Honorato: «When I separated from you and crossed the sea, I was in indecision and doubt about what were the things I should retain or abandon; This indecision increased day by day since I heard the man who was promised to us as sent from heaven and that as such we were waiting for him to clarify those questions that had us full of confusion, and I saw that he was like the others, except for a certain level of eloquence that he possessed. When I was already in Italy, I reflected and thought not about whether I would continue in that sect, into which I already regretted having fallen, but about what would be the method to find the truth, whose love you know better than anyone how much it made me sigh" (Util 8,20). However, Augustine continued to be linked to Manichean positions, especially those that acted as a sedative on his conscience. He still continued to believe that it was not he who sinned, but another evil nature that acted within him (Conf V 10,18). For him it was a comfortable belief and, therefore, one of the last to detach from his being. Augustine's situation of losing hope of making progress in doctrine and in the sect shows us what the previous situation had been: a longing, moved by hope, to progress, to fully achieve what he had perceived as the Manichean promise: a rational Christian religion. Evidently it would be limiting the scope of words too much to reduce this progress only to the moral field. Augustine speaks of progress in doctrine (Conf V 8,10). The retreat begins; Not only has it lost hope of progress, but positions previously achieved are also beginning to slip from its grasp. They were retained by remissius et neglegentius (Conf V 10,18). It was reasons of friendship on the one hand and a greater hopelessness of finding the truth outside of Manichaeism that kept him linked to it (Conf V 10,19). If it had fallen into it as if by necessity when all other exits had been cut off (Useful 1,2), for that same reason it continues without establishing the definitive break. The difference is only in Augustine's spirit: he entered joyfully and hopeful and now he finds himself disappointed and without hope; but just like before, without paths that allow him to change course.
Augustine soon saw, as we already said, that the Manichaeans were more skilled in destroying the positions of others than in building their own on a solid basis, and he experienced this in

own person. He was able to get rid of the setup they provided relatively quickly, but he was not able to overlook the wall they had built in front of the alleged ruins of the Catholic Church. Manichean criticism had reduced everything to ruins, and Augustine felt unable to even come close to seeing whether those ruins really existed or were invented.

The Manichean Secundino asks Augustine, as if surprised, who it was that changed him so suddenly (Secund 3). He considers Augustine's abandonment of the sect as the abandonment of the high ideals that had always distinguished him. At the same time, he reminds him that his conversion to Catholicism was dictated by fear 124 or the ambition to achieve greater honor within the Catholic Church (Secund 2.5; Contra Secund 1). Augustine answers him by acknowledging that, certainly, his abandonment of Manichaeism was the result of a fear, but not the one Secundino suspects, but rather the fear of the words of the apostle Paul to Timothy (1 Tim 4:1-4), which clearly point to the Manichaeans. He also recognizes that, at the moment of abandonment, he burned with a desire for honors, but not just any honor, but the one mentioned by the Apostle in Rom 2:10 (Contra Secund 2). However, it does not support the first statement, namely, that the change had been sudden. Perhaps he did not need to do so because the answer had already been given in the Confessions, a work written previously and which Secundino shows signs of knowing,25. The Confessions clearly indicate how Augustine's conversion to Catholicism began the same day he became a Manichean, in the sense that he accepted this faith by searching for what he could only find precisely in Catholicism, and which he could not see, blinded by the Manichean propaganda to which he did not know how to resist or, better yet, he lacked the means or criteria to judge it. Augustine became a Manichean, we have said, because they knew how, with perfect skill, to destroy the building in which he was housed and promised him another that exactly responded to the young man's desires. We saw previously how, despite all his personal dedication, full acceptance was conditional on the acquisition of that promised abode, and equally how, little by little, all hopes of seeing that promise become a reality fell. But, since the skill of the Manichaeans had consisted precisely in closing the other roads, even when hope was lost, he had nowhere to turn. Once converted, he asks his friend Honorato, whom he is trying to attract to the Catholic faith, what prevented him from seeking the Catholic faith, and he answers that it was not any law, nor the strength of the adversaries, or the persona vilis sacratorum, the bad reputation, the novelty of the institution or having to live in secret (Util 7,18). The return to the ancient faith had to go through the recovery of what had been kidnapped by Manichean propaganda. That would correspond again to the acceptance of the Catholic faith. In effect, one thing is the abandonment of the Manichaean faith and another is the acceptance of the Catholic one, although both are related127. The fact that Augustine completely separated himself from Manichaeism had his part in having felt deceived by the Manichaeans on the other point. Before they had deceived him by promising him what they could not give him; Now he feels deceived by having been presented with a ghost of the Catholic Church, not what it really was. He had been presented with a Catholic Church defending points of view that he now discovers do not belong to him. He discovers that he has been fighting ghosts (Conf V 10,20; VI 3,4). This discovery did not automatically lead him to the Catholic faith, which he began to consider as a valid reality; but it did serve to separate him from Manichaeism completely. The major reason that prompted Augustine to decide to break with Manichaeism is not of a religious order, but of a rational and scientific order (V 14,25). To return to the Catholic faith, he needed, above all, to overcome the consequences of the Manichaeism that had nourished his spirit for years. Dropouts had to be frequent. Secundino talks about

a personal crisis: he also perished (Secund 5). Faust thanks his teacher because he did not allow him to abandon his faith (Faust XIX 5). So much so, that they already had a kind of catechesis on abandonment to prevent it from infecting others or plunging them into a deep crisis. In such cases they used to say: lumen per ipsum transitum fecit (Useful 1,3), that is, it was something temporary, not permanent. Abandonment was translated as a being abandoned by the light 128. It is needless to remember the role that Saint Ambrose played in the definitive abandonment of Manichaeism by Augustine. His work was not to dismantle the Manichean system, but to rebuild in the eyes of Augustine the Catholicism that he saw collapsed. It is true that the Augustine who heard him was an already deflated Augustine, far removed from the fanaticism and blindness of other times. Perhaps this is why he let the contents pass next to the words, without intending it positively. Specifically, its main work is on two points that represent two achievements for Augustine: the existence and value of a spiritual exegesis, the key to interpreting Scripture {Conf V 14,24) and the exposition from the authentic Catholic point of view of the biblical affirmation that man was made in the image and likeness of God (Conf VI 3,4). The positions that had previously seemed unsustainable, little by little, were presented to him as defensible; then as comparable to the Manichean positions and finally as winners. Manichaeism had been defeated.

Before entering, specifically, into Augustinian criticism, both at a general level and at a particular level, it will be useful to dwell on some previous aspects such as the starting point, the motivations, the underlying attitude, and the recipients. Augustine bases his criticism on his own knowledge of the doctrine of the sect. We have already presented what Agustín knew about it based on his own writings that transmit fundamentally faithful information, if nuances from the controversy are left aside. This knowledge will give you personal security in criticism and guarantees for the reader. The saint presents himself as a doctor who is all too familiar with the ills of those who once were his coreligionists (Costum I 1,2). By virtue of this knowledge he has of them he also knows what they can understand and what they cannot (Costum I 17,30). Augustine makes great efforts to make clear the motivations for his actions and the attitude in which he places himself towards the Manichaeans themselves. We find a wonderful declaration of principles at the beginning of his refutation of the Letter called "of the Foundation": "I have begged and continue to beg the only true and almighty God, from whom, by whom and in whom all things exist, that in refuting and refuting your heresy, to which you adhered more out of imprudence than out of malice, grant me a pacified and serene mind, which thinks more about correcting you than about knock you down. For God, although he uses his servants to destroy the kingdom of error, as regards men as men, commands that they be corrected, not that they be led to perdition" (Fund 1). It is up to him to choose and desire the best to have access to his correction, not with a desire for rivalry, emulation or persecution, but consoling, exhorting and disputing with meekness, benevolence and softness; to God to grant what is good to those who want it and ask for it (ibid.). Excellent statements, but only in principle, because the writings seem to be from someone else based on different budgets or motivations, where meekness, benevolence and softness do not always have a place. We must not forget, neither in one case nor in the other, neither in the solemn prologues, nor in the subsequent development, the part that corresponds to rhetorical training, undeniable in Augustine. She perfectly explains the visible opposition between declared principles and concrete implementation.
They must be read, therefore, from the literary genre in which all controversy moved. Without this calling into question the pastoral zeal of the bishop.

Augustine starts, on the one hand, from the fact that the Manichaeans, although they are deceivers, have themselves been deceived before (Fund 2; Conf IV 1,1). It also starts from the fact that they are not capable of understanding certain realities, since in order to judge divine things, which are much higher than what they think, they have a totally gross and morbid mind due to the pestiferous food of corporeal simulacra (Costum I 17,30). A frequent accusation in this regard and which constitutes a fundamental criticism, is that of being carnal, which prevents them from understanding the spiritual (Costum II 26,40) 133. "It is foolish to discuss this with you: if you are not yet capable of understanding God as incorporeal, what can you understand that is incorporeal?" (Against Second 20). They are trapped in the bonds of the flesh and are unable to overcome their prejudices (True Religion 9:16). The truth cannot be hidden from those who love it, but they must seek it properly. If you do not desire it with all the strength of your soul, there will be no possibility of finding it (Costum I 17,31). Although he knows that there are those who are incapable of understanding, he also knows that there are others who do not succeed, not because they lack ingenuity, but because of the ill will that will make them lose that same ingenuity (Costum II 2,2). It is the perdition of the soul, which, wanting to overcome man, is defeated by its own error (Adiman 28,2). On the other hand, to avoid hurting them with his judgments, he stands before them and applies them to himself. One example is enough. The text of Mt 7:16 refers to the Manichaeans: Do not throw what is holy to the dogs; but then he continues: «Do not feel offended. I too was a dog and barked when, instead of the bread of doctrine, I was rightly given lashes of rejection" (Costum I 18,33). Although with a bit of irony, so frequent in anti-Manichean writings, he tells them that he does not appear before them as a teacher, with which attitude they would perhaps consider him arrogant, but rather as a student, to learn what he could not in nine years (Fund 10). On the other hand, he writes that only someone who has not experienced that being free from error is due to divine mercy can have an insulting attitude toward past errors (Fund 27). From these assumptions arises the famous and beautiful text at the beginning of the refutation of the Letter called "of the Foundation" (2-3). The good rhetor, who is also an excellent shepherd, does not lack sweetness in his words. What it aims to do is heal them more than

attack them. That is why he affirms that he plans to maintain restraint in his criticism and, in this way, place himself above those who so fiercely attacked what they did not know. He recognizes that it will be difficult for him, which is why he notes: "If I am capable" (Costum I 1,2). The aim pursued is none other than to make them see that the Christian faith that leads to the summit of wisdom and truth, in whose joy happiness consists, is not in the Manichaeans, but in Catholic discipline (Costum I 18,33). He only asks them to listen to the Catholic doctors with the same peace and the same longing with which he listened to them during the nine years that they had him as a toy in their hands (Costum I 18,34). In another text Augustine goes even further. It offers both parties to place themselves in a fictitiously neutral situation; That is to say, that no one starts from being in possession of the truth, and goes in search of it, as if it were unknown to both contending parties. Such will be the condition to seek it in harmony and with care. And if they are not willing to grant him this, he asks them to allow him to hear them as strangers and, as such, discuss with them. The only condition would be that he did not have to pray with them, nor take the name of Manichaean until they had given him a clear reason, free of all obscurity, for things related to the salvation of the soul (Fund 3). Particularly with respect to Scripture, he proposes that they put aside personal points of view and turn to experts who can elucidate the issues in one direction or another (Almas 9). It is clear that these are nothing more than concessions of the rhetor who seeks to capture the reader's benevolence; at most methodological and formal concessions, because Augustine would never renounce the acquired positions from which he writes or speaks, as he also knew that they would not be accepted by the Manichaeans themselves whom he allows to understand that he directs the writing, although his words are directed, in his intention, to Catholics preferably, to avoid them falling into error, rather than to the convinced Manichaeans, against whom he knew he could do little,34. If it is true that he reminds them that he writes with sincerity of which God is a witness, without any desire to argue, he also does not remain silent that he does so without doubting the slightest about the truth, although this does not prevent further study (Genes II 29,43). To systematize the criticism that Augustine makes of Manichaeism we are going to establish two sections, one of general criticism and another of particular or specific criticism of each of the specific elements of the system. The external criteria that Augustine uses most are two: their small number and the fact that they are recent, their novelty. Augustine resorts to the fact of their small number repeatedly (Costum I 34,75; II 20,75; Útil 14,31; Faust XIII 5; XX 23; Contra Secund 26). In Secundino's reply, Augustine invites him not to be deceived by their numerical simplicity to affirm that they are the authentic Christians, taking refuge in the Gospel text that there are few who follow the narrow path (Mt 7:14). The fact that Augustine comes out in front of this argument seems to indicate that it was common in the sect, which would show the real numerical scarcity. Augustine speaks of the species paucitatis, that is, of the only apparent value of the criterion that is based on the small number of followers, because although it is true that there are very few who do not harm anyone, among those who harm, there are fewer criminals than thieves and fewer incestuous people than adulterers. In other words, the lower number is related to the seriousness of the crime. Hence Augustine's warning: "Be careful lest what causes your poverty is nothing other than the excessive horror caused by your impiety" (Contra Secund 26). In his reply to Faustus, Augustine resorts again to numerical smallness, but in a moral context: to the Manichaeans who are usually skilled in showing the scourges of others (of the Catholics), he argues that the same thing occurs among Read about this the beginning of the work Commentary on Genesis in reply to the Manichaeans.

Augustine's critical work focuses, in a further step, on the Manichaeans as critics of the Catholics. In this counter-criticism the Bishop of Hippo highlights several aspects, the first of which is their ignorance: they harshly attack what they do not know (Costum I 1,2). The name that best fits their attitude is boldness, daring to accuse what they do not know (Genes II 13,19). Catholics believe what is in Scripture, not what the Manichaeans imagine (Faust XXVI 3). In effect, they have been victims of their own suspicions (Faust XXII 21). Consequently, the defense is easy: it is enough to deny—as corresponds to reality—that Catholics understand things as the Manichaeans believe they understand them (Util 5,12). That is to say, sometimes the accusation has weight in itself, but not in the subject to whom it is accused. It is not unusual for Augustine to defend himself with a simple "That is not what we think" (Adiman 12,5). He is very careful to distinguish the truth professed by the Church from the opinions of certain members of it; That is why he will be able to state categorically: «Your criticism does not affect us, but rather certain senile or even childish opinions; criticism is all the more inept the more it is accompanied by oratory apparatus. Consequently, whoever converts to Manichaeism does not condemn the discipline of the Catholic Church, but rather shows ignorance of it" (Costum I 10,16.17). This distinction must also be established on a moral level; but the Manichaeans forget it in order to base their attacks, something that would be impossible for them otherwise. Augustine's reply could not be more than one: "Cease cursing the Church for the bad habits of some, since she also condemns them and strives to correct them" (Costum I 34,76). Particular subjects do not always represent the full truth found in the Church. On the other hand, ignorance leads them to not believe that there could be someone who takes the gospel, reads it "with knowledge" and discovers in the meadows, where the Lord feeds his flock, the man who hides snares for the unwary and less cautious (Adiman 15,2). It is the reproach he addresses to Adeimantus. Their attitude is based on a false assumption: that there are no learned Catholics who can discover their fallacies. In addition to the negative and devastating aspect, Manichean propaganda also had the positive, the offer of one's own principles.

The offers are valid and the terms that contain them are irreproachable, but we must not lose sight of the fact that such words can come from the mouths of both real doctors and scammers (ibid.). Double reproach, then: either that under a beautiful presentation they hide something unpresentable; or that it is something really positive and valuable, but offered by a scammer. The criticism of the Manichean system, as such, will occupy most of the Augustinian pages. Such criticism does not respond to a global plan, but has been dictated by circumstances, as well as the method used or the goals sought. To carry it out he uses two types of documents: the writings of Manes and the Manichaeans on the one hand and the Holy Scripture on the other. Occasionally he introduces quotes from the Treasury or the so-called "Letter of the Foundation" into his writings or discussions to criticize or ridicule them. He systematically refuted this last work, although not in its entirety, analyzing not only what it textually says, but also the consequences of its contents. Augustine uses a literal interpretation, the same one that Adeimantus and Faustus had applied to the Old Testament and against which Augustine never ceases to protest. The same writings of these two Manichaean doctors give rise to a fine and accurate criticism of the system. Perhaps it is in the little work in which he answers the letter of the Manichean Secundino where Augustine is more clearly aware that the other has allowed himself to be taken in his hands: «I am not going to provide more documents showing Manes' error than those that your letter offers me...; In it I see no other way out for your naivety, but to regret having put yourself in the letter in a quagmire from which you cannot get out. Even more: "Lament that Manes ever existed, for the very truthful frontispiece of your letter, like a battering ram, has struck down all your deceitful machinations" (Contra Secund 3). Augustine's security is based precisely on the fact that he can establish his anti-Manichean positions not only in scriptural documents, but also in data taken from the writings of Manes themselves (Felix II 3.5), even trying to show their contradiction.

He was merely trying to repeat the same attitude that the Manichaeans adopted towards the Old Testament, trying to prove that it was opposed to the New and, therefore, could not be true (Faust XXVIII 5).

Although the recourse to internal contradiction in the Manichean writings is comparatively rare, the recourse to Scripture is constant, which is the fundamental criterion of authority, which we will discuss below. It is enough to anticipate that he does not hold his fingers, and to do so he resorts to those testimonies that they must necessarily believe, that is, to the Gospel and Paul (Faust XXIII 5). At the same time he tries to focus the target or recipient of his arguments, since there are documents that may not be valid for pagans or Jews, but may be valid for Manichaeans, who pride themselves on being Christians (Faust XVI 14). In some text he resorts to the authority of Cicero, but he is quick to excuse himself by stating that he does so because in the specific case what is being discussed is not content, but words; In fact, the fundamental difference between Scripture and profane authors is precisely in that: the former is interested above all in the contents, the latter almost only in the words (Adiman 11). Augustine bases his formulations on reason and authority, looking interchangeably at the double addressee to which we referred. In The Customs of the Catholic Church he asks where he should begin, whether with reason or authority. And the answer is: The natural order requires that authority precede reason... But since he has to deal with people who feel, speak and act everything against that order, stating that first of all one must begin by providing reasons, he will continue such a way of acting, despite considering it vicious (Costum I 2,3). It matters little to him whether his interlocutor prefers to rely on authority or reason, because both sources provide him with sufficient arguments. If you rely on authority, here is this; If in reason, here is something else, he will say in his reply to Faust (Faust XXXIII 9). He will resort to one or the other, as circumstances require (Fortun 19). However, when there is evidence of reason, he will resort to them before any others (Faust XXII 23.26). "Thus reason teaches" is a way of arguing by Augustine (Costum II 11,20). To his friend Honorato he indicates with these words the approach of the little work he dedicates to him: "Leaving aside the trifles of common places, combata res cum re, causa cum causa, ratio cum ratione" (Util 1,3). But there are other occasions when reasons cannot be given because the listeners are not capable of understanding them. In such cases, recourse to authority is necessary.
Its precise expression is that we must urge them with authority

It is the recourse to the most faithful truth of the apostolic doctrine (Faust I I I 3). This was necessary not only thinking about the Manichaeans, but especially about the Catholics. Along with the tests of reason and authority, Augustine frequently resorts to common sense. Thus, he says, embracing the Christian faith, abandoning Manichean fables, is not a matter of being wise, but of having just a little common sense. "If they had, not only the Christian faith to believe the Apostle, but a minimum of human sense to see the obvious, each of them would see and consider in themselves how true, how true, how great things there are in the small and how many good things there are in the smallest" (Faust XXI 8). He will remind Fausto that great wit is not required to understand what he is going to say. In fact he appeals to everyone, wise and ignorant, to hear him, pay attention and judge (Faust XXII 22; Almas 12.22). Secundino will remind the listener that it is enough to read as one should (Contra Secund 10). At a formal level, Augustine responds with implacable logic to the same logic that Faust used. You can read about it Against Faustum XXII 26. Other times he will use the same language of the Manichaeans in his anti-Catholic campaign: "Do not terrify me with the name of the Paraclete, for I have not come to believe unknown things, but to know certain things" (Fund 13). There is no lack of mockery as when he exposes the theory of beings existing before the mixture of good and evil and the speeches given there; comments: «Wonderful and fully divine eloquence; and they had not heard any grammarian or rhetor, nor had they learned such things among the tears caused by the rods and rules" (Faust XXI 10). In his response, Augustine will sometimes be long, other times short, depending on the case. Sometimes it becomes long-winded on one point and then brief on the rest, given that the argument is fundamentally identical (Faust VI 9). In any case, he always responds to everything, whether in the Manichaean criticism of Catholic positions, or in regards to the offer itself.

Just as Faust did not limit himself to accusing the patriarchs in a generic way, but went down to details, in the same way Augustine proposed to give a punctual and precise response to all the statements of the Manichaean bishop (Faust XII 48). That desire for

Augustinian criticism also goes through the personal conditions of his opponents, both referring to the intellectual and moral aspects. On the one hand, they do not know how to maintain the logical order of the steps to be taken. Their intellectual activity is also tainted by the carnal sense they use to judge all things: what offends Faust is the supreme criterion, without stopping at other considerations (Faust XXXII 20). Augustine usually contrasts the Catholic faith with Manichean "perfidy" or "opinion" (Contra Secund 10; Felix II 21). In The Usefulness of Faith Augustine presents three levels of knowledge that are expressed by the verbs intellegere, credere and opinari. About them he states the following: the first always exists without any vice, the second is sometimes found with vice and the third never exists without vice. Indeed, understanding (intellegere) the great good and divine things brings happiness; Knowing superfluous things does not harm anything, although it can be harmful to spend time learning them that more necessary things require... Belief is guilty when one believes something unworthy of God or when one believes too easily something from a man; That is, the vice can be either in the object of faith or in the believing subject; In this last case, there is credulity rather than faith. The problem of faith, therefore, is closely related, to the point of being identified, with that of authority, insofar as man must resort to some authority to reach the truth. To embrace faith is to embrace an authority. The problem of the legality—according to the rational nature of man—of recourse to it is intertwined with its function in the human cognitive process, particularly in the religious field. In the human cognitive process there is a natural order. And this order precisely asks, according to Augustine, that authority precede reason (Costum I 2,3). Human life in its daily manifestations is based on faith (Conf VI 5,7). The goal to be reached is the direct perception of the truth; but first it is necessary to travel the path of submission to an authority. The fact that faith precedes reason, when the subject is not yet capable of understanding with reason, and cultivating the soul through faith to receive the seeds of truth, is not only extremely healthy, but so necessary that without it the sick soul cannot recover health (Util 14,31). Such is the function of faith: to heal the soul so that reason can understand. Consequently, there is nothing in the Church more healthy than the fact that faith precedes reason (Costum I 25,47). That is why Catholic discipline teaches that the Christian mind must first be nourished with simple faith, in order to enable it to grasp superior and eternal realities. This is what the prophet affirms: If you do not believe, you will not understand (Is 7:9), a text to which the saint frequently resorts (Faust XII 46; Nature 24). He describes as sacrilegious and reckless the Manichean attitude of criticizing those who, before they can see the truth that is perceived with a pure mind, protect themselves in advance through faith and prepare themselves for God to enlighten them (Util 1,2). Faith is the milk that, taken within the Church, strengthens the child and enables it to take solid food (Fund 23; Faust XII 46). The foot credere leads to a sapienter intellegere (Contra Secund 23). The consequence is that it is lawful to follow those who command belief (Util 10:24; 11:25). It must be clear, however, that accepting faith does not mean that reason is condemned, nor that reason is no longer used to discern what is true from what is false (Faust XVIII 7).

The Manichaeans required to believe that faith be preceded by an apertissima et indubitata ratio (Util 14,32). They are answered in the first place that this would no longer be faith, if it refers to its object. But this does not mean that faith has to be reckless or that it is reduced to credulity, to "opinion" 152. Augustine's position remains halfway between the theoretical demands of Faust (Faust XVI 8), which are excessive, and the demands that he attributes to them on a practical level, which are otherwise. Both the Manichaean and the Catholic ask for faith in Jesus, although Jesus is different in each case. What can move a pagan, that is, a neutral subject, to prefer one Christ to another, the Manichean to the Catholic or vice versa? That is, what could move you to accept one religion over another? The Manichean cannot offer more than the word of Manes; The Catholic will be able to offer, if only as a historical document, the antiquity of the Scriptures that announce him and show his arrival, the power of his miracles, the sanctity of customs and the truth of reason, all realities of which the point of view of the Manichaeans is deprived (Faust XIII 3). In a text, beautiful for the capacity for synthesis it denotes and for its strength of expression, it establishes the chain of steps that has led the Christian religion, that is, Catholic, to that robustness: «He (Christ) by providing the medicine that was going to heal the extremely corrupt customs, with his miracles he gained authority; With his antiquity he deserved faith; with faith he gathered a multitude; With the multitude he obtained antiquity and with antiquity he strengthened religion. Thanks to that robustness, neither the inept novelty of the heretics acting with deception, nor the cave-dwelling error of the Gentiles who violently opposed it, has been able to uproot it” (Util 14,32). The Catholic religion, in opposition to Manichaeism, has with it antiquities and multitude. The value of this multitude, as a founding authority, we will see when talking about Scripture.

Although both parties recognize divine origin and inspiration, they cannot present any endorsement perceptible by human eyes, that is, external, that confirms this recognition. The term must be deprived of all legal content to transfer it to the field of sociology 155. Today we could translate it by acceptance, prestige, normative capacity over men, but from their freedom. Authority in this context has nothing to do with taxing power; rather, it places itself at the opposite extreme 156, without wanting to deny with what has been stated the normative and binding nature of Scripture for those who have already accepted it. Here we are at a previous stage: in the situation of someone who has several options and has to choose one; That choice is not imposed on you by anyone, but is the result of personal discernment of the values ​​of both parties. It is not power, it is prestige; or, if you want, it is power, but power that does not come from the law, but from the values ​​inherent to the subject who bears that auctoritas. Once the correct reading is established, as far as possible, it remains that all Scripture is true and that only Scripture is true in its entirety; that only from it can one argue with courage and clarity. It is the procedure of Augustine: "I have proven it through the holy, ecclesiastical and canonical Scriptures" (Felix I 12). "Outside of the ecclesiastical, canonical and Catholic Scriptures, none other has any weight of authority" (Faust XXIII 9). This means that the same credibility must be given to one text as to another, as long as it is contained in them (Faust VII 2); that is, Scripture must be believed in its entirety (Faust XV 13). This is what Catholics believe; the Manichaeans only pretend to believe it (Faust XXVI 3). Its interpretation Having now recognized the authentic Scripture, recognized its truth and authority, the next step is to know how it is to be interpreted. But before even exposing the norms and criteria on the basis of which this interpretation must be guided, it is necessary to stop at another fundamental aspect, at least because of the frequency with which the Bishop of Hippo refers to it and because of the importance that he assigns to it: the disposition with which the reader or commentator must approach the biblical text. While clarifying why the Manichaeans have erred so manifestly, it indicates what attitude will avoid error. The Manichaeans have clearly erred because they have lacked the necessary conditions to approach Scripture. Referring to Faustus who had claimed to have found nothing in the Old Testament that was a proclamation of Christ, Augustine stated that he did not feel any surprise, since although he had eyes to read, he lacked the "heart" to understand; placed before the door of the divine mystery, instead of knocking with the confidence of piety, he began to insult with the pride of impiety (Faust XII 30). What Augustine above all reproaches the Manichaeans is that, from the outset, they placed themselves in a critical attitude towards Scripture. Instead of approaching with the spirit typical of one who seeks, they do so with a spirit of animosity against her (Faust III 2.3; Util 3.9; Genes II 2.3; I 15.24). With accurate expression: "the Manichaeans, whom we suffer as judges of divine Scripture" (Faust XXII 12). queer. It is what he reminds the Manichaeans that they should have done and reproaches them for not having done it (Adiman 3,4; Faust III 4). There are many pages of the Augustinian anti-Manichean polemic dedicated to exposing the criteria for interpreting Scripture. For reasons that are easy to understand, in most cases it refers to the Old Testament. The Manichaeans denied its authority, its divine origin and objected to its contents. A proper interpretation will remove any basis for such criticism. Augustine starts from a dispensatio, a plan, of the Holy Spirit in relation to Scripture. Its reading must tend precisely to capture that dispensatio (Adiman 15,3) to whose fulfillment everything tends (Adiman 17,6), enclosed in both words and events (Contra Secund 26). In other words, Scripture contains great mysteries; Its discovery will dictate the feeling regarding the vanity of the heretics: either of pain because they are men, or of ridicule because they are arrogant (Genes I 3,5). The correct understanding of Scripture requires starting from the existence of figures. The Manichean who, accepting the New Testament, denies it for the Old, has his neck crushed by the authority of the Apostle who explicitly states it in 1 Cor 10:11: Everything happened to them in figure (Faust XII 37). The darker the texts that heretics reproach seem, the more wonderful treasures they hide if they are carefully examined and scrutinized. It is necessary to believe that there is nothing written in the prophetic books that is not a sign of some future reality. And if there is something that does not directly mean it, its presence is not superfluous, but rather supports what it does mean. Augustine writes a work that deals exclusively with the agreement between both Testaments, the Reply to Adeimantus. First of all, he tells them that they are incapable of understanding it because they do not know what it means to think about holiness and justice (Faust XXII 6). Secondly, it tells them that they are missing the mark, since what they criticize does not correspond to what Catholics teach (Adiman 12,5; Util 5,12). Furthermore, the method they use, removing the texts from their context, is not fair, since applied to the New Testament it would give the same results that the Manichaeans obtained applying it to the Old Testament. With it it could be shown that the Old is good and the New bad. According to this criterion, two Testaments could even be found within each one of them (Faust XXII 77). Furthermore, whoever reads Scripture with pious eyes will find in the New what the Manichaeans reproach in the Old and in the Old what they praise in the New (Adiman 13,4; 27; Faust XXII 21). In this sense Augustine strives to show the identity of contents in both Testaments: in both they speak of the mercy and severity of God (Adiman 17,5; 7,3). Because they were written by a single God, both are in agreement and are adjusted in terms of their patience that invites penitence, indulgence that forgives those who repent, and justice that punishes those who do not want to correct themselves (Adiman 7,5). The just measure of revenge and total forgiveness of injuries is not only commanded in the New Testament, but also pre-announced in the Old (Adiman 8); In both Testaments one can read the same attitude towards wealth: object of desire or flight, acceptance or rejection, although according to the degrees corresponding to each era (Adiman 19,2). On the other hand, the Old Testament is that of figurative promises, while the New is that of manifest fulfillments; the first is intended for carnal men, the second for spiritual men (Adiman 20,3); the former to servants to whom it is a burden, the latter to freemen to whom it constitutes a glory (Adiman 16,3); In the former it is moved by fear, in the latter by love. In the words of the saint: «This is the briefest and clearest difference between the two Testaments: fear and love; fear belongs to the Old, love to the New, but both have been dispensed and united by the most merciful dispensation of the only God” (Adiman 17,2). In the first stage, that of fear, the severity of God was praised above all, while in the other, that of love, his goodness; As for men, in that they served the law through the flesh; in this they adhere to God through the Spirit (Adiman 22). What was meant by the Old Testament was already known by some saints; but the difference is that in the New One, once revealed, it is announced to all peoples. Then it was the moment of significance, now that of manifestation. «Scripture, which then was the collector of significant works, is now a witness of the signified realities; what was then meant as an announcement is now read as proof” (Faust VI 9; XVI 32). The Manichaeans reproached the Catholics for their inconsistency with respect to the Old Testament: on the one hand they claim to accept it and, on the other, they discriminate some parts in favor of others; They fulfill some prescriptions while dropping others. They relied on this attitude to maintain their own attitude towards the New Testament: accepting it globally, but rejecting some specific points. Augustine responds to them by establishing the distinction between the precepts vitae agendae and the precepts vitae significandae. The former continue to have validity, but not the latter, which fall once their significance has been revealed (Faust X 2-3). It is not true, then, that they accept one part yes and no other; They accept it in its fullness, but not everything in the same way: the former in its literal reality, the latter in its meaning.

The Catholic does not accept the Old Testament to obtain its promises, but to perceive in them the announcement of the New (Faust IV 2); He does not fulfill like a servant what was ordered as a prefiguration of ours, but rather reads in freedom what was written to confirm us (Faust VIII 2). "We not only affirm, but also

We show and teach with the apostolic writings that the contents of the Old Testament that we did not observe were appropriate for that time and for that people, and that in those same contents that we did not observe we understand what they mean and we appropriate it spiritually" (Faust XXXII 8). Let us make a brief reference to those spiritual meanings of the Old Testament. They are none other than Christ and the Church. Everything contained in the Old Testament is written either about Christ or in attention to him (Faust XII 7). If the Manichaeans preferred to investigate with piety, rather than speak lightly, they could easily see it (Faust XII 25). The Gentile could also perceive what is affirmed there, whether of Christ or of the Church (Faust XIII 7). The entire Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ and in the Church, or if you want, in Christ, Head and Body (Faust XXII 94; XVIII 7; XXII 24.38). This congruence and unity between both Testaments should not be surprising, since the God of both is the only one; They are two voices of the one God (Costum I 17,30; I 30,64). For those who understand well, in both the music of the unity and peace of the one Holy Spirit is perceived (Adiman 3,3; 11). The author is unique: God, although he has manifested himself in a different way: as Lord who incites fear to the old man, and then as Father who invites love to the new man who returns to him (Adiman XVI 3). To conclude this section we can affirm that Augustine's relationship with Manichaeism, first acceptance and later rejection and refutation, was fundamental for the formation of Augustine as an exegete. If the saint has put so much effort into defending the truth of Scripture, into showing the harmony among the evangelists or the unity between the Old and the New Alliance; if it has accentuated the dividing line between the canonical books and the apocrypha; If he insisted on the authenticity of the canonical writings against the theory of interpolations, and, finally, if he attached so much importance to the comparison between the different manuscripts containing the sacred books, all of this is largely due to Manichaeism. He also owes his preferential dedication to the Old Testament to Manichaeism, especially in the first stage of his life as an exegete, and also his interest in allegorical exegesis 1M. The opposite is to act praepropere and praepostere, and the result is none other than ghosts without content and situations with no way out (Costum II 2,2; Fund 31; Nature 4). At the crux, Augustine poses his first battle. One by one, he presents the various answers, real or deducible, that they give: 1.a Evil is, with respect to any being, what is opposed to its nature. But, admitting this, and there is no one so blind that he does not see it, the entire heretical construction collapses. If evil is what goes against any substance, it cannot be a substance. The Manichaeans admit the existence of two souls in it: one that derives from God as it is part of its substance, and the other that derives from the kingdom of darkness, of which it is also a part (Souls). That there is no other soul, the one called by the Manichaeans a bad soul and opposed to the good one, can be seen by just paying a minimum of attention. All life, by the fact of being life, and as life, belongs to the supreme source and supreme principle of life. Consequently, these "bad" souls either lack life and then cease to be souls, or if they live to be able to be souls and do what is attributed to them (want-not want, desire-refuse) they cannot live except through life, that is, bringing their life from Life. Since Christ is the life (Jn 14:6), there is no reason not to confess that all souls, since they can only be by living, have been created by him (Almas 1). Creation is one of the Christian truths that Augustine defends most vigorously against the Manichaeans, and from there he confronts them. The first result of the doctrine of creation is to maintain distances between creator and creature, and in the context of the anti-Manichean controversy, to separate God from the evils of the creature. The workmanship can never be equal to the maker. The creature is corruptible, without that corruption affecting the creator and without disgracing him. It does not affect him, Augustine will say, because that corruption does not come from the being that he gave him, but from the lack of being, as a consequence of the fact that he is not the supreme being, but rather a participation, by creation, in the being of God. Nor does he disdain because as a divine artist he shows his art in knowing how to combine forms in wonderful harmony, since being great in large works he is no less in the smallest ones. The art is the same, although the works are different, some major and others minor. He does not create the universe in individual beings; rather, he creates each thing for the universe as a whole. Art gives itself in its entirety in the creation of each one, producing and arranging each thing in the places and orders that are congruent and ordering what corresponds to all in particular and as a whole (Faust XXI 5; Contra Secund 8). Even sin has its place in the whole, contributing to beauty, like the color black in a painting (Conf V 2,2). In contrast to them, who spoke of the "fabrication" of the world, Augustine uses the term creation in its precise meaning. The world has not been made from a previous reality, as was the opinion of the Manichaeans, but from nothing (Fund 24.25.36; Contra Secund 4.5.8.9...). And it has not been the result of God's need, but rather a free decision of his will. He did not create looking at himself, but at the result of his decision; that is, not to benefit himself, but rather what came out of his hands. And this creation, in the sobriety of its conception, is very far from the fantasies that Manes' imagination created. We are not going to dwell here on the observations and criticisms, mocking and ironic most of the time, that Augustine makes of his image of the world, as it came from the hands of the one sent by the Father of lights. At a doctrinal level they contribute little, although they are rich in data to show Augustine's sarcastic streak.

Augustine's criticism suffers from two flaws. One is general, that is, the strictly literal interpretation of the Manichean myth, and the other is real or fake misinformation. When we speak of misinformation we refer to the identification that Augustine makes between Christ and the soul, as both parts of the one God. But we already saw how Fortunatus distinguished very well between Christ and the soul, the first being similis Deo, while the second is not 183. In this sense there is no identification between Savior and being saved, nor can it be affirmed that it is man, that is, the elect, who frees the Savior. One may wonder if Augustine knew of such a distinction. We thought that he could not ignore it, given the degree of knowledge of Manichaeism that he possessed and the eagerness with which he devoted himself to reading his books. So, is it possible to speak of ill will, in the sense of arguing from a conscious falsification of data? This may not be the case, or at least not necessarily. In the controversy Augustine is speaking above all for Catholics and argues from Catholic positions. In Catholic theology, the being of God does not admit these divisions between substance and nature, between equal and unequal "divine beings", by virtue of its absolute simplicity. Consequently, although Augustine knew these Manichean positions, he overlooks them as inconsistent with Catholic theology, and presents the consequences that follow from the postulates of that same Catholic theology. If it is true that this had no value before the Manichaeans who saw their thinking betrayed, it could have had value before the Catholics, who reasoned with the same meter as Augustine. In any case, it is worth not forgetting that the polemical tone allowed him to very consciously confuse causes and occasions, as in the case of food. Making the positions of the opponents ridiculous was the desired effect, although to do so he did not tell the whole truth, but rather part of it.

The data are confirmed by the Manichaeans themselves in the Letter called "of the Foundation" (Nature 42), 86. Where there are variations, and notable ones, is in their interpretation. Few data from the entire Manichean system have been recalled more times by Augustine than that referred to this "globe", where he found occasion to ironize and ridicule his former coreligionists. Also here you can see the debater skilled in distorting, if not the data, then the interpretation thereof. The Manichaeans who recognized the existence of this "globe", which on the outside was covered by particles of light not yet completely purified, and which had the positive function, established by God, of preventing the kingdom of darkness from seeing the pure light and again feeling the desire to attack the kingdom of light again, never spoke of it as a condemnation, which will be the point at which Augustine becomes strong as the indicated texts indicate 187. In either of the two poles of the dilemma, the Manichaean God comes out badly. But other texts show that it was the Manichaeans' intention to show that their faith and God are more benign and less cruel than the Catholic faith and God. While the latter condemns something done by him to hell, the Manichean God only condemns the

They refute Augustine's arguments precisely by showing that in that case Jesus Christ who commands eternal fire would be more cruel. At the same time, Augustine tries to present this situation as irremediable, as one of eternal punishment. But in reality the data provided by the Manichean writings and the controversies with the Manicheans themselves do not allow us to confirm this. It always remains true that Felix speaks of the eternal fire to which Christ will send the wicked; but when he presents the doctrine of Manes he limits himself to indicating that unpurified souls will be applied to the "globe", without indicating that it is forever, although this is to be assumed, given the function assigned to it. Everything seems to indicate that between Manichaeans and Catholics there was a certain competition to show a more benign and less cruel God. The Manichaeans showed such benignity in the fact that they did not punish with eternal fire anything that had a relationship with their own God, while their severity had no limits towards the adverse party. That is why Augustine will tell them that they pretend to be too good (Adiman 7). Augustine, on the contrary, will try to force the argument: The Catholic Christ who condemns to eternal fire one of his creatures, who has freely chosen the path of evil and who, therefore, takes responsibility for his damnation, relieving God of that responsibility, is always infinitely more merciful than the Manichaean God who condemns to eternal torture a part of himself, which has been involved, without its own consent, even more so by God's command, in an unwanted situation. At the same time, the Manichaeans, their interlocutors, are extremely sparing in using the data of the myth, preferring with obvious constancy the language.

With reference to morality, we will first briefly show Augustine's defense of Catholic morality, against the attacks of the Manichaeans, and then move on to the critique of Manichean morality itself. We have already seen how a strong point of the Manichean advertising campaign was precisely the moral and ascetic life of its followers, mainly the chosen ones, which they compared with that of Christians. Augustine's response takes several directions. In the first place, he reproaches them for not distinguishing between men who profess doctrines and the doctrines themselves; or, in other words, he reproaches them for generalizing particular cases. From the bad example of some Catholics they conclude that all Catholics are equal (Costum II 20,75). «When it comes to your followers, you evade the issue or, even more shamelessly, you do not evade it, and you want to convince others by all means that in your very small number there are hidden who, I know, who faithfully practice the precepts; while when it comes to the multitude of the Catholic Church, you follow a contrary procedure, wanting to hide its immense holiness, which shines brighter than the light of the sun" (Costum II 20,75). It is malevolent error that directs the eye only towards the chaff of the Catholic harvest; If they wanted to be wheat, they would instantly see the presence of wheat there as well (Faust V 11; Costum I 31,68; 34,75). Even admitting the presence of good and bad in the Catholic ranks, the comparison between Catholics and Manichaeans can be established. The work The Customs of the Church and those of the Manichaeans aims nothing more than to show the superiority of the Catholics over the Manichaeans from a moral point of view. SURVIVAL OF MANICHAEISM IN AUGUSTINE

It is worth asking now if Augustine's criticism of the Manichaeism to which he belonged in his young years supposes and testifies to a complete disassociation from it. Already in life he had to hear the most contrary statements about his relationship with the faith of Manes. While the Marachaean listener Secundinus claimed that he had never been truly Manichaean and that he had not come to know the mysteries revealed by the Persian, the "Pelagian" Julian of Eclana repeatedly accused him of continuing to be a Manichaean. The Donatists had previously spread the same point of view, questioning Augustine's Catholic baptism and forcing him to defend himself in a sermon preached in Carthage (Commentary on Psalm 36 III 19). INTRODUCTION In the Revisions (I 14) Augustine informs us that he wrote this work when he was a priest. It is, therefore, after the spring of the year 391 and before the last months of 395, the date on which he was already bishop. But we can specify the date more by taking into account the placement of the work in the catalog of the Revisions: it is located after The Utility of Faith and before the public debate with Fortunatus, for which we have an exact date: 28-29 AD 392. On the other hand, taking into account that The Utility of Faith was written before our work, but always during his priestly period, we must leave a margin of time from its order so that he could compose that one Thus, we can place it in the period of time that goes from the summer of 391 to the summer of 392. We do not know external reasons or circumstances that led to the writing of such a work. Already located in Africa, a priest of a Church, he must have felt like a burden his Manichean past and his former work as a proselytizer. That is why his first writing, as we indicated, from the priestly period is The Utility of Faith, an attempt to win over Honorato to the Catholic faith, whom he had once brought to Manichaeism from paganism. Possibly suspicions on the part of the Donatists about the veracity of his conversion were even beginning to insinuate themselves,1 and he undertook the task of dismantling them all, renouncing that past in another public writing, in a tone of lamentation. Despite being directly an anti-Manichean writing, the air in which it moves is very different from the violent criticism that he uses in his first work against them: The Customs of the Catholic Church and those of the Manichaeans. The center is not constituted by them, but by himself; He speaks about himself directly, about them only as a consequence of the other. It is a meditation out loud on what he should have done and did not do, because if he had done so he would have avoided falling into that Manichaeism. He alludes to them in Reply to the Letters of Petiliano III 17,20 and defends them in Commentary on Psalm % III 19.

In this sense, the book abounds in autobiographical data, for example, his fall into the networks of the Obra sect of a few days (n.l), his Christian education (n.l), the friendship and the triumphs that led him astray (n.ll), the attribution of the triumphs to the Manichaeans (n.ll), his attitude towards the Manichaeans themselves (n.ll), along with aspects of his intellectual situation: the "weakness of his inner eye" by which he did not know how to distinguish the sensible from the intelligible, the carnal from the spiritual (n.12), that the Manichaeans separated him from the consideration of manifest realities (n.23). As for the Manichaeans, whom he considers Christian heretics, his tone is rather mild, despite some outbursts, such as when he doubts that they are men (n.3.9), or proclaims their ignorance (n.10) or their sacrilegious pride (n.18). As Décret 2 has warned, the work marks a turn in Augustinian's anti-Manichean controversy, in the sense that it abandons the defensive line that had characterized all of his previous treatises, except for the aforementioned Customs. In this book he no longer defends the Catholics, but attacks the Manichaeans, from that reflection on himself. And not so much to the Manichaeans, as we have just indicated, but to the Manichaean doctrine, with reference to a specific point in his anthropology: the two souls. And he begins with this point because he considers it the foundation of the sect (n.22). It is a work very close to the theme, without major deviations, so frequent in it, although with some reiterations. If we ignore that central point, there is little information that it gives us about Manichean dogmatics. He does not go into the particulars of the myth to ridicule it as he will do later. He completely dispenses with cosmology and soteriology to focus on anthropology. The points of his argument are the following: Every soul, as the source of life, must have as its origin God, the source of all life. If every soul is life by definition and God is the source of life, it must come from God, and thus the Manichean dogma of the existence of two souls falls to the ground, one that would belong to the substance of God and another foreign to him, coming from the kingdom of darkness. The comparison between the sunlight that the Manichaeans consider divine and life occupies several pages. If this sensible light is divine, life will be much more so, since it is evident that what is perceived through a superior means is superior. Therefore, if this light that we perceive

We see with our eyes is divine, even more so will the life we ​​perceive with our mind and, consequently, our soul. There cannot be, therefore, a soul, a life-giving principle, that does not come from God. Such is the theme of numbers 1-8. No. 9 is dedicated to presenting a correct, non-dualistic interpretation of Jn 8:44: You do not hear precisely because you are not of God; You have the devil for your father. Number 10 presents the origin of evil from the Manichean point of view, which, after an autobiographical parenthesis (n.ll), goes on to refute in the following numbers, from the definition of sin and will. The argument is based mainly on rational arguments. The use of Scripture is minimal. In the entire work, only fourteen biblical quotations are counted, all from the New Testament, both explicit and implicit; but nine of them are in n.9, which deals precisely with the interpretation of Jn 8:44. This fact, however, must not be attributed to a specific intention, but is the result of the moment in which Augustine writes, having just been ordained a priest, who has not yet had time to familiarize himself with the Scriptures. Finally, it is worth noting the extensive note dedicated to it in the Revisions, undoubtedly the longest of all the anti-Manichean works, even taking into account the brevity of the writing. There are ten texts on which he returns, but in none of them he has anything to correct, although he does specify his thinking more along the anti-Manichean line or, in most cases, he tries to show how what was written then does not contradict what he said later in the anti-Pelagian polemic, making the appropriate distinctions. The points in question have been pointed out in a note in the same text.

3. I also said: Sin does not reside anywhere else but in the will (n.12). Pelagians may think that such a statement favors their point of view, thinking about children. In effect, they deny that they possess original sin, which can be forgiven in baptism, arguing that they have not yet used the free will. As if the sin which we affirm that they contracted from Adam already from their origin, that is, as involved in his guilt, and which keeps them subject to punishment, could ever have existed but by the will! It was committed voluntarily when the transgression of the divine command took place. The statement can also be considered false: sin does not reside anywhere else but in the will in virtue of the words of the Apostle: If therefore I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me. It is so true that this sin does not reside in the will that it even says: I do what I do not want. How then does sin reside nowhere else but in the will? But this sin of which the Apostle spoke with such words is called sin because it is the fruit and punishment of a sin. In fact, the text refers it to the lust of the flesh, as it reveals next when it says: I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh, because although the desire for it is found in me, the realization of it fully is not. The full realization of good consists in the fact that the concupiscence of sin does not even exist in man. When he lives holyly, the will does not give its assent to this concupiscence.

Certainly, however, the good is not given in fullness, because (man) still lives within concupiscence, although his will resists it. Baptism annihilates what is to blame for such concupiscence, but the weakness remains, against which every baptized person who progresses in good fights with the utmost effort, until he is cured. The sin that does not reside anywhere but in the will must be understood above all that which is the result of a just condemnation - such a sin, in fact, entered the world through a single man - although even the sin by which the concupiscence of sin is consented to is committed only by the will. That is why I also said in another place: For one does not sin except voluntarily (n.14). 4. This definition seeks to distinguish those who want from those who do not want; and in this way the gaze is transferred to the first ones who existed in paradise, who caused evil for the human race, by sinning without suffering coercion from anyone, that is, by sinning of their free will, since they acted with full knowledge against what was commanded and the tempter induced them, not forced them to do so. It can be said, therefore, without being incongruous, that he who sinned in ignorance sinned unintentionally, even though he did willingly what he did in ignorance. Consequently, not even in this case there can be sin without will. Thus, the will was, according to our definition, a movement of the soul,

Consequently, since life and, therefore, the soul cannot be perceived by any bodily sense, but only through intelligence, and, on the other hand, the Manichaeans themselves affirm that this sun and this moon and all light that is perceived with these mortal eyes must be attributed to the true and good God, it is the height of madness to proclaim that what we see through the body belongs to God, and, on the other hand, to think that what we perceive through the body must be deprived and stripped of the authorship of God. and with the soul, but with the highest of it: the mind and intelligence, that is, life, whatever it may be, but always life. In fact, if I had invoked God, I had asked myself what it means to live, although it is a reality closed to all bodily sense and absolutely incorporeal, could he not have given me the answer? Or do they not also confess that those souls they detest not only live, but even live without ever dying? Truly, what Christ said: Let the dead bury their dead, he did not say it in reference to those who were totally lifeless, but to sinners. Sin is the

only death of the immortal soul, as Paul writes: The widow who lives among pleasures is dead. She affirmed at the same time that she was dead and that she was alive. Therefore I would no longer have focused on how distorted the life of the sinful soul is, but only on the fact that it lives. Not being able to perceive this except through intelligence, I think it would have occurred to me that any soul must be preferred to the light that we experience through these eyes, to the same extent that we prefer intelligence to the eyes themselves. The Manichaeans also affirm that this light comes from the Father of Christ. Can I doubt, then, that any soul comes from him? But I, not even in that my ignorance nor in that my age would have doubted in the slightest that not only the soul, but even any body, came from him, if only I had thought with pity and prudence what is the form and what is a formed being, what is beauty and what is a being clothed with beauty and finally which of these things is the cause of the other 4.

If I had meditated on it, if I had reflected, I would have passed on the problem to the Manichaeans, I would have made them see what the strength of intelligence is, how there is nothing in man that we can put in comparison with its excellence. It is what gives strength to those tiny limbs, what moves its legs in just the right proportion when it runs, or what moderates and makes its small wings vibrate when it flies. Whatever it is, for those who reflect properly it stands out as something great in a small thing, to the point of being preferred to any glare that dazzles the eyes. What, then, I ask, is what we perceive with thought, if we do not perceive that one thing is to understand with the mind and another to feel through the body, and that this is separated from this by an incomparable sublimity and that, therefore, it is not possible not to prefer the intelligible to the sensible, since the same intelligence is put before the senses by far? 5. From here, perhaps he would also have known what follows as an obvious consequence. Since injustice, immoderation and the other vices of the soul are not perceived by the senses, but by the intelligence, despite the fact that we detest them and consider them condemnable, it follows that, since they are intelligible realities, even they can be placed before this light, despite the fact that in their kind they are the object of praise. The soul that submits rightly to God is first made to see that not everything we praise should be put before everything we disapprove. Indeed, not because I praise lead in the highest degree of its purity enim, quid illa membra tam exigua uegetet, quid huc atque illuc pro naturali adpetitu tantillum corpusculum ducat, quid currentis pedes in numerum moueat, aut quid uolantis pennulas moderetur ac uibret. Quod qualecumque est, beneconsideratibus in tam paruo tam magnum eminet, ut cuiuis fulgori ptaestringenti oculos praeferatur. (V). Certe quod nemo dubitat, quicquid id est, intellegibile est, quod omni sensibili et ob hoc huic etiam luci diuinis legibus antecellit. It had been indicated that the investigation did not have to be done on vicious souls, but on the vices themselves. Since they are not known with the senses of the body and yet they are known, one cannot but accept that they are intelligible realities; And if these are superior to the sensible ones, how can we agree among ourselves that God is to be considered the author of light if, on the other hand, no one, except a sacrilege, will affirm that God is the author of vices? I would have responded to that man either on the fly and in an improvised way, if God had inspired me to solve this problem; or with a previously prepared response. And in the event that neither one nor the other had been deserved, he would have deferred the question raised, confessing that the proposed problem was difficult and arduous to elucidate. I would have returned to my interior again, I would have prostrated myself before God, I would have groaned from the depths asking that I not have to suffer being stuck in the middle of the road, as far as I had already arrived with valid arguments; that I should not be forced by a two-headed problem either to subject and subordinate the intelligible to the sensible, or to affirm that God is the author of vices, since both constitute the fullness of falsehood and impiety. There was no way I could have thought that he would have abandoned me in such a situation. He, then, would have admonished me in the ineffable ways that are characteristic of him to consider again and again whether the vices of the soul, the origin of my desires, were to be counted among intelligible realities. Taking into account the weakness of my inner eye, a just consequence of my sins, para desde ipsis uitiis esse quaerendum —quae quoniam sensu corporis non cognoscetentur, et tamen cognoscerentur, non nisi intellegibilia posse accipi; quae si sensibilibus omni[57]bus antecellunt, cur luzem deo auctoti esse tribuendam Inter nos conueniret, uitiorum uero auctorem deum nemo nisi sacrilegus diceret—respondem homini, si aut statim et sudden, ut bonis dei culturaribus solet, diuinitus infulsisset huius solutio quaestionis, aut Fuisset antea praeparata: quorum si neutrum meruissem atque potuissem, coepta differrem; quodque esset propositum, difficile. esse ad dinoscendum atque arduum confectioner.

His knowledge would not be more secure for us, but custom would give him greater confidence. And thus he would have investigated what properly belongs to the sense of the eyes. I would have found the colors over which this light dominates. They are realities that no other sense perceives. In fact, although the eyes also perceive the movements of bodies and magnitudes and intervals and figures, it is not specific to them, since such realities can also be experienced by touch. From this I would have deduced that this light stands out above the other corporeal realities, all the more so the more sight stands out over the other senses. Choosing, then, among the other things that are perceived by the senses, this light on which to lean and on which to place that necessary step for my investigation, I would have gone on to consider what I should do next, and I would have dialogued with myself in the following way: if this sun that stands out for its great brilliance and whose light is sufficient for the day were to diminish little by little before our gaze, like the moon, what else would we feel with our eyes but the light still resplendent in less measure, although searching, without seeing it, for the light that existed before, and welcoming with sight what remained? Consequently, we would not see that decrease, but the light that survives the decrease. By not seeing, we would not feel anything; In fact, everything we feel through sight cannot be unseen. Therefore, if that decrease is not perceived either by sight or by some other oculi mei, quae mihi peccatis meis iure accidisset, aliquem mihi ad inuisibilia contuenda in ipsis uisibilibus machinarer gradum: quorum esset nobis nullo moda certior cognitio, sed consuetudo fidentior. Non ergo illum defectum uideremus, sed luzem, quae defectui remaneret. Cum autem non uideremus, non sensibleemus; quicquid enim sentimus aspectu
The vices, superior to this sensitive light

sense, could not be counted among sensible realities. There is nothing sensible that cannot be perceived by the senses. Let us now focus our reflection on virtue. We rightly affirm that its intelligible light makes the soul shine. A certain diminution of this light of virtue is called a vice, which does not make the soul perish, but darkens it. Consequently, the vice of the soul cannot rightly be considered among intelligible realities, in the same way that the loss of light is precisely excluded from sensible realities. However, what remains of the soul, that is, the very fact that it lives and is a soul, is a reality as intelligible as what continues to shine to a certain extent in this visible light after the waning is sensible. With all reason, then, the soul is placed before any sensible reality inasmuch as it is a soul and participates in life, without which it could in no way be a soul. The consequence is that it is the greatest error to affirm that there is some soul that does not come from God, from whom you boast that the sun and the moon come. 7. Suppose that it were your pleasure to call sensible not only all the things that we perceive through the senses, but even those realities that, although we do not feel them, we judge of them through the body, such as darkness through the eyes and silence through the hearing - we know the former by not seeing and the latter by not hearing - and in turn designate as intelligible not only those realities that we see if

Our mind is illuminated 9, like wisdom itself, but also those from which we depart, because the mind is deprived of such illumination, which is insipidity, which we can properly call darkness of the soul; In this case there would be no problem of words, but it would have solved the difficulty with a simple division, and would have immediately shown those who know how to pay attention that, by virtue of the divine and incorrupt law of truth, intelligible substances take precedence over sensible ones, but not the respective deficiencies or deficiencies, even if we want to call them intelligible in the first case and sensible in the second. Those who confess, therefore, that these sensible lights and those intelligible souls are substances, without any other possibility, are forced to grant and grant the most prominent position to the souls; On the other hand, the deficiencies of both genders cannot be put before each other. They are nothing more than privations and indicate non-being, and have no more consistency than the negations themselves. In fact, when we say: "It is not gold" and "It is not virtue", although the distance between gold and virtue is great, there is none between the negations that we attach to it respectively. However, no one in his right mind doubts that the lack of virtue is worse than the lack of gold. And who does not understand that this happens not because of the denials themselves, but because of the realities to which they are attached? The more virtue is superior to gold, the greater the misery is to lack virtue.

We value more or less not the deficiencies themselves, but the things in which they occur. From this it follows that the deficiency in the life that is an intelligible reality is much more miserable than that of this sensible light, because the life that is perceived with intelligence is of much more value than this light that we see with the eyes. 8. Things being this way, will anyone dare not grant that all kinds of souls come from God, which in truth are not so except through life, which is so far above this light, if he attributes to God the sun and the moon and everything that shines in the stars, and even in our fire and this visible and earthly light? And if he who affirms the truth is true: "To the extent that it shines it comes from God," will I then lie, great God, if I say: "To the extent that it lives, it comes from God"? I wish that mental blindness and torments of souls do not reach such levels that men do not understand this. However, regardless of their error and pertinacity, I think that, equipped and armed with such reasons, once I had presented them with the reality thus considered and examined, and had discussed peacefully with them, I would have feared that none of them would deserve any interest to me, if I tried to put before or at least compare intelligence and those realities that are perceived by intelligence, although not in their diminishment, to the corporeal or to the realities that equally belong

to sense as far as knowledge is concerned. Having established this, when would he or anyone else have dared to deny to me that souls, as bad as you want, precisely because they are souls, are included in the number of intelligible realities and that they cannot be understood through their diminishment? Because souls would not be such except for the fact of living. Even if it were understood that they were vicious due to some deficiency, it would be noted that they are vicious due to a lack of virtue, but not due to a deficiency in their being a soul, since it is because of life that they are souls. And it cannot be that the presence of life is the cause of the deficiency, since the deficiency of something is in proportion to the extent to which life leaves it.
