And I would have exhorted those men—if I had found them being men,0—not to presume to have found something, but rather to seek with me teachers who would show us how these texts that seem to us in mutual opposition are in agreement and harmony with each other. Since within the same and identical authority of the Scriptures it is stated in one text: Everything comes from God, and in another: You are not from God, and it is not lawful to recklessly condemn these books, who would not see that it was necessary to find a competent doctor who knew the solution to the problem? This one, if he were endowed with a good capacity to understand and were - as the word of God says - a spiritual man, would undoubtedly support the true reasons, regarding the intelligible and sensible nature that I have exposed and on which I have discoursed, as far as I could; Furthermore, he himself would clarify them much better and in a way more appropriate to teaching. Regarding this question, we would hear nothing from his mouth except the possibility that there is no kind of soul that does not come from God and that, nevertheless, sinners and infidels are rightly told: You are not of God. Well, perhaps we too, imploring God's help, could have easily seen that it is one thing to live and another to sin, and that, although the life of sin is called death in comparison with the righteous life, both realities can be found.

in the same man, who is both alive and sinful. But the living being comes from God, and the sinful being comes from himself. In this division we use, from the two parts, that which is appropriate to our affirmation, so that when we want to indicate the omnipotence of God the creator we say, even to sinners, that they come from God - and we also say it to those who are part of some kind of being, we say it to animated beings, to rational beings, and finally we say it, which fits perfectly, to living beings, since these beings are gifts of God in themselves; On the other hand, when our purpose is to reproach the wicked, we rightly say to them: You are not of God. We say it to those who deviate from the truth, to the unfaithful, to the criminals, to the lustful and to the sinners, this name that includes all of the above. Who will doubt, in turn, that none of this comes from God? And so, what is so strange that Christ, reproaching sinners precisely for being sinners and not believing in him, told them You are not from God, leaving standing, referring to the other perspective, the affirmation that everything comes from God? If not believing in Christ, if rejecting his coming and not welcoming him, indicated with certainty which souls are not of God and therefore it had been said: You do not hear me precisely because you are not of God, how would the apostle's phrase in the famous beginning of his gospel be true, in which he says: He came to his own and his own did not receive him? How were they his if he did not receive him?

Although it is said with all reason and truth that they come from God, to those who are ignorant and less capable of examining dark things in depth, it seems that, as if by a certain chain, evils and sins are linked to God. In this area, the Manichaeans consider themselves invincible, as if asking was equivalent to knowing. I wish it were so! No one would be found wiser than me! But I do not know how often the person who proposes a great question in disputes assumes the role of great doctor, and most of the time he is more ignorant than the one whom he instills terror, precisely at that point in which he intends to frighten him. I would like to know what men would answer when I asked them if they thought that someone had sinned whose hand another had written, while he was sleeping, something shameful; any men, as long as no madness has deprived them of the common sense of the human race, whatever their studies, or their ignorance, or even their rudeness of ingenuity, that they bring to their judgment. Now at peace with them, to the extent that I could have achieved it, and won over again for my project, I would ask them not to feel offended if I asked them something else that was identically obvious and known to everyone. The usefulness of repentance

Is it possible for the human being to be weary, indecisive between one side and the other, either inclining towards sin, or feeling moved to do good, in order to be forced to accept the existence of two kinds of souls, whose nature comes in one case from God and in the other not? Is it not possible to conjecture numerous other causes of this pendular thinking? But any good estimator of reality warns that these things are dark and that souls whose eyes are sick will investigate them in vain. Consequently, let us rather reconsider what was said about will and sin, which - I repeat - supreme justice does not allow anyone who has the use of reason to ignore; which, if we are deprived of it, there is nothing to support the beginning of the path of virtue or the evasion of the death of vices. All this, reconsidered again and again, shows in a sufficiently clear and intelligible way that the Manichean heresy is false.

Not even a barbarian will dare to say that, if he has sinned, he should not repent. Things being this way, I ask what kind of souls it is to repent of sin. I know with complete certainty that it cannot correspond either to the one who cannot do evil, nor to the other who cannot do good. Therefore—using your terminology—if the soul of darkness repents of sin, it does not proceed from the substance of the supreme evil; If it is the soul of light that repents, it does not come from the substance of the highest good. That feeling of pain testifies that the one who repents did wrong and could have done good. «How then, one will say, is there no evil in me, if I have done evil? Or how is my repentance just, if I have done no wrong? Listen now to what the other would say: «How is there no good in me if good will exists in me? Or how is my repentance such, if there is no good will in me? The Manichaeans, then, must either deny the great benefit of repentance, eliminating it not only from the Christian name, but also from all human reason, even that which borders on imagination, or they must desist in their acceptance and teaching that there are those two kinds of souls, one of which is devoid of all evil and the other of all good. But, if they do so, they most certainly cease to be Manichaeans, since the entire sect is based on the variety of souls, more than double, leading to the abyss31. 23. Personally, it is enough for me to know that the Manichaeans make mistakes with the same certainty that I know that they must repent.

MINUTES OF THE DEBATE WITH FORTUNATO

INTRODUCTION The Revisions tell us that the debate and, therefore, the work belong to the time of Augustine's presbyterate. But in this case we did not need the Revisions data because the date is known to us from the same text that has been transmitted to us. As the minutes of a public debate between a Manichaean presbyter, Fortunatus, and another Catholic, Augustine, they include the date: the sixth and fifth of the calends of September, under the second consulship of Arcadius Augustus and that of Q. Rufinus, that is, August 28 and 29, 392. The circumstances that led to the debate are known to us from the Life of Augustine written by Possidius. According to him, the heresy of Manes had infected many in Hippo, both residents and passers-by, mainly through the work of a presbyter named Fortunatus (Life 6). This fact is confirmed by Augustine himself in the Revisions, where he says that he had lived there for a long time (I 15), Augustine does not indicate having known him personally, since he speaks of him in an impersonal way: a certain, although we know that this way of speaking does not indicate ignorance in Augustine in any way.' Possidius, however, does expressly say that he had met him in the years of his youth in Carthage 2. Fortunatus himself seems to confirm this information from Possidius 3. The success of the Manichean caused some Christians in the city and region, both Catholics and Donatists, to present themselves to Augustine and ask him to visit the Manichean presbyter and discuss with him "about the law." Agustín agreed instantly. They appeared before Fortunato with the same request. According to Posidio, Fortunatus was reluctant to enter the fray with Augustine. But in the end, urged by the insistence, and to avoid the shame of his people, he agreed to hold the debate with his Catholic opponent. Once the day and place had been appointed, Augustine's biographer continues, the debate was held. See M. TESTARD, Saint Augustin et Cicero. I. Cicero dans la formation et dans l'oeuvre de saint Augustin (Paris 1978) p.11-19. Life 6. Fortm 1.
Arts of the debate with Fortunato

with a large influx of people, some motivated by interest in the subject and others by curiosity. There were notaries who transcribed everything said and what happened. So much for Posidio. We have to add that the minutes are not official, but ecclesiastical records; which, contrary to what was indicated by Possidius, does not seem to be a full transcription of everything that was said there 4. The debate took place in the baths of Sosius (n.5), that is, in a neutral place, where both Catholics and Manichaeans undoubtedly attended. These attendees have a certain participation in the debate, either indirect or direct. Indirectly they are protagonists in that Augustine appeals to them by saying: "those who listen to us had imposed on us that we discuss faith in the two natures with rational arguments" (n.19). Directly too, because at a certain moment they caused an uproar when they found, the minutes say, that Fortunatus did not want to admit the Apostle's text in its entirety (ibid.). Its duration was two days: August 28 and 29, as we have indicated. Such duration was not agreed upon from the beginning, but was the result of its progress. Without the reason being clear, since the argument adduced is not convincing, namely, that "he did not want to admit what is recorded in the text of Saint Paul", despite the fact that Fortunatus' quote was perfectly orthodox, at a precise moment there was an uproar among the attendees, who began to argue among themselves, which caused the session to be adjourned (n.19). Curiously, what became a topic of discussion among those present had not been affirmed by Fortunato, who, even more, had explicitly denied it; On the contrary, these were attributions made by Augustine to the Manichaeans, but already beforehand. All this allows Décret to suggest that Fortunatus's sharp argument, based on Scripture, forced Augustine to go on the defensive, before which his horrified "parishioners" had come to his aid, who on the other hand did nothing to silence them, and thus session 5 was adjourned. The debate is slow, both in the first and the second part, with the exception of the last moments of this second. The interventions of both parties are frequently long. In general, one can speak of a correct combat in which the answers correspond to the questions, despite the fact that some are avoided from time to time, especially by the

of Fortunatus, who sometimes prefers the counter-question to the answer, something that bothers Augustine, who reminds him that he has always personally answered 6. At first, however, a misunderstanding appears between the two, which cannot be said to be malicious or the result of circumstances 7. Augustine insists on talking about faith, Fortunatus prefers the moral theme, that is, the customs of the Manichaeans. Here Fortunatus was clever in getting Augustine to implicitly withdraw the accusations leveled against the chosen Manichaeans in the work The Customs of the Manichaeans. According to the text (n.3) the debate had been arranged to discuss the (Manichean) faith, and in fact the first session begins with an exposition of the Manichean faith made by Augustine, which Fortunatus acknowledges responding to the truth (n.l). In the second, it is Fortunatus himself who begins by establishing some fundamental points of his faith, which gives rise to Augustine to explain the Catholic faith (n.20). In the Revisions he will say that it was about the origin of evil, which corresponds to the truth as a topic really considered (n.15.21), but that it does not seem to have been a specifically programmed topic. Possidius in turn speaks, as we saw, that the invitation to Augustine was to speak "about the law." The formulation is very generic and will be consistent with reality if it is given the meaning of faith. The work is important as an information source. Regarding Augustine, there is little that he gives us, except for the first bars in which he tells us that he was a Manichean (n.l), that he attended the prayers of the sect (n.2.3), that he was only a listener (n.3), that he never found an answer to a question, the one that Nebridius had presented to him (n.37; Nebridius' question in Conf VII 2,3). All data that is known to us from other sources, particularly the Confessions. That he was revoked from Manichaeism by divine mercy (n.37) is a constant interpretation. More difficult to interpret is the information about the divine warning to abandon the error (n.37), if it refers to something very specific and not to the entire process narrated in the Confessions. The greatest contribution he offers us refers to Manichaeism. Particularly it allows us to understand what the public presentation of the sect was, perhaps not so much what refers to the contents of the internal catechesis. In this regard they are worthy

Minutes of the debate with Fortunato

to highlight the following data: a) Maximum effort to present themselves as authentic Christians. Hence the extensive recourse to Christian Scripture (New Testament) as the foundation for Manichean dogmatics itself. This is how Fortunato bases dualism in the Gospel (n.14.21: Mt 15,13; 3,10); sin and condemnation in Paul (n.21: Gal 5,17; Rom 7,23-24); the human condition (n.22: Mt 10,16), Christology (n.3: Jn 14,6.9; 5,24, etc). b) No recourse to Manes' writings. Presumably that was left exclusively for internal catechesis; From the outside there was no book other than the Christian Scripture. It must be recognized, however, that in a debate of this type "authorities" that were not accepted by both parties could not be used, c) Not once is Manes mentioned: everything develops as a dispute between two Christian groups that defend the authenticity of their own interpretation of the message of Christ, d) What is most strange is that Fortunato never attacks the Old Testament. It may be a matter of tactics, that is, to prevent Augustine from attacking the Manichaean myth in the same way, or to not enrage a perhaps largely Christian public, or it may also be due to Fortunatus's firm conviction that he does not need to attack the opposing positions, since his own faith is sufficiently founded. At the same time, Augustine's behavior must also be highlighted: he does not bring up the Manichaean myth at all either. After reading the minutes of the debate, the Manichaeism found in him is very different from what his reply to the Letter called "of the Foundation" would allow us to glimpse, if only that work had been preserved. It is possible that there was an implicit pact of non-aggression, or simply that the course of the debate did not give rise to outbursts, without giving the impression of not having to respond to the adversary's objections. Regarding Manichean dogmatics, it is abundant in data. First of all, the radical dualism (n. 14.18.20) that Fortunatus proves by resorting to the opposition of things among themselves, to the Christian Scriptures, to the existence of evil and to the redemptive work of Christ. Regarding God, the insistence on his incorruptibility is notable (n.1.3.6.7, etc.).

Fortunatus never speaks of the three times, nor of the initial combat of his own initiative, but only as a reply to Augustine: thanks to this combat God prevents evil, he does not suffer it (n.15.16); If he had not faced it, he would have been complicit in evil (ibid.). On the other hand, God's victory is assured, since He is invulnerable in

its nature. The instrument of this victory is the soul, which is not similar to God (n.12), that is, in its nature, although it is similar to its substance (n.ll). She, the soul, has been sent by God so that, through her own passion, she may set limits on the contrary nature (n.33). There is also abundant data referring to soteriology. First, the insistence on the involuntary sin of the soul, whose root, the substance of evil (n.21), is in us and is what leads us to sin, even if we do not want to. Here the duel with Agustín is not without interest. Despite involuntary sin, man can be responsible for it, a reality that takes place after receiving enlightenment. This is how Fortunatus justifies the fact that repentance and penance are so highly valued in the sect, contrary to all of Augustine's arguments (n.21). Thus "science" acquires a fundamental value, as in every Gnostic system: knowing one's own origin and present situation is the starting point for penance, a means of salvation (n.20-21). The very frequent recourse to Christ, path, truth and door (n.3) could not be missing, but what is missing, as we already indicated, is the mention of Manes and his function in that path of salvation, which will appear in the debate with Felix and in the Letter of Secundino (n.3). In the present debate, Christ appears as the only teacher, liberator and savior. A Christ obviously seen from doctrinal positions (n.7), similar to God (n.3), born at the beginning of the world; a Christ who, as savior, is above all a teacher, granting the heavenly precepts; Its mission is to grant knowledge and precepts that bring health to chained souls (n.20). Eschatology is absent, except for the fact that God recovers the soul for himself, once he has fulfilled his mission of setting limits on contrary nature (n.33). Not even in Augustine's mouth does the "globe" appear so present in the debate with Félix and in the replies to Faust and Secundino. He is also sparse in data on the organization of the sect. The only information is given by Augustine when he indicates that he was a listener and not elected. The same is said regarding prayer made towards the sun, and the Eucharist. Finally, it is worth asking what the result of the debate was. Possidius (Life 6) states that Fortunatus, not knowing what to answer, slipped away, stating that he had to consult with the leaders of the sect about what he could not answer, and that if they did not give him satisfactory solutions he would know what to expect.
And so, full of confusion, he disappeared shortly after, never to return.

more to Hippo. Certainly, at the end of the debate Fortunato asks: "What can I answer you, then?" (n.36). But the question can be interpreted in two ways: either as a recognition that he has nothing to say, or as a confession that anything he says will be useless, since Augustine would be incapable of understanding. What is the authentic interpretation? Augustine certainly considered it in the first sense, that is, as a triumph and perhaps the public as well. The truth is that Fortunato left and ceased his fruitful propaganda, although he did not become a Catholic. Possidius, we remember again, indicates that he never set foot in Hippo again. His successor was Félix, with whom Agustín will once again have another public debate. But the circumstances will be very different.

MINUTES OF THE DEBATE WITH FORTUNATO MANICHAEUS. SINGLE BOOK 1. At the same time that I was a priest I had a debate with a certain Fortunatus, also a priest, but a Marachaean, who had been residing in Hippo for a long time and had seduced so many that he liked to live there for their benefit. The debate was recorded on the fly by notaries and written up as public minutes, as they include the date and the consulate. I took care to turn it into a book to perpetuate his memory. It addresses the question of the origin of evil. I affirmed that the evil that man does comes from the free will of the will; Fortunatus, on the other hand, strove to persuade of the existence of a nature of evil coeternal with God. Answer me to this if it pleases you and deign to also explain to me in what sense the Apostle said that we were by nature children of wrath, the same ones who are said to be reconciled to God. If they were children of wrath by nature, how do you say that the soul is by nature a daughter and a portion of God? Fortunatus: If the Apostle had said that we are by nature children of wrath, referring to the soul, the same word of the Apostle would have made the soul a stranger to God. With this reasoning you now show that the soul is not of God, because, as the Apostle says, we are by nature children of wrath. If, on the other hand, the same Apostle, who expressly acknowledges that he descends from the lineage of Abraham, spoke in this way as he was linked to the law, it follows that he said that we were children of wrath in terms of the body, like all the others. He showed that the substance of the soul comes from (ex) God and that the soul cannot be reconciled with him in any other way, except through the mediation of the teacher Christ Jesus. But even after the enmity was eliminated, the soul seemed unworthy of God. We, however, confess that it has been sent by omnipotent God and that it comes from him and that it was sent to do his will, just as we believe that Christ the Savior came from heaven to fulfill the will of the Father. Nam dictum Note Fortunato's insistence on affirming the presence of evil everywhere. He has already said twice before that it is found all over the world and now he indicates that44"everywhere." The same is true for his intervention in the following issue. Here Fortunato clearly tells us about the Manichean conception of sin in its proper sense: what it consists of and when it occurs. There are, then, two kinds of sin: one involuntary, prior to Gnostic enlightenment, when the contrary nature forces the soul to sin, and another for which the soul is already responsible, when, after having been enlightened, it adheres to material things. INTRODUCTION The Revisions place this writing after the debate with Fortunatus, that is, after August of the year 392. It is also later than the work Faith and the Symbol, based on the exposition that the same Symbol made to the bishops of all Africa gathered in council in Hippo, a council that took place on October 8, 393. It is, therefore, after this date. But since between the last mentioned work and the one at hand there are four others, although not very long, its composition must be delayed for a reasonable time. Taking into account above all its relatively considerable volume (the second largest anti-Manichean work, after the Reply to Faust) it cannot be placed before 394. The origin of the work must be seen, according to Revisions (I 21), in the occasional fact that certain disputations of Adeimantus came into his hands, which the Manichaeans used in their propaganda against the Catholic Church. The text does not tell us who sent them to them, although it is assumed that they were the faithful; Nor does it mention when. In this regard, we do not know if this is the work referred to at the end of The Two Souls, even as a project, in which it would show how the Scriptures can be defended (Almas 24). The relative distance in time and the nature of urgency perceived in the composition of this writing lead us to think not. Who was Adeimantus? This work provides us with little data, although it explicitly mentions him 14 times. It is said that he was one of the disciples of Manes, great doctor of the sect (n.12,1). The first data is confirmed in Revisions (I 21) and the second by Faustus, also a Manichean, according to whom he was a very learned man to whom only Manes should be put before him as an object of study (Faust 12), data that Augustine collected. These works are: Literal Commentary on Genesis (incomplete), The Sermon on the Mount, Psalm against the sect of Donatus and Reply to Donatus's letter. Although the last writing has not been preserved to us, we can deduce that it was not very long from the fact that it consisted of only one book.

also (Faust VI 16). In the work Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets he indicates that he is designated by the name of Addas (II 42). But there are extra-Augustinian data that allow us to complete this information. According to the Acts of Archelaus (XIII 4), probably written in the first half of the 4th century, Adeimantus is one of the first three disciples of Manes; commissioned by him to preach Manichaeism in Egypt according to the documents discovered in the Chinese Turfan. He was there between the years 244 and 261, reaping abundant successes in his missionary work. In this last year he changed the scene of his activity: he left Egypt and went to Adiabene 2. During the period of his stay in Egypt it is likely that he also came to North Africa, being, therefore, the apostle of Manichaeism also in this area, which would explain the great prestige that he enjoyed there 3. His work was not only as a preacher, but also as a writer. His works were well known in Africa, as Faust himself shows. The Manichean bishop alludes to him when, when speaking about why they do not receive the prophets, he affirms that the writings of the ancestors (stop them) have sufficiently demonstrated that they did not prophesy Christ (Faust XII 1); In another text, however, he mentions him explicitly with these words: "the most learned Adeimantus has already brought to light and abundantly discovered the fallacy common to Jewish superstition and semi-Christians" (ibid., I 2). Possibly it was these writings of Adeimantus that were condemned by Diocletian 4. The work that came into the hands of Augustine was a catechesis writing through controversy with Catholic positions regarding the Old Testament. Agustín has not transmitted it to us as it came to him, but he allows us to know it in its general tenor. As we have already said, it was a work against the Old Testament. To attack him he used the New, precisely by establishing a systematic opposition between the two. Augustine has transmitted to us only 28 of these texts (chapter), which we divide, following Decret 5, into three groups: A) The evil God of the Pentateuch and the prophets of the Old Testament (11 chapter). B) The curse against "everyone who hangs on the tree of the cross" and the carnal anthropology of Deuteronomy (2 chapter).

C) Morality and the rude rites of the law (16 chapter). That Adeimantus's work was broader is information that Augustine himself gives us in the Revisions (I 21). After telling us that he responded to some chapters twice because some answers he had already prepared were lost and appeared after the response had been prepared the second time, he adds that to others he gave a solution in sermons to the people 6, and, finally, that he did not respond to others because more urgent tasks got in the way, which forced him to abandon that task and then he forgot. Augustine's refutation broadly follows the method that is usual for him whenever he has to refute works by other authors: first give the text and then refute it. But in this case Augustine does not give it in a literal tenor, but limits himself to presenting the text of the Old Testament that is the object of Adeimantus' reproach and then the text of the New Testament that opposes him, sometimes summarizing the argument that explains the opposition. Agustín used what we could call a token system, that is, answers to each of the questions separately. This explains why some could be disclosed and even lost and others could not and that others were left unconsidered, since it seems that everything is dominated by haste. At the same time we can assume that he has not followed the faithful and exact order, as it appeared in Adeimantus' writing. But that he disclosed them in a predetermined order can be deduced from the precise reference to chapter 3 referred to in chapter 23. The information he gives us about the life of Augustine is null; The information on Manichaeism is extensive with regard to the specific aspect of its understanding and use of Scripture, both the Old and New Testaments, but very poor with regard to Manichaean dogmatics and morals. Let's start with the first thing. Regarding Scripture, in addition to what has already been repeatedly stated about the frontal opposition to the Old Testament, it informs us that they also rejected the Acts of the Apostles (n.17,5); that they had great appreciation of certain apocrypha, such as the Acts of Thomas (n.17,2) and Acts of Peter (n.17,5); at the same time he denounces the defects of the exegetical method of the Manichaeans, the main of which are the following: easy recourse to the theory of interpolations (n.3,2; 15,1); interpret the texts in isolation and out of their context (n.3,3; 14,2, etc.); keep silent about what is not appropriate (n.12,4; 28,1). Of less interest is a piece of information about the corruption of the codices, at least insofar as it warns us that Augustine was aware of this possibility and that he took it into account in his polemical work (n.28,1). On the other hand, Augustine's exegesis is allegorical and spiritual, as he had already done in the previous scriptural work written to refute the Manichaeans, namely, the Literal Commentary on Genesis, an unfinished work. To escape the accusation of being arbitrary, he relies on the fact that such a method was already used by the apostles, particularly by Paul: "they expounded a few mysteries to leave us the standard according to which the rest were to be understood" (n.12,5). Although information on Manichaean dogmatics is scarce, some data is not missing, although none of it is new. Of course, in its pages we find references to substance dualism (n.26), to the initial combat (n.20,3), to the condemnation of the race of darkness (n.7,1), to Jesus patibilis (n.17,4.6), to metempsychosis (n.12,1-2) and to the belief that trees also have a rational soul (n.22). Finally, it also informs us of the disproportion in favor of the listeners and against the chosen ones among the members of the Manichean church. While the "saints" are few, the listeners constitute a mob, a multitude (n.15,2), but without the data having absolute value, that is, in relation to Catholics. Another interesting point is the statement that they sought to gain the sympathy of the pagans (n.ll and 13,1), a fact that Augustine repeats in Against Faust (XX 5). *

That king who at his son's wedding found among the diners a man without his wedding dress, whom he first called a friend and then ordered, tied hand and foot, to be thrown into the outer darkness, says well. Anyone could take that same chapter of the Gospel and, as Adeimantus does with the Old Testament, slanderously accuse the Gospel, praising rather the books of the Old, in which it is written: Praise the Lord for he is good, for his mercy is eternal, and reproaching in the New that the one called to the banquet is thrown into such great torment because of his dress. If he did this systematically with fraudulent perversity, collecting all the texts in which meekness appears in the Old Testament and those in which severity appears in the New, pretending that the texts are opposed to each other, praising the Old and recriminating the New, he would also find those ignorant and unaware of the divine Scripture, whom he would convince that the Old Testament and not the New Testament had to be retained. This is the same thing that the Manichaeans do, but in the opposite direction, that is, reproaching the Old as contrary to the New. And I am amazed that you do not think that someone could ever read one and the other and, understanding them with divine help, praise them both and feel pain for the fraud and evil of the Manichaeans or warn them off as heretics, or mock them as ignorant and proud.

14 [1]. About this text from Deuteronomy: According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all flesh according to the pleasure that the Lord has given you. Beware, however, of eating the blood; pour it out like water on the earth. Adeimantus believes that these words of the law are opposed by those of the Lord in the Gospel: Do not let your hearts be dulled by gluttony, wine and worldly cares; and to those of the Apostle: It is a good thing not to eat meat or drink wine, and to these others: You cannot take part in the table of God and that of demons. We, on the other hand, affirm that all these texts, both those of the Old and the New Testament, have been written as particular reasons required, and we show that they are not opposed to each other. Adeimantus himself could have warned, regarding the words he took from the Old Testament, that this text does not refer to unbridled voracity: According to the desire of your soul, kill and eat all flesh, since it says next: According to the pleasure that the Lord has given you. The Lord has not given you immoderate pleasure, but enough for the sustenance and health of your nature. On the other hand, whoever follows his unbridled voracity follows his own vice, not the pleasure that the Lord gave him. Therefore it is not contrary to what is found in the Gospel: Do not dull your hearts with gluttony, wine and worldly cares. When one satisfies nothing more than the pleasure it gave [148] 14 (XJV.l). De eo, quod scriptum est in deuteronomy: Secundum desiderium animae tuae oc(149)cide et manduca omnem carnem iuxta uóluptatem, quam dedit tibi dominus. About this text from the prophet Amos: If it can happen that two walking together on the road do not know each other and that the lion returns to its cubs without prey; if a bird falls to the ground without a hunter there; if he sets the trap without reason, so as not to catch anything; If the trumpet sounds in the city without the people being filled with terror, in the same way no evil will happen in the city that is not caused by the Lord. Here evil is not to be understood as sin, but rather as punishment, since evil is spoken of in a double meaning. The evil that man causes is one thing and that which he suffers is another. The one he causes is the sin, the one he suffers is a punishment. The prophet, then, was speaking of punishment when saying the above. Under the moderation and government of divine Providence, man does the evil he wants, in such a way that he suffers the evil he does not want. The Manichaeans reproach the prophet with such words as if they did not read in the Gospel: Are not two birds sold for an ace? And yet, none of them falls to the ground without your Father's will. God works evil; evil that is not for himself, but for those he punishes. Consequently, as far as Himself is concerned, God works good because everything that is just is good, and that punishment is just. Three kinds of visions

Have you seen the invisible God? If, on the other hand, they answer negatively, rather, if they dare, accuse the Apostle who says: The invisible of God has been made visible since the creation of the world through the understanding of created things. First he talks about invisible and then he indicates that he becomes visible. Are you not forced to confess here that it is invisible to the eyes of the body, but visible to the mind? In the same way, the prophet also saw God who is invisible to the body, not with the body, but with the mind.

Many things are not in the proper sense, but in a figurative sense, and many are also shown in an equally figurative sense. The third kind of vision is that of the sight of the mind, through which truth and wisdom are seen and understood. Without this last class, the two indicated above are either useless or lead to error. Perfect revelation occurs when the things that God shows, either to the senses of the body, or to that part of the soul that captures the images of the bodies, are not only experienced in this way, but also understood by the mind. To this third class corresponds that vision that I mentioned, in accordance with the words of the Apostle: The invisible of God becomes visible from the creation of the world through the understanding of created things. To see God through this vision it is necessary to purify hearts with good customs, by the piety of faith and by the action of God. What good did it do for King Balthazar to see a hand writing on the wall before his eyes? Since he could not apply the gaze of the mind to this vision, he sought to see even what he had already seen. Daniel, endowed with that luminous gaze through which these realities are understood, saw with his mind what the king had seen with his body. Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream, with that part of the soul that captures the images of bodies; but since his mind's eye was not capable of seeing better what he had seen, he sought the gaze of another person, that of Daniel, so that he could interpret what he had seen.

REPLAY TO THE LETTER CALLED “OF THE FOUNDATION” INTRODUCTION The Revisions (II 28) place this work immediately after Various Questions to Simplician, the first of those written while he was already a bishop. The problem is knowing the exact date of composition. Augustine himself indicates that he sent them to Simplician, bishop of Milan, successor of Saint Ambrose. Given that he died on April 4, 397, this work would have to be placed after that date, and consequently also the one at hand. But it is most likely that Augustine wrote it when Simplician was still a priest. Otherwise Augustine would have gone almost two years without having written anything, which is difficult to understand; On the other hand, it must be taken into account that Augustine says that he composed it at the beginning (exordium) of his episcopacy'; Although it is impossible to specify how far this exordium goes, it must be given the meaning of beginning. We have another point of reference in letter 37 that accompanied the writing: had it been written after the consecration of Bishop Simplician, Augustine would hardly have passed without referring to the event. On the other hand, our work must have been written very soon after the one sent to Simpliciano; Otherwise, there would be no time left for the composition of the other three works that, always according to the Revisions, precede The Confessions, which in all probability began in the years 397-398. Regarding the Letter called "of the foundation" there are several statements that we find in Augustinian work: "It contains almost everything they believe" (n.5); "by reading it, the faithful are enlightened" (n.5); "It is well known by all the enlightened", unlike other letters of Manes (n.5) and "it contains the beginning, the middle and the end" (Felix II 1). All important statements in that they shed light on the title and show his celebrity and the extent of his knowledge in Africa, something that cannot be stated at the same level as any other writing by Manes.! A first study was carried out by Alfaric, who identified it with Fataq, Manes' father, through a series of phonetic changes2; A second, more convincing contribution by Décret identifies him with Patig, the missionary sent by Manes to Egypt, along with Adeimantus 3. As we have already indicated, Augustine refuted only the beginning although it was his intention to refute it all when he had time. For this purpose he had already noted down the points that seemed appropriate; notes with which, according to him, "it was completely demolished" (Revisions II 28). The truth is that either he lacked time, or the controversy took other paths, but the work remained uncompleted. We also already indicated that the refutation does not seem to follow the text in detail, but rather selected parts either because it was easy to ridicule or for other controversial reasons. The system is the usual one: present the text and then refute it. But two things are surprising: the extensive introduction, overflowing with benevolence and understanding, before entering into the refutation itself; and then the absolute disproportion between what is a quote from Manes' letter and what is typical of Augustine, so that in the last 28 chapters he does not present any new text; the last had been cited in chapter 15. The work can be considered in a certain way as the complement to the one written against Adeimantus. He had composed a writing attacking the Old Testament from the New. Agustín gave him a quick answer, of an exegetical nature, for the needs of the moment. Most likely, the same work of Adeimantus suggested that he go on the attack, focusing on the writings of Manes, particularly the Letter of the Foundation. Why precisely this one? No doubt because he had it in his library, but also because it was the best known and most used. In his desire to harm the sect's proselytism, he wants to pay them in the same coin: doing the same thing that they did with the Old Testament. In this sense the work represents a novelty, since until then it had never directly dealt with a writing by Manes. He had indeed refuted his doctrine in a work like The Two Souls, but not in a specific writing. And when he refutes the Charter he does so by focusing only on its mythical aspects, which are not lacking; that is, what was easiest for him to ridicule. Take the

It is strong in the argument that the kingdom of darkness, as described by the Manichaeans, is composed of natures, all of them a good and full of goods that allow their existence, since if such goods disappeared, they would also disappear. At this level Augustine is concerned above all with cutting off the sect's anti-Catholic propaganda and making it ridiculous; for presenting his own thoughts and that of the Church, more than for making known that of his adversaries. It is not surprising, then, that Agustín has not continued to refute the letter, according to his notes. In the same writing he had already ceased the practice. If I had nothing else to believe in the matter, before admitting that he had already come through Manes, I would still wait for his arrival. In the aforementioned book it is written: First, O Theophilus, I spoke about all that Jesus began to do and teach on the day when he chose the apostles by the Holy Spirit, and commanded them to preach the Gospel. He manifested himself alive to them after his passion with many tests. He appeared to them for forty days, instructing them about the kingdom of God; I narrated how he lived with them and commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father that you have heard, he told them, from my mouth. But if he had said such a thing, who would not have answered him: "If I have to believe unknown things, why should I not rather believe those that are already celebrated by the consensus of the learned and the unlearned, and are already established in all peoples by an authority of great weight?" » 40 He, fearing that he would be argued in this way, covers the ignorant with fog, first promising them the knowledge of certain things, and then imposing on them the faith of uncertain things. If he is told to at least let it be known that these things were shown to him, he faints in the same way and commands us to believe that too. Who could endure such great fallacy and such arrogance?

16. But what will I say about the truth and wisdom that surpasses all the powers of the soul, if the nature of the soul itself, whose mutability is obvious, does not occupy, with a certain mass of its own, a place in space? Everything that has any volume cannot but be smaller in its parts, having one thing in one place and another in another. In fact, the finger is smaller than the entire hand and one finger is smaller than two and one finger occupies one place and another finger another, and another the rest of the hand. We see this only in the articulated masses of bodies. Nor is one part of the earth where the other is, because each has its own place; and a smaller part of a liquid occupies a smaller place and a larger part a larger one, and one part of it is at the bottom of the container while another is at the edge of it. Likewise, the parts of the air each fill their place, and it cannot be that the air with which this house is filled can have with it at the same time in the same house also the air that the neighbors have. Regarding the light, some of it enters through this window, another through that, the larger part through the larger window and the smaller part through the smaller window. There can be no body at all, celestial or

terrestrial, gaseous or liquid, which is not smaller in one part than in the whole, nor can it have at the same time a part in the place of another, but by having one in one place and another in another, it extends thanks to its distant mass through spatial places and divisible or, so to speak, sectionable. The nature of the soul, on the other hand, although it is not considered that its faculty by which it understands the truth, but rather that other inferior one by means of which it contains the body and feels in it, in no way is it the case that it extends through space by virtue of any mass. It is present to itself in its entirety in each of its parts, since it feels all of itself in each of them, nor is one part of it less in the finger and greater in the arm, in the proportion in which the finger is less than the arm, but in every place it is equal, because in every place it is whole. When a finger is touched, the soul does not feel through the entire body and yet it feels entirely. That contact is not hidden from her entirely, something that would not be possible if she were not present to herself entirely. Nor would she be present to herself in her entirety when she touches the finger and feels in the finger, so that she abandons the rest of the body to concentrate on that one place where she feels. Rather, when all of it feels in the finger of the hand, if it touches another place on the foot, it does not stop feeling all of it in that place. And if it is whole at the same time in the different places, far from each other, without abandoning one to be whole in another, nor does it have one and the other in the way of having one part here and another there, but is capable of showing itself entirely at the same time in the different places; how you feel whole

17. What to say? If we think about their memory, not the one referring to intelligible realities, but the one referring to these corporeal realities that we see that beasts also have - since donkeys walk without mistake through known places, beasts return to their burrows, dogs recognize the bodies of their masters and while sleeping they emit sounds and sometimes even break into barking, something that they would not be able to do if they did not find in their memory the images of the things seen or in some way perceived by them. the body—who will be able to consider as deserves where these images are taken, where they are held, and where they are formed? In fact, if they could not be larger than the volume of our body allows, someone could say that the soul forms and keeps these images in the interior spaces of its body within which it itself is located. But, despite the fact that the body occupies a very small part of the earth, the soul wanted to form images of the immense regions of heaven and earth, for which it is not narrow even when they leave or follow one another in droves; Here it shows that she was not extended by places, since it is not the images of those enormous places that in a certain way welcome her, but she to those images, not in any bosom, but by virtue of an admirable force and power by which she is capable of adding or taking away something from them, sufficiens exhibite se singulis locis simul totam, quoniam tota sentit in singulis satis otendit se locorum spatiis non tenerí. 17 (XVII). Crux? 18. What should I say about that faculty by which the truth is understood and by which it resists with great vivacity these same images, figures obtained through the senses of the body, which are offered to it as if they were truth? Through it you can see that one is, for example, the authentic Carthage and another one that is created with the imagination, modifying it with great ease according to your whim. From it easily come innumerable worlds through which the imagination of Epicurus wandered without limit; and, so as not to dwell on it, from it also easily comes that land of light diffused through infinite spaces and the five dens of the race of darkness with its inhabitants, in which the fantasies of Manes dared to usurp for themselves the name of truth. What then is this faculty that discerns all this? No matter how big it is, it is bigger than all these things and you think of it without having to imagine it. Find spaces for it, if you can; spread it in places and lengthen it with the swelling of an infinite mass. If you think about it, you can't do it. Whatever occurs to you, with the same imagination you judge that it can be divided into parts and you make some larger, some smaller, as you like. And you also see that the very thing with which you judge such things is superior to them, licet eis et addere quodlibet et detrahere et in angustum eas contrahere et per immense expandere et ordinare, ut uelit, et perturbare et multiplicare et ad paucitatem singularitatemue redigere. 18 (XVIII). Quid iam de illa loquar potentia, qua intelleginie ueritas, qua istis ipsis, quae de corporis sensu haustae figurantur, imaginibus sese pro ueritate obponentibus magna uiuacitate resistitur? Qua uidetur aliam uerbi gratia ueram esse Karthaginem, aliam, quam cogitans fingit et pro suo arbitrio tota facilítate commutat, ex eadem uenire facilítate innumerable worlds, in quibus Epicuri cogitatio innumerabiliter peregrinata est, et, ne fines consecter, ex eadem uenire facilítate istam terram lucís per spatia infinite diffusam et quinqué antra gentís tenebrarum cum habitatoribus suis, in quibus Manichaei phantasmata ueritatis sibi nomen ausa sunt usurpare. Quid est ergo haec potentia, quae ista discernit? Profecto quantacumque sit, et his omnibus maior est et sine ulla tali rerum imaginatione cogitatur. Huic inueni spatia, si potes, hanc diffuse per locos, hanc infinitee molis tumore distende. Profecto si bene cogitas, non potes.
Quicquid enim tale tibi oceurrerit, judicas ipsa cogitatione secari posse per parte facisque ibi aliam partem

19. Therefore, if you experience that the soul, so often mutable, whether due to the turmoil of different desires, now because of the affections that yield to the abundance or scarcity of things, now because of the innumerable games of fantasies, now because it forgets and remembers, knows or is ignorant; If we experience that the soul, so mutable, as I said, by these and other similar movements, does not spread or extend through places, but surpasses all those spaces by the vivacity of its power, what can we think or how to value God himself, who, remaining untouched and immutable above all rational minds, gives to each one what is to be given? It is easier for the soul to speak to it than to see it, and it speaks of it the less the more purely it is able to see it. If, as the imaginations of the Manichaeans shout, it extends, limited locally on one part, while on the other it is infinite, then the parts that are in it, however large they may be, and its innumerable fragments could be measured, some as larger and others as smaller, according to the whim of the one who imagines them. For example, a two-foot part would be eight feet smaller than another ten-foot part. This necessarily happens to all natures that, extended through such spaces, cannot be found entire in all minorem, aliam maiorem, quantum placet; illud autem ipsum, quo ista indicas, cernís esse supra ista, non loci altitudine, sed potentiae dignitate. [216] 19 (XIX.21). Quare si animam totiens mutabilem siue uariarum uoluntatum turba siue adfectibus pro rerum copy uel inopia sese flectentibus siue ipsis innumerabilibus ludis phantasmatum siue obliuione et memoria siue doctrina et inperitia: si ergo animam, ut dixi, his atque huiusmodi motionibus totiens mutabilem Sentis non diffundi extendique per locos, sed omnia talia spatia potentiae uiuacitate superare, quid de ipso deo cogitandum aut existimandum est, qui supra omnes tationales mentes inconcussus atque incommutabilis manens tribuit, quod cuique tribuendum est? Quem facilius eloqui audet anima quam uidere, et quem mucho minus eloquitur, quanto sincerius uidere potuerit. Id enim necesse est bus contingat

20. However, perhaps it is not necessary to act in this way with carnal spirits, and it is preferable to descend to the level of the ideas of those who either do not dare or cannot reach with their minds the incorporeal and spiritual nature, so that they do not even reflect with their thoughts on their own thoughts, and do not notice that, without any space of place, they judge on the same local spaces. Let us descend, then, to the level of their ideas and ask them, next to which "part" and to which "side of that luminous and holy land" - as Manes says - "was the land of darkness." It says like this: "To one part and to one side", without indicating which part or which side, whether the right or the left. But, whichever one you choose, it is clearly clear that one cannot speak of one side except where there is a second side. On the other hand, where there are three or more sides, either the scope of a figure is conceived as limited everywhere, or, if it appears as unlimited in some of its parts, it is absolutely necessary that it have limits where we speak of sides. If on one side was the land of darkness, then say what it bordered on the land of light on the other side or sides. They don't say it; but when forced to do so, they affirm that the remaining sides of what they call the land of light are infinite, or naturis, quae per talia spatia diffusae ubique totae esse non possunt, quod in ipsa anima non inuenítur et ab eis, qui haecconsiderare non ualent, deformiter de illa et turpiter creditur. 20 (XX.22). Verumtamen cum carnalibus animis fortasse non sic agendum est, sed descendendum est potius ad eorum cogitationes, qui naturam incorpoream et spiritalem cogitando persequi uel non audent uel nondum ualent, ita ut nec ipsam cogitationem suam eadem cogitatione considerent et inueniant eam nullo locorum spatio de ipsis locorum spatis iudicantem. [217] Descendamus ergo ad eorum sensus et quaeramus ab eis, "iuxta" quam "partem" aut auxta quod "latus", sicut Manichaeus dicit, "inlustris illius ac sanctae terrae erat tenebrarum terra." Dicit enim: «Iuxta unam partem ac latus», nec dicit, quam partem uel quod latus, dextrum an sinistrum. Sed quodlibet eligant, illud certe manifestum est non dici unum latus, nisi ubi est alterum latus. Vbi autem uel tria uel plura sunt latera, aut figurae ambitus intellegitur undique terminatus aut, si ex aliqua parte in inmensum patet, ex iis tamen, quae latera dicuntur, necesse est finiatur.
Dicant ergo, ex alio latere uel ex aliis lateribus quid adiungebatur terrae lucis, si ex uno latere erat gens

If, on the other hand, we say "next to a nose" or "next to a navel," both learned and unlearned will laugh at us, since there is only one and one. others, thrown off the path by I don't know what blindness, that only the land of darkness had been or was corporeal, while it was necessary to believe that what you call the land of light was incorporeal and spiritual? And so that it does not appear that the land of darkness is simple compared to that of light, which is double, they still limit it on two sides. With this example you can see what was said more easily: think of a loaf of bread made with four parts in the shape of a cross, three of which were white and one black. Now remove all distinction from the three white parts and imagine them infinite in all three directions: up, down and back. This is what they believe is the land of light. The other room, black, imagine it infinite downwards and backwards, but having an immense void above it: this is what they think the land of darkness is like. These things are revealed, as if they were secrets, to those who pay close attention and investigate eagerly.

22. However, if this is so, it follows that the land of darkness is touched by the land of light on two sides; and if he touches it on two sides, it also touches the other on two sides. Indeed, "on one side was the land of darkness." Then it also appears how ugly the shape of the land of light is: like that of a hoof split by a certain black wedge that narrows downwards, limited only by the place where it is split, open and exposed from above, with the void intervening. All space above the surface of the land of darkness is infinite. Furthermore, how much better the shape of the land of darkness turns out to be! If she cleaves, the other is cleaved; If she enters, the other opens; She does not leave any empty space in herself, the other is only not hollow at the bottom, where the enemy wedge fills it. Thus, ignorant and avaricious men, giving greater honor to the multitude of parts than to unity, to the point of attributing six parts to the land of light, three downwards and three upwards, preferred that the land of light be penetrated, rather than it being the one that penetrated the other. With such a figuration, although they deny that it is mixed, they cannot deny that it has been penetrated. 22 (XXII). Verumtamen si ita est, adparet terram tenebrarum a terra lucis duobus lateribus tangi; et utique si duobus tangitur, duobus etiam tangit. "Certe iuxta unum latus erat terra tenebrarum." (24). Deinde quam foeda figura terrae lucis adparet, tamquam fissa úngula nigro quodam cuneo subter artato, illac tantum finita, qua finditur, hians etiam et patens desuper interposito inani, quicquid a surface terrae tenebrarum sursum uersus inmensum est. Quam deinde melior ipsius terrae tenebrarum figura ostenditur, si quidem illa findit, haec finditur; illa inseritur, haec interpatet: illa in se nulli inanítati dat locum, haec ab inferiore tantum parte laxa non est, qua hostili cuneo subinpletur. Indocti ergo homines et auari cum maiorem honorem tribuunt multitudini partium quam unitati, ut sex parts darent terrae lucis, tres deorsum uersus, tres sursum uersus, maluerunt penetran terram lucis quam penetrare. Tali (189) enim figura etsi conmixtam negant, penetratam tamen negare non possunt. In the writings of Augustine the image of the cuneus had already appeared in the work The True Religion 49,96 and will appear again in Faust IV 2.

Reply to the letter called "of the Foundation" THE NUMBER OF NATURES IN THE IMAGINATION OF MANES

24. Since I read: "God the Father and his kingdoms founded on the lucid and blessed earth," I want to be told if the Father, his kingdoms and the earth are of the same substance. If this is so, that wedge of the race of darkness does not split and penetrate - which would be enormously shameful due to its ineffable deformity - another nature that would be like the body of God, but rather it would split and penetrate precisely the very nature of God. I beg you to think about these things, since you are men. I beg you: think of them and flee from them; uproot and expel from your faith the sacrilege of such ghosts, tearing, if possible, your hearts. Or are you going to say that those three realities are not of one and identical nature, but that the Father is of one, the kingdoms of another and the earth of another, so that each of these three realities has its nature and substances distinct and ordered according to the degrees of being? If this is so, Manes must have proclaimed not two, but four natures. If, on the contrary, the Father and his kingdoms have a single nature, and the earth another, he had to have spoken of three. Or, if he preferred to speak of two because the land of darkness does not belong to God, I ask how the land of light belongs to God. For if it has a different nature, and God did not generate it or make it, it does not belong to him and its kingdoms are located in another foreign realm. Or if they belong to him because of their proximity, the land of darkness must also belong to him 24 (XXIV.26). Deinde uolo mihi dicatur, quoniam lego deum patrem et supra lucidam beatamque terram fundata regna eius, uttum [222] unius et eiusdem substantiae atque naturae sint et pater et regna eius et terra. Quod si ita est, iam non quasi aliam naturam, quod quasi corpus sit dei, cuneus ille gentis tenebrarum diffindit et penetrat —quod quidem ipsum esset ineffabili deformitate turpissimum— sed ipsam omnino naturam dei cuneus ille terrae tenebrarum diffindit et penetrat. Rogo, cogitate ista, homines estis, rogo, cogitate ista et fugite taliumque phantasmatum sacrilegia dilaniatis, si fieri potest, pectoribus de fide uestra eradicate atque propellite. Quod si uerum est, non duas, sed quattuor naturas Manichaeus praedicare debuerat.
Si autem unam naturam habet pater et regna, terra uero sola diuersam, tres naturae fuerant praedicandae. Aut si propterea duas dicere maluit, quia terra tenebrarum non pertinet

25. Therefore, if you are convinced that the almighty God can do some good out of nothing, come to the Catholic Church and learn that all natures, made and created by God, ordered according to the degrees of being from the highest to the lowest, are all good, but some better than others, and all of them made from nothing, since the divine craftsman works with his power, so to speak, through his wisdom, so that it may be what he It was not and as far as it is, it is good; and, on the contrary, insofar as it is deficient, it shows that it was not begotten by God, but made by him out of nothing. All you have to do is confess that God made the land of light out of nothing, but you don't want to believe that. Quare si uobis iam persuadetur posse aliquid boni omnipotentem deum de níhilo faceré, uenite in catholicam et discite omnes naturas, quas fecit et condidit deus, excellentiae gradíbus ordinatas a summis usque ad Ínfimas, omnes bonas, sed alias aliis esse potiores, easque factas esse de nihilo, cum deus artífex per sapientiam suam potentialiter, ut ita dicam, operaretur, ut posset esse, quod non erat, et in quantum esset, bonum esset; in quantum autem deficeret, se non de deo genitum, sed ab ipso de nihilo factum ostenderet.

So, by taking away its beauty and turning it from straight to crooked, so that concord disappears where there was concord and there is disharmony where there was concord, is it perhaps deprived of any substance? Learn that substance is not an evil, but that, just as a body that changes its shape for the worse loses its beauty or, more precisely, it diminishes and what was previously called beautiful is called ugly and a body that was previously pleasant is displeased, so also the beauty of the right will present in the soul, a beauty by which it lives piously and justly, is lost when that will changes for the worse. 27. What should I do with the extremely miserable souls lost by error and chained by custom? These men do not know what they say when they say such things, because they do not pay attention. I beseech you: no one urges you, no one urges you to combat, no one insults you for past errors, except for those who have not personally experienced divine mercy. To avoid error, let us only worry that it will ever come to an end. Look a little, without animosity or bitterness. We are all men; We do not hate ourselves, but we hate errors and falsehoods. I beg you, pay a little attention. The God of mercies helps those who look and turns on the inner light of those who seek the truth. Well, what can we understand if we do not understand that what is straight is better than what is crooked? 28. The text continues: "In that land lived igneous bodies, that is, a pestiferous species." By saying "they inhabited" he certainly wants it to be understood that they are living beings. But so as not to give the impression that my reproach is based only on the term, let us look at how he distributes all the inhabitants of that land into five classes of living beings: «Here existed infinite darkness, springing from nature itself, immense and with its own offspring. Beyond them were the muddy and murky waters with terram, in cuius lateris rectitudine inuenio, quantum ad corpus adtinet, non paruae pulchritudinis bonum, [228] et ab omnipotent atque optimal deo eam uult esse penitus alienam, cum id ipsum bonum, quod in illa inuenimus, cui alü tribuendum sit nisi auctori bonorum omnium, non inueniamus? Sed malum erat, inquit, etiam illud latus. Puta malum esse: deterius esset certe, si non rectum, sed distortum esset. Quomodo est igitur summum malum, quo potest aliquid cogitan deterius? Deinde necesse est aliquid boni sit, quo carendo fit res quaecumque deterioration; carendo autem rectitudine ieront latus illud deterius: inest ergo illi boni aliquid, rectitudo. Et numquam mihi dices, unde inest, nisi ad eum te contuleris, a quo siue magna siue pama, omnia tatnen bona esse fateamur. Sed iam a lateris huius consideratione transeamus ad alia. 28 (XXVHIJ1). "Habitabant, inquit, in illa terra ignea corpora, genera scilicet pestifera." Cum dicit «habitabant», animata utique atque uiuentia uult intellegi. Sed ne de uerbo slander uelle uideamur, adtendamus istos omnes habitatores terrae illius, quemadmodum in quinqué genera uiua distribuat. «Hic infinitee, inquit, tenebrae ex eadem manantes natura inaestimabiles cum propriis fetibus; ultra quas werent aquae caenosae ac turbidae cum suis inhabitatoribus; quarum interius

its inhabitants; within them horrible and impetuous winds with their own prince and parents. Within, in turn, was the region of fire, incorruptible, with its leaders and nations. Likewise, further within, a race full of darkness and smoke, in which dwelt the prince and chief of all, having at his side innumerable other princes, of which he was the mind and origin. These were the five natures of the pestiferous earth. We consider that these five natures are like parts of a single nature which they call pestiferous earth. They are the following: darkness, waters, winds, fire, smoke. He orders these five natures in such a way that the darkness, by which he began to count, is exterior to all the others. Inside them he places the waters; within the waters the winds; within the winds the fire and within the fire the smoke. Each of these five natures also had their respective classes of inhabitants; There were five, therefore. I ask, then, if in those five natures there was a single class of inhabitants, or were they diverse as the natures were diverse. They answer that they were diverse, and in other books they teach that the darkness contained the serpents, the waters the natal animals, such as fish; the winds are volatile, as are the birds; fire to quadrupeds, such as horses, lions and others of the same species; smoke to bipeds, such as men 49. uenti horribiles et uehementes cum suo principe et genitoribus. Rursum regio ignea et corruptibilis cum suis ducibus et nationibus. 29. Who then established this order? Who distributed and distinguished the different classes? Who gave them the number, the quality, the forms and the life? All these realities are good in themselves and no one can be found who has given them to each nature other than God, the author of all good things. In fact, they do not describe it as if it were chaos, nor in the way in which poets usually refer to a certain formless matter without external form, without quality, without measure, without number and weight, without order or distinction: I don't know what is confusing and lacking absolutely any quality - which is why certain Greek doctors call it axoiov 50 -. No, this is not how the Manichaeans strive to make understood what they call the land of darkness; but in a completely distant and different way. They associate and align one side to the other, which is not only diverse, but also the opposite. They enumerate five natures, they distinguish them, they order them, they state the qualities that are their own and they do not even allow them to be sterile and infertile; Rather, they fill them with their own inhabitants and assign appropriate and comfortable forms to those inhabitants. And, what surpasses everything else, they grant them life. To enumerate so many goods and proclaim them alien to God, the author of all goods, is equivalent to not recognizing in things the great good of order, nor in themselves the great evil of error 51. 29 (XXIXJ2). Quis igitur is this ordinauit? Quis distribuit atque disún(195)xit? Quis numerum, qualitatem, forma, uitam dedit? Haec enim omnia per se ipsa bona sunt nec inuenitur, unde cuique naturae nisi ab omnium bonorum deo auctore tribuantur. Non enim sicut chaos describere, uel quo modo insinuare etiam poete solent informam quandam materiem sine specie, sine qualitate, sine mensuris, sine numero et pondere, sine ordine ac distinctione confusum nescio quid atque omnino expers omni qualitate —unde iliud quidam doctors graeci á-rroiov uocant—, non ergo sic isti hanc quam uocant terram tenebra[230] rum insinuare conantur, sed omnino aliter longeque diuerse atque contrarié latus lateri adiungunt atque conliniant: naturas quinqué numerant, distingunt, ordinant, qualitatibus propriis enuntiant nec eas desertas infecundasque esse permittunt, sed suis inhabitatoribus conplent eisque ipsis congruous forms et suis habitationibus adcommodatas adtribuunt et quod antecellit omnibus, uitam.

30. It continues: "But these species that inhabited those five natures were cruel and pestiferous." As if I had praised cruelty and pestilence in them! Consider that I reproach you for what you reproach as evils in them; Praise with me the good things that you yourself mention in them: thus you will realize that you want to make goods mixed with evil pass off as the supreme and supreme evil. I reproach with you the pestilence that is there, you praise with me the health; In fact, those species could not have been generated or nurtured, nor populated that land if they had not enjoyed some health. I reproach you for the darkness present there; Praise with me his fruitfulness. You call the darkness "immense", but you add: "with its own offspring", although the darkness is not corporeal and this whole name indicates nothing other than the absence of light, just as nakedness is a lack of clothing and emptiness is a deprivation of bodily plenitude. And that is why darkness could not generate anything, even though the earth, being dark, that is, lacking all light, could have generated something. But for now, let's skip this. When children are born, there are conditions suitable for health, and a harmony regulated by numbers orders and constitutes unity the members of those who are born, mutually accommodating each other with peace, the fruit of just proportion. Who does not understand that in all this I30 (XXX.33). "Sed ista, inquit, genera quinqué illas naturas inhabitantia saeua erant atque pestifera." Quasi ego in eis saeuitiam pestemque laudauerim. Ecce, ego tecum uitupero, quae in illis mala esse criminaris, lauda tu mecum, quae in illis bona ipse commemoras: ita uidebis bona malis permixta te uelle constituere pro summo et extreme malo. Vitupero ibi tecum pestem, lauda ibi mecum salutem; non enim genera illa uel gigni uel nutriri uel inhabitare illam terram sine aliqua salute potuissent. Vitupero ibi tecum tenebras, lauda ibi mecum fecunditatem; tenebras enim dicis "inaestimabiles" et addis tamen "cum propriis fetibus", quamquam tenebrae non sunt corporeae totumque hoc nomen lucis absentia est, sicut nuditas carere uestitu et inanitas uacare corporis plenitudine; ac propterea tenebrae nihil gignere potuerunt, quamuis terra potuerit tenebrosa, id est carens luz aliquid gignere. Sed interim hoc omittamus.

Fetus tamen ubi [231] exoriuntur, et temperamentum est aptum saluti et quaedam concordia numerosa ordinat atque in unitatem coaedificat membra nascentium sibimet inuicem moderationis pace congruentia. Pray more praise than rebuke darkness? There I reproach you for the disturbed silt of the waters; Praise there with me the form, the quality of the waters, the limbs adapted for swimming of its inhabitants, the life that contains and governs the body and all the conditions adapted to the health of each class. No matter how much you reproach those muddy and murky waters, for the very fact of saying that these waters are such that they can generate and contain their own animate beings, you cannot take away from them the form that any body possesses or the similarity of its parts by which they find form and peace united in the same quality, for if you take it away, there will no longer be any body. If you are a man, you will notice that all these things are worthy of praise. And however much you exaggerate the cruelty of those inhabitants and the impetus with which they tear and devastate each other, you do not deprive them of the harmonious limits of their forms by which each body is at peace with itself by virtue of the adjustment of its members, nor the conditions of health, nor the government by which the soul maintains the parts of the body in the unity of friendship. If you look at all these things with human sense, you see that this is more worthy of praise than what displeases you in them is reproach. I revile there with you the horror of the winds, you praise there with me their nature, which allows us to breathe and nourish ourselves, and equally the form of the body that extends and diffuses through the harmony of its parts. Also pay attention to other things that force you to praise his nature? This one had a soul and a body; she giving life to him, he animated by the breath of life; she ruling, he obeying; she going in front, he behind; she maintaining the body, he not dissolving; she moving her body in the harmony that is her own, he remaining stable by the harmonious union of his members. Do you not feel moved to praise the peace in order or the order in peace present in this one prince? And what I have said about one, it is possible to understand it about all the rest. "But he was also fierce and cruel towards others." It is not this that I praise, but those goods so great that you do not want to consider. Anyone who has recklessly believed Manes, if, at least once warned, he looks and considers these things, he will know without a doubt that, when he speaks of these natures, he speaks of certain goods, but not of supreme and uncreated goods, which is God, the one Trinity, nor of those created that have been ordained in the highest, such as the holy angels and the fully blessed powers, but of insignificant and ordered goods in the lowest part of the scale of the beings, according to their own category. 32. Having wanted to order in his imagination the natures of the race of darkness as if they were the same as those he has known here, Manes is clearly convicted of error. First of all, because darkness cannot engender anything, as I have already said. "But," he says, "that darkness was not like what you know here." So, how do you know what you're telling me? Do you, evil charlatan who promise doctrine, force me to believe? Suppose I believe. In any case, I believe that if they did not have some form as this darkness does not have, they could have engendered nothing; If, on the other hand, they had it, they were better. You, however, by saying that they were not like these, want people to think that they were worse. You could also say that silence, which is to the ear the same as darkness to the eyes, engendered there some animals sornatantia, uolantia, quadrupedia, bipedia: in quibus ómnibus exceptis tenebris, quae, ut dixi, nihil sunt aliud quam lucís absentia, quae oculis non uidendo discernuntur —sicut silentium auribus non audiendo— non quia tenebrae sunt aliquid, sed quia lux non est —sicut non quia silentium est aliquid, sed quia sonus non est— exceptis ergo tenebris in hac enumeratione ceterae naturae sunt et ómnibusnotae, quarum specíem, quia, in quantumcumque est, laudabílís et bona est, nemo prudens abalienat ab auctore omnium bonorum deo. 32 (XXXII.35). Nam Ule Manichaeus, sicut uoluit naturas, quas hic didicit, ordinare in phantasmatibus suis uelut in gente tenebrarum, omnino falsus esse conuincirur. Primo quia tenebrae nihil possunt gignere, ut dictum est. Sed non, inquit, such [2341 erant ilke tenebrae, duales hic nosti. Vnde ergo me illis twelves? An forte tam uerbosus doctrinae Dollicitator cogis, ut credam? Sed fac me credere. Illud tamen scio. quod si non habebant aliquam speciem, sicut istae non habent, nihil generare potuerunt; si autem habebant, meliores erant. Secondly, it was easy for him to notice what is typical of animals that swim in water and transfer it to those ghosts. In the same way he did the same with those that fly in the winds, since the force of this denser air in which birds fly is called wind; On the other hand, I don't know how it could have occurred to him to put the quadrupeds in the fire. I'm not just saying it; but he lacked attention and erred too much. The reason usually given is that quadrupeds are voracious and experience great ardor when mating.
