They have wings and sometimes fly, the truth is that they do not belong to the smoke, according to their distribution. As for the ardor during mating, I think that Manes saw the horses neighing and throwing themselves at their females even with the bit in their mouths. But, wanting to quickly write down what he has seen, he does not pay attention to the wall sparrow compared to which any stallion horse is made of ice. When asked why Manes established the bipeds in the smoke, they respond that the biped species tends to exalt itself and is arrogant. From here, therefore, they say that men come from their origin. And since the smoke rises into the air like an inflated balloon, it is not without reason that they noticed its similarity to the arrogant. This observation must have been enough to show some similarity of what the proud man is, either to form or to understand the comparison, but without going from there to believe that bipedal animals were born in smoke and from smoke. In truth, they must also have been born in the dust because it frequently rises to the sky with no less breadth and height. And also in fog, because most of the time it is exhaled by the earth in such a way that those who see it from a distance are not sure if it is smoke or fog. Finally, why has the argument taken from the ability to inhabit the waters and winds been passed on to the inhabitants themselves? Because we see that those who swim live in the waters and those who fly live in the winds. On the contrary, how did the fire and smoke not terrify that lying man, until he felt ashamed of placing such inhabitants in them? I couldn't put anything more absurd. Indeed, fire [235] ad ignem certe secundum eius distinctionem non pertinent. Quod autem adtinet ad feruorem concubitus, credo eum animaduertisse hinnientes equos et saepe morsis frenis raptos in feminas: quod animaduersum dum uult cyto scríbere, non adtendit passerem parietinum, in cuius conparatione quiuis admissarius frigidissimus inuenitur. Bipedes uero in fumo cum ab eis quaeritur quare ordinauerit, respondert elatum et superbum esse bipedum genus; hinc enim nomines trahere originem dicunt; et quoniam fumus globosus et quasi tumidus in auras erigitur, superbis esse similem non absurde adtenderunt. Quae animaduersio suificere debuit ad aliquam similarityinem dandam de superbis hominibus, siue allegoriam uel formadam uel intellegendam, non tamen, ut ideo bipedes animantes in fumo et de fumo nati esse credantur.

Nam et in puluere nasci debuerunt, quia saepe non minore ambitu et elatione surgit in caelum; et in nebulis, quia plerumque de terra ita exhalantur, ut longe intuentibus incertum etiam faciant, fumusne an nebulae sint. Postremo cur in aquis et uentis de habitandi patientia ad habitatores ductum est argumentum? Qui uidemus et natantia in aquis et uolantia in uentis uiuere. shame to repeat; but in such a way that he tried to separate it from that God whom he confesses as the author of all good things. He did not see such goods, focusing only on what he disliked. It is the case of someone who, terrified by the roar of a lion, and seeing it drag and destroy the bodies of the beasts and men it had captured, found himself overcome with a childlike weakness and with so much fear in his soul that, considering only its ferocity and cruelty, and totally disregarding the other things it possesses and overlooking the nature of that animated being, he cried out that it was not only an evil, but a great evil, with exaggeration proportionate to his fear. If, on the other hand, he saw a tamed lion carrying, its ferocity already tamed, especially if it had never terrified him before, he would stand calmly and without fear to contemplate and praise its beauty. In this regard I will not say more than what particularly concerns this matter, namely: that it may happen that some nature is annoying for some reason and from there arises aversion towards all of it, although it is clear that the form of a living and true beast is much better, even when it instills terror in the jungle, than that of another, pure imitation and simulation, when it is praised painted on a mural. Perhaps Manes will not deceive us with this error nor make us blind to contemplate the beauty of nature, when he reviles some things in them in such a way that forces us to feel total displeasure in the face of what he cannot revile in its entirety. 35. Who will doubt that all that we call evil is nothing other than corruption? Certainly the different evils can be designated with different terms, but the evil of all things in which one can notice any is corruption. But the corruption of a wise soul is called ignorance; the corruption of the prudent soul, imprudence; the corruption of the just soul, injustice; the corruption of the strong, weakness; the corruption of that which is in stillness and tranquillity, ambition or fear or sadness or boasting; then, the corruption of the health of an animated body, pain and disease; corruption of forces, fatigue; that of rest, fatigue. The corruption of beauty in a single body, ugliness; that of righteousness, crookedness; that of order, perversity; that of integrity, division, fracture or diminution. It is a long and difficult thing to mention by name all the corruptions of these things that I have mentioned and of innumerable others, since many that are found in the body can also be found in the soul. There are countless things in which corruption is given a specific name. However, it is already easy to see that corruption does not harm anything, except as

EVIL AND CORRUPTION
Reply to the letter called "of the Foundation"

destroys the natural state, and that, therefore, it is not a nature, but something against nature. And if there is no other evil in things than corruption, and corruption is not a nature, no nature is truly an evil. If perhaps you are not able to understand this, consider that everything that is corrupted is diminished in some good, since if it were not corrupted, it would be incorrupt; If, on the contrary, it could not be corrupted at all, it would be incorruptible. It is necessary, however, that if corruption is an evil, both incorruption and incorruptibility be a good. But now the problem about incorruptible nature does not arise; We deal with natures that can be corrupted. These, while they are uncorrupted, can be called incorrupt, but not incorruptible. In fact, only that which not only cannot be corrupted, but also cannot be corrupted in any of its parts, is properly called incorruptible. Therefore, any natures that remain incorrupt, although they can be corrupted, when they begin to suffer corruption, by that very fact they are diminished in that good for which they were incorrupt, a certainly great good, because corruption is a great evil. And as long as corruption can increase in them, so long is also the time in which they possess the good in which it can decrease. Consequently, those natures which, according to the imagination of Manes, existed in the land of darkness, either could be corrupted or could not; If they could not, they were incorruptible, a good greater than the

which there is no other; If they could, they either suffered corruption or they did not suffer it; If they did not suffer it, they remained uncorrupted, which we see cannot be affirmed without being an object of praise; If, on the contrary, they suffered it, they saw that their great good was diminished. If they decreased in those assets, they possessed an asset that decreased them. And, if they had a good, those natures were not the ultimate evil, and the entire Manichean fable turns out to be a falsehood.

Only God is extremely good

They are words, but the one who teaches is the only true teacher, the same incorruptible truth, the only inner teacher s4. He also became an external teacher to call us from the external to the internal, and taking the form of a servant, he deigned to appear humble to those who were lying, so that, when they rose, their sublimity would be shown to them. Let us supplicate in his name and, imploring the mercy of the Father through his mediation, let us investigate these things. Those who ask where corruption comes from can be answered very briefly at the outset, saying: it comes from the fact that these natures that can be corrupted have not been engendered by God, but have been made by him out of nothing. Since higher reason has shown them to be good, no one can rightly say: "God should not have made these things good"; If, on the contrary, he says: "I must have done them extremely good," he must understand that the greatest good is the one who did these good things.

Some Catholics reported what had happened to Augustine, who took advantage of the opportunity to take him at his word and challenge him to a public debate and, if he did not accept, invite him to leave the city. Letter 79 is understood in this context: "As you see, I urge you in the name of Christ: if you are willing, face the difficulty to which your predecessor Fortunatus succumbed... and if you are not willing, leave here." Fortunatus had succumbed to the argument that Nebridius had already used to remove Augustine from Manichaeism, and this will be the weapon that Augustine will use to corner Felix as well. Those who brought him the letter probably had a first meeting with him, not as solemn of course as those of the following days. This is how Possidius's data that speaks of two or three discussions (Life 16) can be explained, that is, depending on whether this first one is included or not. This time the debate took place on Augustine's own ground, in the Catholic Basilica Pacis (Felix II 1), in the presence of a Catholic audience, although some hidden Manichaeans were not missing. Augustine feels himself invested not only with religious power, but also in a certain way with civil power. At least Felix sees it that way (Felix I 12). This is a defendant and defeat in the debate, taken by notaries, could mean for him to fall victim to his own words, according to which he was willing to be burned with his books, if any error was found in them. This different personal situation of the protagonists partly explains the progress of the debate. Félix has not gone to him voluntarily, as Agustín ironically indicates, but forced by some inopportune statements. He is terrified of the consequences that may arise for him from the outcome of the debate. Without a doubt he knew that he could not impose himself on Augustine in dialectical force, and even less so on his terrain, and with a Catholic audience (I 15). That's why he chooses to dodge the questions, to "get out of the way," preferring to ask the counter-question rather than answer what he is being asked about, which bothers Agustín 6.

That once he could not avoid the debate with the argument that he did not have his Scriptures that had been confiscated, since Augustine, as if foreseeing the objection, was prepared and brought to public light the Letter of ' See I 2.8.10.17.19; II 7.8-9.U44.

Fundamental, insisting that this text be discussed, undoubtedly because it was one of those requisitioned and because he had already refuted it, at least in part, in a specific work. In fact, the texts that Augustine reads to focus the debate on them are the same ones that he had refuted in his Reply to the Letter called the Fundament7. Félix tries, with whatever means his imagination dictates, to block the debate: according to him, the fear of sinning prevents him from responding (I 19); each one must limit himself to interpreting his own Scriptures without interfering in those of the other (I 17); he insists that the codices be given to him (I 14), first the Letter of the Foundation and then the Treasure (I 17); He claims to be forced, without freedom, oppressed by the strange force of a bishop and by the laws of the emperor (I 12); He asks for a deadline, first of three days and then of five, which Augustine grants him, but tying up the dots so that victory does not escape him: he demands that he declare that he is defeated if he flees (I 20). In the second session, always as a delaying tactic, he requests a new postponement, but relying on arguments that were obviously worthless, so it is not granted; Rather, you are instantly presented with the books you request and that you had "forgotten" to claim your time to consult. Felix's entire tactic loses strength as Augustine manages to focus the debate on his preferred terrain: the nature of God, and particularly the famous argument of Nebridius (Conf VII 2,3). The interventions, increasingly brief, corner Félix. Especially when Agustín threatens to be condemned along with Manes, Félix relents. Evidently the sentence had a different meaning for Manes and for him: for him it meant falling under imperial rule. Therefore, in order to preserve his life or at least his freedom, he had no other option than submission, at least apparent. Thus he agrees to Agustín's conditions and signs a condemnation of Manes, which in all probability has been dictated by Agustín himself, but a purely "material" signature. «The Manichean has simply agreed to lend himself to material gestures that do not tarnish his faith» 8. Such behavior is very far from having meant Felix's conversion, as Possidius interprets, based on the text of the debate, to which he explicitly refers (Life 16).

He might have been deceived by the cunning Félix, as he is called in the Revisions: versutior. Maybe he was a doctor of cunning. The work is rich in information. On the one hand, it allows us to know the air of insecurity and risk in which the heretics moved and the balances they had to make to save freedom or life, without betraying their faith. This even if the persecution was not always current or the laws issued against them were dormant. The writing does not provide us with special data about Augustine, other than his dialectical preparation for this type of debate, where one must not only be attentive to the movement of ideas, but also to the tactics of the opponent. The patience, sometimes on the verge of losing it, that he shows in the face of Félix's departures and his continued focus again and again on what was personally convenient for him is still notable. The most information, obviously, is given to us about Manichaeism. If in the debate with Fortunato Manes or his writings were not mentioned once, here they are. Felix is ​​not afraid to quote his "theologian" trying to show the identity between his teaching and that of Christ or Paul (n.II 2). We hear in it about the five "authors" (the works of Manes) and two of them are nominally mentioned: the Letter of the Foundation, from which he quotes five fragments 9, all known from other works, with the exception of a phrase from one 10, and the Treasury from which he gives a quote (II 5), also already known from other sources. Important is Felix's recourse to Scripture. It is worth highlighting in this regard that he cites three texts from the Old Testament; two of them do not cause surprise because they are taken directly from the New Testament n, but the third does, an explicit quote from Genesis, although adapted to its dogma '2. Perhaps it was an extreme resource to capture the sympathy of a Catholic public. Regarding Manichean dogmatics, Felix makes explicit mention of the three times (n.I 6.9.10.12), the great teaching of Manes that makes him worthy of being considered the Paraclete. Following the line of Fortunatus, undoubtedly common in the sect, he makes a strong defense of dualism, relying on texts from the New Testament (II 2: Mt 7,17; 13,27-28; 25,34.41) and on the work of redemption (II 10). The conception of God is expressed above all in the quotes from the Letter of the Foundation

It also informs us about the average time thanks to the text of the same Charter of the Foundation; the initial combat is presented as an initiative of the Father to prevent evil; The calamity of the souls, part of the divine substance (II 20), is temporary, since they will return to the lucid earth; His fall is what explains the coming of Christ (I 19; II 10.16). The very important work of Christ, whose crucifixion Felix speaks, although not of his birth and resurrection; His function as liberator and purifier (II 10.21), and provider of salutary science (II 10) is completed by that of Manes whose magisterial work he accentuates, having provided definitive knowledge (I 2). He is the Paraclete, since the Holy Spirit speaks in him (I 6.9). At the basis of this soteriology is the Manichean conception of sin: involuntary sin, certainly, but which does not exclude all responsibility on the part of the soul, insofar as it may be negligent, according to the testimony of the Treasury (II 5). Regarding the end time, Felix strongly contests Augustine's interpretation of the doctrine of Manes, that is, of the condemnation of a part of God (11 16), alarming that it is not a condemnation, but rather an assignment of another function. At the same time he refutes the accusation of cruelty against the Manichaean God, since in that case the cruelty of Christ would be even greater (ll 7.8). Augustine, for his part, frequently brings up the "globe" to which the souls that do not acquire total purification at the end of time will be attached (II 8.15.16.22). When writing the Reviews there is nothing to review; He limits himself to giving information about the circumstances of the debate and about his interlocutor, but he adds something worth taking into account. He indicates that in the second of the books the free will of the will to do both evil and good was discussed, but not about Christian grace, because the needs of the debate did not lead him to do so. It is a fact that informs us more about the motivations he had when writing the Reviews than about the writing at hand. He was interested in coming forward to confront the accusations of the Pelagians, according to which the positions they defended then were the same ones that Augustine had defended against the Manichaeans. He, he says, spoke there

Aug. dixit: Adparuit te provere non potuisse apostolum Christi esse We must not forget that the Emperor Constantine made the bishops officials of the State and, to a certain extent, they enjoyed imperial power. The Manichaeans, considered heretics, fell under general antiheretical legislation. On the other hand, they suffered the rigors of legislation specifically directed against them. See Coa. Teod XVI 5. Manes is an apostle of Christ. I will briefly explain why you couldn't try it. You said that you proved that Manes was an apostle of Christ from the promise of Christ himself to send the Holy Spirit Paraclete; Not finding when the one promised by Christ came, you believed it was Manes himself. But when I proved by the holy, ecclesiastical, canonical Scriptures, the moment in which the Holy Spirit came manifestly, whose coming Christ the Lord promised, you went on to say that you should be shown what he had taught and whether he had destroyed the doctrine of Manes. It was answered that Manes had lived after the apostles and that they preached their doctrine before Manes was born; I also told you that one of the apostles, Paul, had prophesied through the Holy Spirit, present in all the apostles, about that doctrine of yours that was to appear, and that he called it the doctrine of lying demons. After having shown that what Paul said about that doctrine is found in what you profess, such as the prohibition of marriage 22 - for you say that all sexual relations, even with the wife, are fornication - and abstinence from foods created by God 23 - for I know that you call some of them impure, despite the fact that the Apostle himself continues to say: Every creature of God is good - by asking you at that point in the discussion to If you answered, you said that Manes taught you the beginning, the middle and the end, the course

of the sun and the moon and other similar things. I showed you that these things do not belong to the scope of Christian doctrine, but you responded that the apostle Paul himself had recognized that his knowledge was partial and his prophecy partial. I maintained that while we are in this life we ​​cannot know divine things, and that here we see through a mirror and in an image whereas then we will see face to face. Since you think that the apostle Paul had said that Manes would come to teach what he himself had not been able to, I asked you if it is not up to you, who claim to have received that same Spirit, to now see God face to face. Since you cannot see God face to face, it is clear that the apostle Paul was referring to that life of which John also says: Dearly beloved, we are children of God and it has not yet been revealed what we will be. We know, however, that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. After having said all this, you claimed that you were helpless before my strength. Such strength is not mine, but if I have any, it has been granted to me, to refute errors, by the one who is the strength of all his faithful and they boast of him with all their hearts. You also stated that the bishop's authority causes you terror, despite the fact that you are seeing how peacefully we are speaking, how calmly we discuss and how the people present do not do any violence to you or terrify you, but rather listen calmly, as befits Christians. You also said that you feared the laws of emperors. Whoever was filled with the Holy Spirit would not fear to suffer this because of the true

The text up to this point already appeared in Fund 11, with slight variations. Note the Trinitarian formulation in the text, although the following text does not mention "the Peace of God" that appears in other manuscripts. Note also the double function assigned to the Son, right hand of the light: to protect from the evil incursion and the snare of the world, and that assigned to the Spirit: to open hearts to see with one's own eyes one's own soul, in perfect harmony with the Gnostic system. Nor did Fund 11 notice anything strange or contrary to the Catholic faith in this text of Manes' letter. Certainly the words are ambiguous and can be accepted as a whole from both Manichean and Catholic dogmatics. What really should have surprised Augustine the most is the title "right hand of light" to designate the Son. It should not have escaped a former Manichaean like him.

Augustine: Pay attention now, so that you begin to know the error of that Scripture. Manes 59 affirms this: that those whom Christ condemns are not of him 60. The apostle Paul says: The prudence of the flesh is the enemy of God, since it is not and cannot be subject to the law of God. Paul also says: The God of this century blinded the minds of the unbelievers so that they would not contemplate the splendor of the gospel of Christ, who is the image of God. Paul himself also writes elsewhere: The thorn of my flesh was given to me, the angel of Satan, which buffets me day and night. Therefore I prayed to the Lord to take him away from me. Manes claims that it is someone other than God who fought against him. This is already proven by the fact that Christ has been crucified, and that all the apostles were crucified by the law of God. Listen now to how Manes himself, so misguided, so arrogant that, introducing another nature, he made himself equal to God and lowered God to himself 65, nevertheless confessed free will. In your Treasury, a book to which you have given such a name in order to deceive men, it speaks in the following way, as you also know: "Those who, due to their negligence, did not allow themselves to be purified at all from the stain of the aforementioned spirits, and hardly obeyed the divine commands in their entirety, and did not want to fully keep the law that was given to them by their liberator, nor govern themselves as was appropriate," etc. ^ You see how in these words with-

even those who speak without knowing what they are saying signify the existence of free will. For he who does not want to keep the law has it in his power to do so, if he wants. He did not say, "They could not," but "They would not." Not wanting to keep the law is not the result of coercion on the part of the race of darkness; Well, if they are coerced, it is not that they do not want to, but that they cannot; If, on the other hand, they do not want to, they are not coerced not to do it, but rather they do not want it of their own free will. The unwillingness that is in his will is certainly a sin, without proceeding from any necessity due to the race of darkness. Book II Blessed are the pure in heart because they will see God? But since only he to whom God grants it has access to it, it is therefore inaccessible by itself. Therefore, no one has access to it if God does not want them to have it. However, he to whom it is granted will have it. How, then, could that race of darkness have access to the abode of God, where is the inaccessible light to which no one has access except the one to whom God grants it? Or, if he had received from God the gift of access to it, he would not have given it to him to attack his kingdom, and he would have had nothing to fear. If, on the contrary, he had not given him the gift of being able to access, and he found himself safe in his kingdom, dwelling in the inaccessible light, what could he fear from the race of darkness to mix it with a part of himself, his substance, what he himself is, which would remain imprisoned, oppressed and defiled? This is a situation in which she would not only be miserably imprisoned, but would also be shamefully purified. Si autem donum tale non dederat, ut posset accesoré, securus in suo regno erat habitans inaccessibilem luzem, quid poterat de tenebrarum gente metuere, ut ei misceret partem suam, substantiam suam, hoc quod ipse est, ligandam, premendam, contaminandam. Vbi non solum miserabiliter teneretur, sed etiam turpiter purgaretur?

Vt enim purgetur inde, dicitis —quod audire nefas est, sed ad uos confun^O)dendos et forte saluandos tacere non possumus— ut purgetur inde pars dei, dicitis in ñaue lucís, quam solem appellatis, facientes inmriam creatori solis et ipsi soli, quem sic dicitis factum, ubi tanta turpitudo celebretur; dicitis enim [835] illic positum deum uirtutes suas conuertere in masculos ad inritandum concupiscentias daemonum feminarum et eosdem rursus conuertere in feminas ad inritandum concupiscentias daemonum masculorum, ut cum daemoniis iniciunt libidinem accensis in

directed towards the forms invented by God, their members relax and thus the part of God that was chained in them escapes 70. You have dared to believe such a great disgrace, such a great sacrilege and you do not hesitate to preach it. This is the means of your doctrine. And the end, what is it? What else, but that God could not purify everything? And since he could not, you affirm that he will make one as a covering for the race of darkness 71, so that there he will find eternal damnation 72 that which could not be purified and did nothing of its own will. Thus it turns out that your God, not real, but fiction, not present somewhere, but imagined in your heart, mixes a part of himself unhappily, purifies it shamefully and condemns it cruelly 73. Answer, then, to this and begin with what I said: Why did God mix a part of himself with what could in no way harm him? Or, if he could, how is he incorruptible? 8. Félix: You accuse Manes of being cruel for having said that; What shall we affirm of Christ who said: Go into eternal fire? 74 Augustine: He said that to sinners. Félix: Why haven't those sinners been purified? Agustín: Because they didn't want to. Félix: Did you say: "because they didn't want to"?

Agustín: That's what I said: "because they didn't want to." Félix: Why didn't they want to? Is there anyone who does not want to be cured? Is there anyone who does not want to be purified, enlightened? What sick person is there who does not want to achieve health? If what Manes says is cruel: that a part of God that could not be purified is tied to a globe, is it not cruel that Christ who had said: I have come for sinners, now sends those who bore his name to eternal fire? But I think they could not fulfill their mandates. If the first is cruel, this is more cruel; If it is cruel that God has not been able to purify them and has tied them to a balloon, it seems even more cruel that Christ has not been able to purify them and sends them to eternal fire. Tell me, Your Holiness, what you think about this cruelty. Agustín: If you had understood what I said, or confessed to having understood it—since by not having to respond you pretended not to have understood what is clear—you would not have said those things. I have already said and proven by divine Scriptures that free will exists; that God is the just judge of free will, who rewards the faithful and those who submit to him and want to be healed, and condemns the proud and impious. Therefore, as he came to heal sinners, he truly heals those who confess their sins, he heals those who repent. But no one repents of another's sin; On the contrary, if repentance is just and true - which is why the Lord Himself says: I did not come to call the righteous, but the sinners -

forma confictas a deo, relaxentur membra eorum, et sic euadat pars dei, quae ibi fuerit colligata. Hoc tantum obprobrium, hoc tantum sacrilegium credere ausi estis et praedicare non dubitatis. Haec sunt media doctrinae uestrae. Finis uero qui est? Quis, nisi quia non potuit deus totum purgare? Et quia non potuit, facturum eum dicitis uelut tectorium genti tenebrarum, ut ibi in aeternum damnetur, quod purgari non potuit et nihil sua sponte commisit. Ita fit, ut deus uester, non uerus, sed fictus, non alicubi constitutus, sed in corde uestro imaginatus, partem suam misceat infeliciter, purget turpiter, damnet crudeliter. Ad haec ergo respond et incipe ab illo, quod dixi: quare deus miscuit istam partem suam, cui nihil nocere poterat? aut si potuit, quomodo sit incorruptibilis. 8. Fel. dixit: Crudelem adseritis Manichaeum haec dicentem; from Christo quid dicimus, qui dixit: Ite in ignetn aeternum? (Mt 25,41). Aug. dixit: Peccatoribus hoc dixit. Fel. say: Isti peccatores quare non purgati sunt? Aug. dixit: Quia noluetunt. Fel. dixit: Quia noluerunt, hoc dixisti? In this regard, see General introduction, p.52. '72l See Manichean Eschatology in General Introduction, p.73ff and 148ff. The statement that such damnation is eternal is only found in the mouth of Augustine, never in the mouth of a Manichaean. Three adjectives that negatively qualify each of the three times of Manichean dogmatics. Augustine had accused the Manichean God of being cruel by eternally condemning a part of himself. Felix's entire intervention is an ad hominem argument, that is, he tries to show that Christ is more cruel from Catholic positions, since he condemns something that comes from him, rather than the Manichean God who condemns something foreign to his being, belonging to the kingdom of evil. On the other hand, if Christ came to save sinners and some are condemned, it is because he has failed.

Aug. dixit: Hoc dixi, quia noluerunt. Fel. dixit: Quare noluerunt? Est, qui non uult curari? Est, qui non uult purgari? Est, qui non uult illuminari? Quis infirmus est, qui non uult ad sanitatem uenire? Si crudele est, quod Manichaeus dicit, quia aliqua pars dei, quae se [836] purgare non potuit, in globo ligata est, hoc crudele non est, ut Christus, qui dixit: ego propter peccatores ueni, moda ad ignem aeternum illos mittat, cuius nomen portauerunt? Sed mandata, credo, non potuerunt conplere. Si hoc crudele est, crudelius est et illud; si illud crudelius est, quia deus illos non potuit purgare et globo ligauit, et id crudelius uidetur esse, quod Christus non potuit purgare, ad ignem aeternum mittere. Hoc mihi sanctitas tua exponat de ipsa crudelitate. Aug. dixit: Si ea, quae iam dixi, uel intellexisses uel te intellegere fatereris —fortassis enim non habendo quod dicas finxisti te non intellegere, quod apertum est— ista non díceres. Iam enim diximus et probauimus per diuinas scripturas esse liberum arbitrium; deum autem liberi arbitrii iustum iudicem, remuneratorem fidelium eique se subicientium et uolentium se sanari, damnatorem autem superborum et inpiorum. Quia ergo ad peccatores sanandos uenit, sanat utique peccata confessos, sanat paenitentes; neminem autem paenitet, cum alius peccauit, sed si est paenitentia iusta et uerax, unde et ipse dominus (541) dicit: Non

repentance - repentance itself indicates that it is not of another nature, but of our will, if perhaps we have sinned. In fact, if one repents of another's sin, this repentance is not that of the wise, but that of the insane. But, according to you, there are no sinners, since the race of darkness does not sin because it acts according to its nature; The nature of light does not sin because what it does, it does by force. You do not find, then, any sin that God has to condemn; You find no sin that can be healed by repentance. Now, if there is repentance, there is also guilt; If there is guilt there is equally will; If there is a will in sin, there is no nature that coerces 75. But if those who cannot do what they desire suffer some weakness—which is why the Apostle says: I see another law in my members that opposes the law of my mind and captivates me in the law of sin that resides in my members—it is clear that it is not a propagation of the first sin and bad habit. Today men create customs by their free will; but once they have created it, they do not defeat it easily. They personally are the cause of a law opposite to themselves dwelling in their members 7 Ó. But those who conceive the fear of God and by their free will submit to be healed by the extraordinary doctor, and just like a good merciful creator healer, they are healed by the humility of confession and penitence. On the other hand, the so-

drunk, either proclaiming themselves righteous or affirming that it is not they who sin, but that something else sins in them and another nature uses them to sin, they become incurable due to their own pride and experience the just punishment of God, who resists the proud while giving his grace to the humble. These words are not unworthy of God: Go into eternal fire, addressed to those who by their free will rejected His mercy, nor these others: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom, addressed to those who by free will accepted the faith, confessed their own sins, did penance, felt displeasure with themselves for what they were and showed their pleasure to God for how He had done them. You, therefore, answer once and for all what I asked you. It's time for me to get it from you, so as not to waste time. If nothing could harm God, why did he send us here? If something could harm you, God is not incorruptible. 9. Felix: If nothing could harm God, why did he send his Son here? Agustín: Consider how you do nothing but ask, without wanting to answer what is being asked of you. Listen to the answer to what you asked, but don't forget that you don't answer my questions, while I answer yours. Nothing can harm God; However, he sent his Son to put on flesh, to manifest himself to men, to heal sinners, to suffer for us in the flesh that he took for us. In fact, in his nature he could not suffer anything, since

ueni uocare iustos, sed peccatores in paenitentiam (Mt 9,13), ipsa paenitentia indicat non alienae esse naturae, sed uoluntatis nostrae, si quid forte peccamus. Nam si alio peccante alium paenitet, non est ista prudens, sed insana paenitentia. Secundum uos autem nulla peccata sunt. Gens enim tenebrarum non peccat, quia suam naturam facit; natura lucis non peccat, quia quod facit, faceré cogitur. Nullum ergo inuenis peccatum, quod damnet deus, nullum inuenis peccatum, quod paenitentia possit sanari. Si autem paenitentia est, et culpa est; si culpa est, et uoluntas est; si uoluntas est in peccando, natura non est, quae cogat. Be si quid infirmitatis patiuntur, qui non possunt inplere, quod uolunt —unde apostolus dicit: Video aliam legem [837] in membris meis repugnantem legi mentís meae et captiuantem me in legem peccati, quae est in membris meis (Rom 7,23)— manifestum est hoc uenisse de translate primi peccati Adam et de consuetudine mala. Nam hodieque libera uoluntate faciunt homines consuetudinem, quam cum fecerint, facile superare non possunt; ipsi ergo sibi de se ipsis fecerunt, quod contra eos lex habitet in membris eorum. Sed qui concipiunt timorem dei et per liberum arbitrium subdunt se sanandos optimal medico et sicut bonus curatori, ita et misericordi creatori, per humilitatem confessionis et paenitentiae

sanantur. Superbi uero dicentes se iustos aut dicendo, quia non peccant ipsi, sed aliud in illis peccat et alia natura de illis peccat, per ipsam superbiam suam et insanabiles fiunt et experiuntur iustum iudicium dei, qui superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam (cf. Iac 4,6). Non est ergo indignum, ut deus dicat: Ite in ignem aeternum eis, qui eius misericordion per liberum arbitrium respuerunt, et dicat: Venite, benedicti patris mei, percipite regnum (Mt 25,41ff.) eis, qui per liberum arbitrium fidem eius susceperunt, peccata sua confessi sunt, paenitentiam egerunt, displicuerunt sibi, quales fuerunt et quales per eum facti sunt, illi placuerunt. Tu ergo iam ad hoc, quod interrogaui, respond—sed impetrem a te, ne moras superfluas faciamus—: si deo nocere nihil poterat, quare huc nos misit? Si nocere poterat, non est incorruptibilis deus. 9. Fel. dixit: Si deo nocere nihil poterat, quare huc misit filium suum? Aug. dixit: Vide, quemadmodum semper interrogas et ad interrogata I will respond non uis. Audi, quod interrogasti, memento tamen te ad ea, quae dico, I will not answer, I autem [838] I will answer. Deo nocere nihil potest; sed filium suum misit, ut carne indueretur et hominibus adpareret, peccatores sanaret, in ipsa carne pateretur pro nobis, quam sumpsit ex nobis. In sua quippe natura pati nihil poterat, quia in

that in the beginning the Word existed and the Word was with God and the Word was God. In this nature nothing could suffer, since the Word was God. But, in order to suffer for us, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Word became flesh by assuming flesh, not becoming flesh; he assumed humanity, without losing divinity. And so he himself was God and man; in divine nature he was equal to the Father, in human nature he became mortal in us, through us, of us, remaining in what he was and assuming what he was not to release what he had made, not what he was. The passion of Christ, then, is not due to indigence, but to mercy. He gave an example of patience to us, from us, that is, to man from man, to the flesh from the flesh. He did not deteriorate in that flesh, but rather the flesh improved in him. On the other hand, a part of your God, without having assumed any flesh that would enable him to suffer, since he was not in the race of darkness, descended in such a way that he was captured, bound, defiled and purified with a purification more shameful than bondage. I already indicated the way in which this purification was carried out n. The more unworthy of God all these things are, the easier they are to understand, since none of them fit with the nature of God. Far from a pious and faithful soul believing in God, the good and true God, such things as you believe, which you have not found, but have invented! Answer once and for all: «If nothing could cause

harm to God, why was she sent here, according to your foolish talk? That pure substance had not assumed any flesh in which to suffer; If he had to suffer something, it could not be in the flesh since he had not received it. 10. Felix: If nothing contrary to him could harm God and no adverse nature could bring harm to Christ, what nature did Christ come to liberate? You, in fact, affirm that he came to free us. Therefore, we were in captivity. If we were in captivity and Christ came to free us from it, the one who held us prisoners was a stranger to God or a force from God. If the one who had us prisoners was a force of God, why did the one who had us prisoners send Christ? If it was in his power to set us free whenever he wanted, for what purpose is Christ crucified? 78 Why was he crucified? If it is a force from God, it would not bring us any harm. If it was a force from God, we were not in its power as captives, but as in the company of our prince 79, as a son with his parents, not as Romans with the barbarians. Since we were accompanied by the strength of God, it was not appropriate for God to send his son, if it is maintained that he came as a liberator. If it seems, then, that we were in the company of the strength of God, the Apostle said: Christ us

principle eral uerbum et uerbum erat apud deum et deus erat uerbum (lo 1,1). In hac natura, quia deus erat uerbum, pati nihil Ule poterat. Vt autem pati pro nobis posset, (542) uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis (lo 1.14). Verbum caro factum est adsumendo carnem, non mutatum in carnem; adsumpsit enim humanitatem, non amisit diuinitatem. Itaque idem deus et idem homo in natura dei aequalis patri, in natura hominis factus mortalis, in nobis, pro nobis, de nobis, manens quod erat, suscipiens quod non erat, ut liberaet quod fecerat, non quod erat. Non est ergo passio Christi ex indigentia, sed ex mercy. Praebuit enim exemplum patientiae nobis de nobis, id est homini de nomine, carni de carne; non tamen in illa carne ipse deterior factus, sed caro in illo melior facta est. Pars uero dei uestri mile carne adsumpta—non enim erat in gente tenebrarum, pro quo pateretur— descendit, ut teneretur, ligaretur, pollueretur et turpius quam ligabatur purgaretur. Iam enim de purgatione eius dixi. Haec omnia quanto indigniora sunt, mucho utique faciliora ad intellegendum, quoniam in naturam dei ista non cadunt. Et absit a pío animo et fideli talia deo credere, deo bono, deo uero, qualia uos creditis, non quem inuenistis, sed quem finxistis. Answer iam nunc: si deo nocere nihil poterat,pura " See Felix II 7.

freed him from the curse of the law, since it is written: Malina substantia ipsius mile carne adsumpta in se passura, si quid passura erat, non in carne quam non susceperat, quare huc missa est secundum our uaniloquy? 10. Fel. dixit: Si nihil poterat noceri deo a parte aduersa et Christo nihil poterat noceri ab aduersa natura, ad quam [839] uenit Christus, ut eam liberaet? Quia, ut dicis, propter libertatem nostram uenit. Ergo in captiuitate Fuimus. Si in captiuitate tenebamur et propterea Christus uenit, ut nos liberaet de captiuitate, qui nos tenebat, extraneus a deo erat aut uirtus dei. Si dei uirtus erat, qui nos tenebat, utquid Christum mittebat ille, qui nos tenebat? If in ipsius arbitrio erat, when uellet resigns, utquid Christus crucifigitur? Neminem ergo latet Christum crucifixum. Quid illum crucifixerunt? Si dei uirtus est, nihil nobis nocebat. Si dei uirtus erat, non Fuimus capti apud illum, sed quasi nos cum nostro principe, quasi filius cum parentibus, non autem Romani cum barbaris. Non oportebat ergo, quia cum uirtute dei constituti eramus, deum filium suum mittere, ut dicatur, quia liberator noster uenit. Si paret ergo nos cum uirtute dei constitutos esse, apostolus dixit: Christus nos liberauit de maledicto legis, quia scriptum est: maledictus omnis, The Manichaeans, who never speak of the birth of Christ, have no difficulty in speaking of his crucifixion, despite their Docetism. The interpretation is not identical to the Catholic one, but is understood from the figure of Jesus patibilis (see General introduction, p.55 note 81). Note also the present: "he is crucified." We assume that it refers to the supreme leader of the sect (Heresies 46).

I say everyone who hangs from a tree. These are the words of the Apostle: If he who curses everyone who hangs on a tree is a force (virtus) of God - since Christ hung on the tree and likewise all his apostles 8I, who were nailed to it for fidelity to his commandments - then who is he who curses everyone who hangs on a tree? 11. Augustine: Those whom Christ rescued from the devil were under his power by their own consent and were in such a situation by God's just punishment. They had freely consented to the seduction of the devil. Just as man had it in his power to give his consent to the devil, ending up his captive, so also the devil, when he was an angel, had it in his power to sin, and ended up deteriorated. The angel who sinned by his free will persuaded the man also endowed with sin to sin, so that just as the devil would not have sinned if he did not want to, man would not have consented if he did not want to. He was a prisoner of the one to whom he had given his consent, not because the devil could do anything, but it was a just punishment from God to deliver into the power of the devil a man who despised the power of God over himself and did not want to obey his law. This is how Christ found sinners: under the power of sin, since sin is linked to free will. Having thus found sinners under sin, Christ rescued them from the power of the proud qui pendet in ligno (Gal 3:13; Deut 21:23). Hoc enim apostolus dicit. Si iste, qui maledicit omnes, qui pendent in ligno, dei uirtus est —-Christus enim pependit in ligno et apostoli ipsius omnes, qui addicti sunt pro ipsius praecepto— quis est iste ergo, qui maledicit omnem, qui pendet in ligno? 11. Aug. dixit: Quos Christus redemit a diabolo, per consensionem suam tenebantur a diabolo et in eius condicione constituti erant per iustum (543) dei iudicium, cui seducenti consenserant per líberum arbitrium. Sicut autem in hominis potestate Fuit diabolo consentiré, ut captiuaretur, sic in ipsius diaboli potestate Fuit, cum angelus esset, peccare, ut in deterius mutaretur. Peccator ergo angelus per liberum arbitrium suasit peccatum homini habenti liberum arbitrium, ut diabolus, si noluisset, non peccasset et homo, si noluisset, non con[840]sensisset.

Cum autem iam ab illo, cui consenserat, teneretur, non quia diabolus aliquid potuit, sed quia dei iustum iudicium Fuit daré in potestatem diaboli hominem, qui contempsit super se potestatem dei et eius legi obtemperare noluit: quia ergo sic inuenit Christus peccatores sub peccato, cum sit peccatum in libero arbitrio, inueniens peccatores _ sub peccato redemit confitentes a superciente. Quod autem in lege positum 80 Note that from half of the text he has deleted the paragraph: "Christ became a curse for us." But the text had already been quoted in full by Faust (Fausf X I V 1). That "crucifixion" of the apostles is their living in the flesh.

to those who confessed to him. The words of the law: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, to which these other words of the Apostle refer: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, do not mean a reproach to the law, but rather they praise the mercy of the Lord. Adam had sinned and all that mass and spread from sin was cursed. But the Lord wanted to assume the flesh of that mass so that the work of grace would undo death, through the assumption of the mortality that came from punishment. That is why the law says: Cursed is everyone who hangs on the tree. Death itself hung on the tree, a death that came from the curse. Therefore, just as by receiving death he put death to death, so by receiving the curse he undid the curse. That is why the Apostle also says: Knowing that our old man was crucified with him on the cross, since he deigned to take the mortal flesh of our old man, that is, of the fate of death originated as a reward for sin, he took from the Virgin Mary the mortal flesh in which to leave us an example of passion and resurrection - that of the passion to strengthen patience, that of the resurrection to awaken hope - in order to show us in the flesh that he took from our mortal flesh the two lives, one tiring, the other blissful; one tiring that we must tolerate, another blissful one that we must wait for. Having to tolerate fatigue is a consequence of our sin; Christ, on the other hand, showed it in this: Maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno, unde apostolus dicit: Christus nos redemit de maledicto legis, factus pro nobis maledictum; scriptum is enim: maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno, non legem reprehendit sed misericordiam domini commendauit. Quia enim Adam peccauerat et omnis illa massa et propago peccati maledicta erat, dominus autem carnem de ipsa massa suscipere uoluit, ut suscipiendo mortalitatem, quae de poena uenerat, solueret mortem, quod de gratia ueniebat, ideo dicit lex: Maledictus omnis, qui pendet in ligno. Mors enim ipsa pendebat in ligno, quae mors de maledicto ueniebat. Quomodo ergo suscipendo mortem interfecit mortem, sic suscipendo maledictum soluit maledictum.

Vnde et apostolus dicit: Scientes, quia uetus homo noster simul confixus est cruci cum illo (Rom 6,6), quia de uetere homine nostro id est de sorte mortis, quae ueniebat ex merit peccati, suscipere dignitus est carnem mortalem de uirgine Maria, in qua nobis et passionis et resurrectionis praeberet exemplum —passionis ad firmandam patientiam resurrectionis ad excitandam spem— ut duas uitas nobis ostenderet in carne, quam suscepit de uita nostra mortali, unam laboriosam, altera beatam: laboriosam, quam tolerare debenmus, beatam, quam sperare debenmus. Toleramus autem laboriosam merit [841] peccati nostri; ill e

his flesh not as the fruit of his iniquity, but as the result of his mercy. So that you may know that the law that you had the whim to reproach is good, the Apostle himself said in a certain place: The law appeared so that crime would abound. Here it seems that he still reproaches him; but listen to what follows: But where crime abounded, grace abounded all the more. The law was given to arrogant men who attributed everything to their own strength, so that, not being able to comply with it, they would recognize themselves as transgressors and, being convicted under the law, would ask for mercy from the giver of the law. That is why the Apostle says shortly after: And thus the law is certainly holy and the command holy and just and good. But lest you say that he refers to another commandment, showing that he is speaking of that of which he had said a little before: The law appeared so that crime would abound, he immediately asked himself this question: Has then what is good become death to me? By no means; but sin, that sin might be manifested, wrought death in me through a good thing. Sin existed, but it did not manifest itself; God gave the law to the proud, he acted against it and the sin that existed but was not manifest came to light. The appearance of sin humbled the proud; The humiliated proud repented and with his repentance obtained mercy. You have heard the answer to what you asked me; You answer what I ask you: «If the race of darkness could not cause any harm to God, autem otendit eam in carne sua, non merito iniquitatis suae, sed officio misericordiae suae. Nam ut noueris bonam esse legem, quam tu reprehenderé uoluisti, ipse apostolus Paulus quodam loco dixit: Lex subintrauit, ut abundaret delictum. Adhuc uídetur illam reprehende; sed audi quod sequitur: Vbi autem, inquit, abundauit delictum, superabundauit gratia (Rom 5,20). Data est enim lex superbis hominibus et uiribus suis totum tribuentibus, ut cum inplere non possent legem datam, praeuaricatores inuenirentur et facti reí sub lege peterent misericordiam a legis conditore. Proinde paulo post dicit idem apostolus: Itaque lex quidem saneta et mandatum sanctum et iustum et bonum.

Sed ne dicas, quia de alio mandat dicit, ut ostendat, quia de illo dicit, de quo paulo ante dixerat: Lex subintrauit, ut abundaret delictum, statim sibi obposuit quaestionem: Quod ergo bonum mihi factum est mors? absit; sed peccatum, ut adpareat peccatum, per bonum operatum est mihi mortem (Rom 7:12-13). Erat enim peccatum, sed non adparebat peccatum; (544) data est lex superbo, fecit contra legem et adparuit peccatum, quod erat, sed non adparebat. Adparens autem peccatum humiliauit superbum, humiliatus superbus factus est paenitens, de paenitentia inpetrata est misericordia. Audisti ergo, quod interrogasti, respond, quod interrogati:

Why did he send a part of himself here to mix and be stained with the nature of demons? 12. Félix: If we have freedom, let no one coerce anyone. I will be a Christian whenever I want. We have the power to be or not to be Christians, according to our will. Augustine: It is clear that we have that power, and I have proven it with the divine Scriptures. Even without wanting it, the person who has led you into this error was forced to recognize it 82. Regarding what you say: «No one coerces anyone; I will be a Christian whenever I want", no one coerces you; only when you want, since by your will you came here and by your will you entered into this discussion83. And woe to the bad will if it is bad! Peace to the good will, if it is good. Be it good, be it bad, it is will. Good will is followed by a crown, evil is followed by punishment. God is judge of wills, as well as creator of natures. If you think that you are being coerced to be a Christian, hear from me that no one is coercing you; think rather about what you hear; consider it, it is in your will, examine as a wise man - in the case where there is some wisdom in you, even if it is human - whether what has been said is based on the truth, if you yourself fail in the defense of your Manes, as it seems, and, whenever you want, become what you are not yet and cease to be what you are. nihil nocere poterat gens tenebrarum deo? Quare huc misit partem suam miscendam et polluendam a natura daemonum? 12. Fel. dixit: Si in arbitrio nostro sumus, nemo neminem cogat; quando uoluero, ero christianus. Voluntas nobis subiacet aut esse christianum aut non esse. Aug. dixit: Quia uoluntas nobis adiacet, manifestum est et hoc de diuinis scripturis docui; quod coactus est etiam [842] inuitus dicere etiam ille, qu uos in ístum índuxit errorem. Quod autem you say: «Nemo cogatur, quando uoluero, ero christianus», nemo te plañe cogit; quando uolueris, este, quia ex uoluntate tua huc uenisti et ex uoluntate tua ista disputasti. Et uae uoluntati malae, si mala est; pax bonae uoluntati, si bona est. Siue enim mala sit, siue bona sit, uoluntas est. Bonam uoluntatem sequitur corona, malam uoluntatem sequitur poena. Deus iudex uoluntatum est, creator autem naturarum.

Si ergo putas cogi te, ut sis christianus, audi a nobis omnino te non cogi; cogita potius, quae audis, perpende, in tua uoluntate es; examine ut prudens, si tamen in te est ulla prudentia uel humano, utrum ea, quae dicta sunt, ueritate fulta sint, utrum tu ipse in Manichaei uestri defensione defeceris, sicut adparet, et quando uolueris, esto quod nondum es, et desine esse quod es. «2 See Felix II 3-6. Irony of Augustine, since we well know that he resisted going to the debate (Private Introduction, p.462). In any case, Augustine is not wrong, since he had said that he was willing to defend his faith and be burned with his books if something wrong was found in them (I 12).

13. Felix: Briefly, as your holiness said, so as not to accumulate documents: if what I previously asked for is okay with you, I have come here; Show me the truth, so that it becomes clear that what I defend is not true, and you have me willing to believe. Agustín: It is already clear enough that what you defend is not true. Far from the hearts of those who seek or possess the truth, to believe that God, coerced by necessity, sank its substance to chain it to the nature of demons and defile it. Far be it from the faithful to believe that, to release his substance, God becomes males in front of females and females in front of males to excite the concupiscence of both. Far be it from the faithful to believe that God will ultimately condemn forever his substance that he himself immersed in the midst of demons. Clearly this is not true. But since you want the truth to be discovered to you instead of that expelled and convicted falsehood, if you still have any interest in knowing the Catholic faith, you will be able to receive instruction about it from its beginning. Indeed, pious faith enables the perception of immutable truth; Whoever does not want to begin with that faith will remain outside in his pride and will not be able to be led to the goal to which he tends or which he wishes to reach. Since that falsehood has already been discovered, reprove it so that you can begin to become capable of knowing the truth. 13. Fel. dixit: Ecce iam competedme, ut dixit sanctitas tua, ne chartas cumulemus: si tibi placet, quod petiui pridem, huc ueni; ostende mihi ueritatem, ut illud, quod teneo, pareat, quia ueritas non est, et habes me paratum ad credendum. Aug. dixit: Iam quidem quod tenes, satis adparet, quia ueritas non est. Absit enim a cordibus ueritatem quaerentium uel tenentium, ut credant deum substantiam suam necessitate coactum mersisse daemonum naturae ligandam atque polluendam; absit a fidelibus credere deum ad liberandam substantiam suam conuertere se in masculos contra feminas et in feminas contra masculos ad eorum concupiscentiam inritandam; absit a fidelibus credere deum substantiam suam, quam ipse daemonibus mersit, postea in aeternum damnare. Hoc ergo quia ueritas non est, manifestum est. Sed quia uis tibi pro ista falsitate expel atque conuicta patefieri ueritatem, si quid de cognoscenda fide catholica adhuc mouet, ab initio fidei poteris erudiri.

Etenim aptum perceptioni ueritatis in[843]commutabilis facit pia fides: a qua fide quisquís incipere noluerit, superbus foris remanebit et ad id, quo tendit uel quo uult peruenire, perduci non poterit. Sed quia iam illa falsitas manifesta est, anathema fal(, J»4.J,)sitatem, ut possis incipere aptus esse ad cognoscendam ueritatem.

14. Félix: That is when such falsehood is revealed to me; Until now it doesn't work for me, since no other one has been shown to me. That's why I can't fail it. Augustine: Should the error that confesses that God is corruptible be condemned, or not? Felix: Repeat it. Augustine: Should the error that calls God corruptible be condemned, or not? Félix: Find out if Manes says that. Augustine: What I have asked is this: Should he who calls God corruptible be condemned? Felix: Whoever claims that God is corruptible must be condemned. Is this what you object to me? Agustín: I'm just asking. Felix: Do you call God corruptible, not what you said before, namely, that he gave a part of himself to his adversaries? Agustín: For now, answer what I ask you: whoever says that God is corruptible, should he be condemned or not? Felix: Totally. Augustine: Whoever affirms that the nature and substance of God is corruptible, should he be condemned or not? Félix: I didn't understand what you just said. Augustine: I say what every man who does not pretend understands 14. Fel. dixit: Cum adparuerit mihi; Quia mihi non adparet, quia altera mihi non ostensa est, non possum anathemare. Aug. dixit: Anathemandus est error, qui dicit corruptibilem deum, an non est anathemandus? Fel. dixit: Iterum dec. Aug. dixit: Anathemandus est error, qui dicit corruptibilem deum, an non est anathemandus? Fel. dixit: Quaeratur, yes dicit. Aug. dixit: Ego hoc interrogaui: qui dicit corruptibilem deum, anathemandus est, an non? Fel. dixit: Qui dicit corruptibilem deum, anathemandus est. Hoc mihi obicis? Aug. dixit: Hoc interrogation. Fel. dixit: Corruptibilem deum dicis, non autem auod primo dixisti, quia partem suam dedit aduersariis? Aug. dixit: Interim quod interrogo responds: qui dicit corruptibilem deum esse, anathemandus est, an non? Fel. say: Valde. Aug. dixit: Qui dicit corruptibilem esse naturam et substantiam dei, anathemandus est, an non? Fel. dixit: Non intellexi, quod dixisti. Aug. dixit: Hoc dico, quod omnis homo intellegit, qui non se fingit

who does not understand: should he be condemned or not who affirms that the nature or substance of God is corruptible, that is, the same as God? Félix: This one must also be condemned, if it is proven that what he says is true. Augustine: I have not yet told you that Manes claims that the nature of God is corruptible; What I told you is that anyone who claims that must be condemned. Félix: And I answered: That's right. 15. Augustine: That part that was mixed with the race of darkness, did it come from the nature of God or from some other nature? Felix: Of (of) that of God 84. Augustine: What comes from the nature of God, is it the same as what God is, or is it something other than God? Felix: That's right; that which comes from (of) God is God, as it is written: The light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not accept it; for God is light and in him there is no darkness. Augustine: You have responded correctly by affirming that what proceeds from the nature of God is God 85; that God is light and in him there is no darkness, and that such light shone in the darkness and the darkness did not accept it. Let us see, then, if it is true that

Manes does not affirm that a part of God was captured by darkness, that she is bound, defiled and polluted, to the point of needing the mercy of someone to free her and purify her. If, on the other hand, he affirms all this, according to your repeated confessions, he must be condemned since he says that a part of God and the nature of God, which is the same as God, was captured by darkness and is bound and stained. You yourself could not affirm it by staying within the Gospel; But what you said is true: that the light shines in the darkness and the darkness did not accept it. Therefore, Manes must be condemned because he said that the light was darkened in the midst of darkness and that darkness captured it. Felix: But whoever is defiled and imprisoned is freed; We also purify ourselves if we are stained. Augustine: But that cannot be accurately stated about the nature of God. Referring to nature that can be stained, it is fair to say that it is stained and purified; On the other hand, referring to that which cannot be stained, you notice how great a sacrilege it is to say: "it is stained and purified"; especially affirming that a certain part of God is defiled in such a way that it will be forever linked to the eternal globe of darkness, because it could not be purified. Whoever does not condemn this responded falsely shortly before, since everyone who considers God corruptible must be condemned. 16. Felix: That a part, which was not purified from the man-

non intellegere: naturam et substantiam dei, id est illud ipsum, quicquid est deus, qui dicit corruptibilem esse, anathemandus est, an non? [844] Fel. dixit: Etiam anathemandus est, si probatum fuerit esse uerum. Aug. dixit: Nondum tibí dixi, quia Manichaeus dicit corruptibilem naturam dei; sed hoc tibi dixi, quia quicumque hoc dicit, anathemandus est. Fel. dixit: Et ego I answered: etiam. 15. Aug. said: Pars illa, quae mixta est genti tenebrarum, de dei natura est, even de alia aliqua natura? Fel. dixit: From dei. Aug. dixit: Quod de dei natura est, hoc est, quod deus est, an aliud quid, quod non est deus? Fel. dixit: Ita est. Quod de deo est, deus est, secundum quod et scriptum est: Lux luzet in tenebris et tenebrae eam non conprebenderunt (lo 1,5); deus enim lumen est et tenebrae in eo non sunt (1 lo 1,5). Aug. dixit: Bene responderi, quia et quicquid de dei natura est, deus est et deus lux est et tenebrae in eo non sunt; et talis lux luxit in tenebris et tenebrae eam non conprekenderunt. Videamus ergo, utrum Until now Augustine had spoken of nature and substance as synonyms. From now on he begins to talk only about nature. Note that Felix does not answer exactly what Augustine asks: if it is or comes from the "nature" of God. He limits himself to answering that it comes from God. For Felix the distinction between nature and substance in God is fundamental. The soul belongs to the substance of God, not to his nature. See General introduction, p.140. Agustín seems not to have exactly noticed Félix's response, since he believes that he has answered in his line and that Je has agreed.

Manichaeus partem dei non dicat conprehensam a tenebris, non etiam teneri ligatam, non etiam maculatam et pollutam, sic ut indigeat misericordia liberatoris et purgatoris. Si autem haec dicit, secundum te etiam et secundum ueras confessiones tuas anathemandus est, quia partem dei et naturam dei, quod est ipse deus, dicit conprehensam a tenebris et liga(546/)tam et pollutam: quod tu ipse secundum euangelium loquens non potuisti dicere; sed uerum dixisti, quia lux luzet in tenebris et tenebrae eam non conprebenderunt. Manichaeus ergo anathemandus, qui dixit, quia lux tenebrata est in tenebris et tenebrae eam conprehenderunt. Fel. say: Sed et qui polluitur et qui tenetur, liberatur; et nos si polluti sumus, mundamur. Aug. dixit: Sed hoc dei natura non recte dicitur. Sed [845] de illa, quae pollui potest, recte dicitur, quia polluitur et mundatur; de illa uero, quae pollui non potest, uides cum quanto sacrilege dicatur «polluitur et mundatur», máxime quia sic dicitis quandam dei partem esse pollutam, ut propterea ligetur in aeternum globo tenebrarum, quia non potuit mundari. Hoc qui non anathemat, falsum paulo ante responder, quia omnis, qui dicit corruptibilem deum, anathemandus est. 16. Fel. dixit: Hoc, quod dixit sanctitas tua, <juia pars, quae se

cha of the race of darkness..., your holiness said it. But Manes does not say that they have been sent to the kingdom of God. It is you who claims that they have been condemned; Manes, however, says that they have not been condemned, but placed in custody of that race of darkness 8Ó. Agustín: Now I am dealing with precisely what you affirm: that that part that had been defiled is purified. Then, if necessary, I will discuss the other part: that it is nailed to its balloon. For now I affirm: the part that is purified was stained. Félix: He who is stained is purified. Augustine: So whoever affirms that the nature of God and the substance of God and that which is God can be defiled, bound, stained by the work of the race of darkness, must he not be reprobated? Felix: What did Christ purify us of? What did he free us from? Augustine: Christ freed us from a part of God, nor from the nature of God, but through his mercy he freed a workmanship of his that had fallen into sin through free will. He purified a reality that could be defiled; freed a reality that could be held captive; He healed a reality that could make us sick. Now we talk about God, about the nature of God, about the substance of God, about what God is. Could it or could it not be defiled?

17. Felix: Our soul is stained; Does it come from (ex) God? If it does not come from (ex) God 87, why did Christ suffer crucifixion for her? If it is clear that Christ was crucified for our soul, it is also clear that it came from (ex) God and was defiled and that he purified it. Augustine: I say that not only the soul comes from (ex) God, but also our body and every creature, both spiritual and corporal, because this is what the Catholic faith maintains. But what God begot from himself is one thing, which is what he himself is; Another, however, is what God did. What God begot is equal to the Father; what God made, being created, is not equal to the creator. One thing is what we say comes from (ex) God, more exactly from (from) him, which is the same as him, as the only begotten Son, as his Word by which he made all things; of others, however, we say that they come from (ex) God, because he spoke and they were made; He commanded it and they were created. The soul belongs to those things that God made, it is not what God engendered in himself. Therefore, the Word that was generated from (from) itself could not and cannot be defiled. On the other hand, the soul, which he made ruler of the body so that it would serve what is superior to it and dominate over what is inferior to it, that is, serve God and have dominion over the body, was defiled by sin by despising the Law of God. But God, granting his mercy to the things he created, sent his son through whom he made them and through him remade them.

non mundauit ab coinquinatione gentis tenebrarum. Et sic dicit Manichaeus, quia non sunt missi in regnum dei. Hoc enim adsetis tu, quia damnati sunt; sed Manichaeus hoc dicit, quia non damnati sunt, sed ad custodiam positi sunt illius gentis tenebrarum. Aug. dixit: De ista parte tecum ago, quam dicis pollutam purgari; Postea, si opus fuetit, de illa, quae figitur in globo eius. Intetim quae purgatur, polluta erat. * Fel. say: Quae polluitur, et mundatur. Aug. dixit: Qui ergo dicit naturam dei et substantiam dei et id quod deus est, posse pollui, ligari, inquinan a gente tenebrarum, non est anathemandus? Fel. say: Christus unde nos mundauit? Where will you free us? Aug. dixit: Christus non partem dei, non naturam dei liberauit, sed invoicem, quam fecit, in peccatum cadentem per liberum arbitrium sua misericordia liberauit. Eam rem mundauit, quae pollui poterat, eam rem liberauit, quae captiuari poterat, eam rem sanauit, quae infirman poterat. Modo autem de deo, de natura dei, de substantia dei, de eo, quod deus est, loquimur: poterat pollui, an non poterat? Felix answers the statement of Augustine, who has attributed to Manes a doctrine that according to the Manichean doctor is not his: Manes does not affirm that the unpurified part of God will be condemned, but that another specific function will be assigned to it: the guarding of the race of darkness, so that they do not attack the kingdom of light again. Note that Agustín replies to Félix and avoids the issue, leaving it for later, but without addressing it again.

17. Fel. dixit: Anima nostra ex deo est, quae polluta est? si non est ex deo, utquid pro illa Christus crucifixus est? Si ergo paret, quia Christus propter animam nostram crucifixus est, paret, quia ex deo est et polluta erat et ipse eam mundauit. [846] Aug. dixit: Ego non solum animam, sed et corpus nostrum et omnem creaturam et spiritalem et corporalem ex deo dico esse, quia hoc habet catholica fides. Sed aliud est, quod de se deus genuit, quod hoc est, quod ipse; aliud autem, quod fecit deus. Quod deus genuit, aequale est patri; quod deus fecit, non est aequale conditum conditori. Aliud autem dicimus ex deo esse, quod melius dicitur de deo esse, quia (547) hoc est, quod ipse, sicut unigenitus filius, sicut uerbum eius, per quod facta sunt omnia (cf. lo 1,3); alio uero sic dicimus ex deo, quia «dixit, et facta sunt; mandauit, et constituta sunt” (cf. Ps 148,5). Hinc est anima, ex his, quae fecit deus, non illud, quod de se genuit deus. Ideo uerbum, quod de se genuit, pollui non potuit nec potest nec poterit. Anima uero, quam fecit rectricem corporis, ut seruiret superiori, dominaretur inferiori, id est seruiret deo, dominaretur corpori, contempta dei lege per peccatum polluta est; deus autem misericordiam praestans his, quae fecit, misit filium, per quem fecit, et per illum refecit. Quando Felix continues to avoid talking about "the nature of God" and limits himself to talking "about God."

When it came to creating what did not exist, he created it through his Word; At the moment of redoing what had gone wrong, he took from there the creature, the Virgin Mary, in order to show man, in his own human condition, what he had to endure and what he should expect. And so the nature of the Word, the substance of the only begotten Son of God, suffered nothing either from the Jews, his persecutors, or from the devil, the persecuting evil angel. As he clothed himself with flesh, he clothed himself with something mortal, passible, mutable. In that reality that he clothed himself in, he suffered what he wanted to give us an example of patience, and he reformed it to show an example of justice. You tell me now if a part of God who is God can be defiled or not; If he can, he is not the immutable God, and whoever says so deserves to be condemned. If, on the contrary, it cannot, you already warn that Manes must be condemned, who affirms that a pure part of God, the nature of God, what God is, came here, linked to the race of darkness and defiled in such a way that it needs to be freed and purified. 18. Félix: Did you say that the soul does not come from (ex) God? Agustín: I didn't say that; I said that it comes from (ex) God as made by God, not as born from (of) him 88. Felix: You said that the soul does not come from (ex) God, but

which is the work of God himself, since without God nothing exists. That is what you say, but you do not want to affirm that the soul comes from (ex) God. Augustine: It comes from (a) God, but as made by him. Félix: Whether he made it, sent it or donated it, the soul comes from (ex) God. Then, if it comes from (ex) God and is stained and Christ came to free it from that stain, why do you recriminate Manes? Augustine: For I maintain that the soul, which is not of the nature of God, but was made by him, sinned by virtue of its free will, was defiled by sin, and, by the mercy of God, found liberation in repentance. On the other hand, you affirm that the very nature of God who is God, God of God, is imprisoned and defiled in the race of darkness. Great is the difference between what God generated from (from) himself and what he made not from himself, but from nothing, that is, he received being when he did not exist at all or, in other words, he was created. Felix: So it's a part of God. Augustine: I have already told you that it is not a part of God; Also listen to how you must understand that Almighty God is a creator. Everything that is made and everything that someone does is done either from (from) itself or from (ex) something else or from (ex) nothing. Man, not being omnipotent, makes himself the son; something is made of (ex) something else when, for example, the carpenter makes an ark out of wood or a vessel out of silver. He could make the glass, but not the silver; he could make the ark, but not

condendum erat, quod non erat, per uerbum conditum est; quando reficiendum erat, quod deprauatum factum fuet, suscepta est inde creatura de uirgine Maria, ut per id, quod erat homo, demonstraretur homini, et quid sustinendum et quid sperandum esset. Itaque natura uerbi, substantia unigeniti filii dei nihil passa est uel a persecutoribus Iudaeis uel a diabolo angelo malo persequente. Sed quia induit se carne, induit se re mortali, re passibili, re mutabili: in eo quod se induit, passus est quicquid uoluit ad exemplum patientiae, et reformauit hoc ad exemplum iustitiae. Your way said mihi de dei parte, quod deus est, utrum pollui possit, an non. Si potest, non est incommutabilis deus, et qui hoc dicit, anathemandus est. Si autem non potest, uides anathemandum Manichaeum esse, qui dicit partem dei, naturam dei, id quod est deus, uenisse hucpuram ad gentem tenebrarum ligatam atque pollutam, ut indigeat solui et mundari. [847] 18. Fel. dixit: Hoc tu dixisti de anima, quia ex deo non est? Aug. dixit: Non dixi; sed dixi, quia ex deo est, tamquam a deo facta, non tamquam de deo nata. Fel. dixit: Dixisti de anima, quia non est ex deo, sed invoice dei, Note the precision and constancy in Augustine's use of prepositions: ex to designate the creation-making; from to indicate the generation and to indicate the origin, without specifying the mode. Félix, on the other hand, uses ex, without giving it the meaning that Agustín gives it. Everything seems like a dialogue between deaf people: using the same words they cannot be understood, because they say different things.

quia sine deo nihil est; hoc enim dicis tu et non uis adseuerare, quia ex deo es anima. Aug. dixit: A deo est, sed facta a deo. Fel. dixit: Aut facta aut missa aut data, ex deo est. Ergo si ex deo est et polluta est et uenit Christus liberare eam de pollutione, quid blame Manichaeum? Aug. dixit: Quia ego dico animam non naturam dei, sed factam a deo per liberum atbitrium peccasse et peccato esse pollutam et per dei misericordiam in paenitentia liberatam; tu autem ipsam naturam dei, quod deus est, deum de deo dicis in gente tenebrarum captum atque pollutum. Et multum interest inter id, quod de se deus genuit et quod fecit non de se, sed ex nihilo, id est cum omnino non esset, a deo acceoit, ut esset, id est ut institueretur. Fel. dixit: Ergo pars dei est. Aug. dixit: Iam tibí dictum est, non est pars dei; et accipe, quomodo inteilegas deum omnipotentem factorem. Omnia, quae fiunt et quod quisque facit, aut de se est aut ex aliquo aut ex nihilo. Homo quia non est omnipotens, de se filium facit, ex aliquo, sicut artifex (548) ex ligno arcam, ex argento uasculum, Potuit enjm faceré uasculum, sed non
Minutes of the debate with Félix

the wood. On the other hand, no man can make something exist from what does not exist at all. But God, since he is omnipotent, begot a Son from himself, made the world from (ex) nothing and formed man from clay, to show us by these three acts of power that his action reaches the three levels. As for what he did from (of) himself, one should not speak of making, but of engendering. Regarding what he made of something else, for example the man from (ex) the earth, he did not do it having made another the earth itself from which he formed the man, as God made the silver for the silversmith from which he made the vessel. Rather, God himself made what did not exist so that it existed and what would then exist a second time and which he himself had already created from nothing so that it existed. Thus, it is understood that the body, the soul, the entire creation has been made by God, not in the sense that it has been generated from God to be what God is. Therefore, perhaps now you will choose what you are going to keep and what you are going to reject. Choose what is best. You will see many mutable things, good although mutable; many other mortals, good although mortal. But the absolutely immutable good is God himself. Choose what is best for you to retain: either that God is mutable or that what God made is mutable; You necessarily have to stick with one of the two options. If you do not want to admit that what God made is mutable, all you have to do is admit that God is mutable. To purify you from the sacrilege and blasphemy that I may faceré argentum; potuit faceré arcana, sed non potuit faceré lignum. Ex nihilo autem, ex eo, quod prorsus non est, faceré ut sit, nullus homínum potest.
