INTRODUCTION Of all the works contained in this volume, the Response to the Manichean Secundino is the most difficult to place in time with a certain precision. The Secundino Letter does not provide data that allows us to date it. The placement in the Revisions (II 36) also does not allow us to refine too much. It is placed after The Nature of Good, which immediately follows the debate with Félix and which also lacks a certain date. But if it is admitted that the debate with Félix is ​​not placed in its chronological place, despite having a certain date, it ceases to be a point of reference. Yes, in a certain way it is the work Reply to the Letters of Petiliano, written between 400 and 403, which occupies fifteenth place behind the Reply to Secundino, which would force us to lower the date to at least 398 to allow time for the composition, even partial, of these works.' But there is no shortage of authors who take the debate with Felix as a valid reference point and delay the composition until 405 at the earliest. If only to decongest the period 397-402, we believe that it is preferable to delay the composition; Otherwise it is not easy to understand how he could have composed so many works in such a short time. It is possible to think that these three works, Minutes of the Debate with Felix, The Nature of Good and Response to Secundino, formed a block of later composition, but that he wanted to associate them with the great work Reply to Faust, thus closing the chapter of anti-Manichean works. The relative chronology between them would be exact, although not their placement in the whole of Augustinian work. These works are: Against Hilary (lost), Evangelical Questions, Annotations to Job, Catechesis for Beginners, The Trinity, The Concord of the Evangelists, Reply to Parmeniano's Letter, Baptism, Answer to the Questions of Jenaro, The Work of the Monks, The Good of Marriage, Holy Virginity and Literal Commentary on Genesis,
Reply to Secundino

As it is a response to a letter, we are interested in knowing it and above all its author. Secundino would be totally unknown to us if it had not been for Augustine's writing, to which he prefixed the letter received. We therefore have no more data than what both writings provide us, together with the Revisions. In them Augustine explicitly states that he was a Manichaean of the category of listeners. When he says that he had not known him personally (Revisions II 36) he seems to imply that he knew him through some other means. In fact, the aforementioned information that he was a listener has been received from another source that he does not mention, since in his letter Secundino does not inform about it. Perhaps they had information about each other from the time of their first stay in Rome in 383-384; It is an untested possibility. Secundinus, for his part, knew Augustine well, at least from his books that he claims and shows that he had read 2. He also knows the rumors that spread in Africa among the Donatists and for which Petiliano is spokesperson (Reply to the letters of Petiliano III 16,19; 25,30) that he had abandoned the Tnanichean sect out of fear (Secund 2). Secundinus must have been one of those fervent listeners like Constantius (Faust 20.74). The difference between Secundino and Constantius is this: while Constantius suffered for the supposedly real sins of the elect, Secundino suffered for the slander raised against the sect. Furthermore, while Constantius was well educated in the liberal arts and eloquently defended the sect, Secundino shows no particular training in these arts and his letter is not a model of composition. Although he manifests a fiery Manichean fervor, he reveals no less an unorganized mind.

Not only because of the different tones with which he addresses Augustine, alternating flattery with the puncture not exempt from irony: heart of gold, your divine patience - possessed of Punic perfidy, armed against the truth, god of all eloquence, etc., since all this was undoubtedly a calculated attitude; but also because of the sloppiness of the ideas and the somewhat contradictions, as when he says that he was never a Manichaean and then invites him to return to the truth.

that he abandoned, or that he left Manichaeism now out of fear, now out of ambition for honors. At several points the letter is dark, although such darkness is only for us and not for Augustine, who could understand its allusions very well. But that does not mean that he has a good training in the theology of the sect and provides us with data that expands our knowledge of it. The fact that he was a listener is an element to be valued and opposes the common opinion that this category of faithful was people without major commitments and generally without specific training. Before we talked about Constancio. It is assumed that the origin of the letter, probably written in Rome 3, is Augustine's first anti-Manichean work: The Customs of the Catholic Church and those of the Manichaeans, particularly this second part that left such a bad image of the elect. Secundinus takes upon himself the trouble and perhaps the honor of addressing Augustine, representing in a certain way the Roman Manichean community, perhaps precisely because of his condition as a listener, since the defense by a chosen one could seem too self-serving. If Secundino's letter really had some relationship with Augustinian work, it would still seem strange that Augustine had completely silenced what he said there, as he also silenced it at the beginning of the debate with Fortunatus (n.2.3). Nor can we think that Agustín did not notice where his correspondent's shots were going. Let's come to the letter as a source of information. Regarding Augustine, we have already alluded to the rumors that spread about his abandonment of Manichaeism out of fear; We must add certain allusions that we understand perfectly from the Confessions, such as the reference to Hortensius and the Academy and the statement that his change was sudden, which contradicts what is maintained in the Confessions themselves. His statement that Augustine was never a Manichaean (n.3) still seems strange to us. He does not provide special data on the sources of Manichaeism. He does not cite or mention any of Manes' writings. From the New Testament it only has one explicit quote, Eph 6:12 (n.l), but the entire letter is full of implicit references to it. From the Old Testament, in addition to numerous allusions, he explicitly cites four texts (Hos 1,2; Gen 1,28; 24,2; 47,29 in n.3) not certainly to use them for his own

cause, but to return to Augustine the mockery that he had dropped about the strange way that God used to purify the divine particles, that is, by means of the androgynous virtutes (Nature 44; Felix II 7.13; Faust XV 7; XX 8). At the same level as the Old Testament there is a quote from the book of the Acts of the Apostles (10:13), which they do not accept. The most abundant dogmatic data refer to anthropology and soteriology and, of course, to the fundamental point of the two natures. Important, as it is the most detailed that we have written by a Manichean, is the treatment of sin in its various stages (n.2). He strongly emphasizes the saving function of Christ, spiritual Savior, as well as Lord and Shepherd, against whom he makes Docetism very clear, without this preventing him from speaking about the different moments of the passion, with explicit allusion to his crucifixion in the whole world and in every soul, that is, to Jesus patibilis (n.3.4). And next to Christ, the figure of Manes to whom he assigns a special role in the final judgment (n.3). The greatest novelty, perhaps, must be seen in the refutation of what is the constant refrain of Augustine's anti-Manichean propaganda. He has always insisted that the Manichaeans promise complete understanding and then demand faith, thus showing a total inability to explain the myth itself. Secundino responds that it is not possible to attempt to explain each point of the doctrine, separately from the others. And resorting to Agustín's old profession, that of a teacher, he reminds him that each point must be understood from the totality. But it goes even further: "There are some realities that cannot be explained until they are understandable, since divine reason surpasses the hearts of mortals" (n.6). It is, therefore, absurd what Augustine demands or claims: a rational explanation of the divine mysteries. In the moral aspect, Secundino addresses two calls to conversion, to follow the spiritual Savior along the narrow path, and to flee from the evil that has deceived so many, including the apostles, and that even wanted to act on Christ. To Augustine's indications that the Manichaeans are few, he responds that there are few who follow the path of virtue, which is far from the mass, particularly the mass of women, thus criticizing the Catholic Church. The response to Augustine's accusations also appears when he alludes to
Augustine's response
the numerous hidden sins of Catholics that he claims he does not want to proclaim to avoid propagandizing evil (n.4). THE ANSWER

The tone of Augustine's response is in line with the first chapters of his Reply to the Letter of the Foundation. Agustín, who could hardly have overlooked the irony of certain of Secundino's words, flattering only in appearance, responds gently, in an almost confidential tone. He understands the Manichean listener: what he thinks of Augustine can occur in man, although in fact it does not occur in him. An author 4 wonders the reason for this affable tone and why he has not moved into the realm of personal controversy, as he did with Julian of Eclana. And he wonders if he was not afraid that Secundino would pull the blanket and discover hidden plots of Agustín's life, since he seems or at least pretends to be well informed about his former life. It seems excessive to us to want to compare the response to a letter, generally affable, with the controversy held with Juliano. The case is so different that it does not seem that conclusions can be logically drawn about Agustín's different behavior. Augustine promptly refutes the personal accusations that he abandoned Manichaeism out of fear and desire for honor, precisely conceding that this was the case. But, evidently, he will say, that fear and that honor was not what Secundino imagines, but rather another that the Scriptures recommend (n.1.2). Say the same regarding the sudden change (n.24). If Secundino insisted twice on his status as a Punic, Augustine replies by repeatedly mentioning the Persian origin of Manes and that of Manichaeism. The accusation was more serious in the latter case, since Carthage had been the enemy of Rome in other times, while the Persian Empire was always there as a force opposed to the Roman Empire and to present it as Persian was to present it as an enemy of the Roman people. Augustine sets out to refute Manichaeism from the very words of Secundino. Thus the first words of his letter are like the battering ram that destroys the entire system (n.26). Consequently, Secundino has to regret having written what he wrote (n.3). The Manichean doctrine is unsustainable

He dedicates extensive development to the theme of sin and evil, in response to Secundino, focusing on this trilogy: the soul, consent and the evil to which he consents (n.13-19), from which he tries to demonstrate how the Manichean affirmation that there are only two opposite and contrary substances is unsustainable. Secundino had cited several texts from the Old Testament, all of them related to the seal of the belly and one from the Acts of the Apostles, related to that of the mouth and the hand. In this case Augustine does not follow his usual practice of interpreting them allegorically, but rather takes his cue from them to attack the doctrine of the three seals. If Secundino reminded him that there are mysteries that human reason cannot explain, Augustine remains silent about it; But he does not remain silent regarding the invitation that his correspondent addressed to him to convert again to Manichaeism: he himself returns the coin, inviting him in turn to convert to Catholicism and not to hide behind the small number of Manichaeans, because the information could turn against him. The Augustinian text provides data on different aspects of the Manichaean dogma but without any novelty, and for this reason we do not dwell on them. In conclusion we will say that to the elderly Augustine this work seemed to be the best of all those written against Manichaeism. Without a doubt the arguments, not new, had been maturing and in this work they acquire their final and most serene formulation.

It is abundantly clear that the substances of both are diverse. As one cannot see or understand the Son without also understanding the Father—for he says: He who has seen me has also seen the Father—so neither can one worship the Son, if one does not at the same time worship the Father. And, therefore, if the creature were a son, he would not be worshiped without also worshiping the creator, nor would those who worshiped the creature rather than the creator be condemned. You already realize, as I believe, that it is not convenient for you to call Jesus Christ the firstborn of the most secret and ineffable Majesty and king of all lights, if you do not stop being a Manichean, in order to distinguish the creature from the creator. In this way, Jesus Christ is the only begotten insofar as he is the Word of God together with God, equally immutable and eternal, who does not consider it a plunder to be equal to God, and the firstborn of every creature insofar as in him all things have been created, those in heaven and those on earth, the visible and the invisible. You recognize, then, as I believe, the words of the Apostle to the Colossians.
THE CREATURE IS NOT A PROLEMENT OF GOD, BUT EITHER ALIEN TO HIM

7. In this sentence there are above all two things that necessarily follow. I beg you to consider them with me. The first: If the creature were alien to God, the Apostle would not say that God is its creator. The other: If the creator and the creature were of an identical substance, I would not reproach them for having served the creature rather than the creator, because whoever they served, they would not depart from the same nature and substance. As no one can serve the son if he does not also serve the father, because the substance of both is the same, in the same way no one can serve the creature without serving the creator, if they were both of the same substance. Therefore, if you have discernment and wisdom, you will notice the great difference that exists between creator and creature. And you must understand that the creature is not the offspring of the creator, since, if it were, it would not be inferior to him, but equal and of the same substance, and, consequently, whoever worshiped and served the creature, would pay worship and servitude at the same time to its creator and father. When the Apostle rebukes and considers detestable those who worshiped and served the creature rather than the creator, there was enough conuersiones fieri posse nisi in creatura mutabili: quae tamen nisi esset ex artífice et conditore deo, non dixisset apostolus: Et coluerunt et seruierunt creaturae potius quam creatori, qui est benedictus in saecula (Rom 1:25). 7. On the other hand, we are persuaded by the Christian faith that it is only contrary to God, the supreme being, which is absolutely not; However, everything that is in some way has the supreme being in some way, and in its kind is good, although some things to a greater degree and others to a lesser degree. And in this way all goods, the work of God the creator, are ordered and distributed hierarchically, partly by intervals of places or positions, like all corporeal things, partly by natural merits, as the soul takes precedence over the body; in part

by rewards or punishments as when the soul is either elevated to rest or subjected to pain. And that is why those princes against whom we have engaged in combat, according to the Apostle, are the first to suffer the punishment for their sins, and that is why they cause harm. In fact, no one feels such envy that it leads him to hurt another, unless he is first a torment to himself. The strongest harm the weakest, because no one defeats another if he is not more powerful than him. And yet these evil princes are weaker than if they had remained in their original state and in justice. It is important, however, to know in which one is stronger than the other: whether in the body, like horses are stronger than men, or by the nature of the soul, how the rational is more than the irrational, or by the dispositions of the soul, how the just is above the unjust, or by the hierarchy of power, like the emperor above the soldier or provincial governor. It is accepted that absolutely all power comes from the supreme power of God; Furthermore, power is often given to the worst over the best, that is, to the wicked over those who either already possess justice or are striving to attain it. It is given so that those of proven virtue may manifest themselves through patience, either to nourish their own hope or as an example to others. The Apostle says: Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven virtue, and proven virtue produces hope. Hence it turns out that they win in something inferior, but are defeated in something superior. They frequently defeat the body that is weaker, and are defeated by the mind that is stronger. One fights against its strength by opposing it with patience; against their snares, opposing prudence, so that they neither subdue us by forcing us to give pernicious consent nor deceive us with their traps. But since all things have been made by the Power and Wisdom of God, when the higher created things slide towards the lower, in which all sin consists and what is called evil, force imitates power and fallacy imitates wisdom; On the other hand, when things that have slipped away rise and return upward, magnanimity imitates power and doctrine imitates wisdom. 11. Fainting is no longer nothingness, but rather a striving towards it. When things that have more being slide towards those that have less, not those toward which they slide, but those that slide, fail. They begin to be less than they were, not in the sense that they are the same as those into which they slipped, but less within their own genre. The soul does not become a body when it inclines towards it, but, nevertheless, in a certain way it does become a body through the appetite that makes it faint. In the same way a certain angelic sublimity, delighting more in itself by its dominion, inclined its affection to that which is less and began to be less than it was and, at its level, tended towards nothingness. This consent, therefore, is evil and therefore also the substance of the soul, if it is the substance of the soul and if both form a single substance. Do you see what you have been forced into? To show that the soul and that evil are no longer two substances, one good and one bad, but rather both bad. At this point you will perhaps try not to attribute guilty consent to the soul that consents to evil, but to the evil itself to which it consents, so that in this way there can be two substances, one good and one bad. In fact, it is affirmed that the soul belongs to the part of good, and that its consent to evil and the evil itself to which it consents both belong to the other part, both being attributed by the soul to the bad substance. Who will have such absurd delusions? For the soul does not consent if the consent is not its own; but it is she who consents, therefore the consent is hers. Furthermore, if the consent is yours and it is evil, this evil is yours. In fact, if this evil belongs to that other person to whom the soul consents, it is necessary to admit that it did not have that evil before consenting to it. What good then is the soul, by whose coming that evil is doubled or, to put it more mildly, increased?

13. But I am already seeing three realities and I think that you also see them with me. In fact, the soul that consents to evil and the evil itself that it consents to are two realities, and the third is consent itself, since you do not say that this is the soul but that it is of the soul. I ask, then, what consent itself is, if you affirm that it is the substance itself or that it is in the substance. If you affirm that it is a substance, you will have to admit that there are no longer two substances, but three. 14. Furthermore: if this consent is a substance, the evil of which is evident, we discover that it is in the power of the soul whether a certain bad substance exists or not, given that this consent is in the power of the soul. For if he is not, then he does not consent of his own free will. You, however, have said that, by virtue of that consent, the soul sins of its own will. So, as I said, the soul has in its power whether or not a certain bad substance exists. But what else is an evil substance but a nature? Consequently, some nature will not be natural either to the soul, because if it does not want it it will not exist, or to that evil to which the soul consents of its own will. You cannot affirm that the evil of the race of darkness is natural, because it is installed there by a foreign will, that is, by the will of the soul. To what nature, then, will this nature, that is, this consent, be considered to belong, if it is a nature that is not natural either to the soul or to the race of darkness, if you do not admit, contrary to Manes, that there are not two, but three natures? For in the case in which there were once two, now, once this consent has been born, they have become three. This third, who was born of the soul that consents and of the evil that it consents to, you are forced to consider as the daughter of both; but since it has been born of two natures, one of which is good and the other bad, I ask: why has not a neutral thing been born? Erit ergo aliqua natura, quae nec animae naturalis sit, quoniam, si nolit, non erit, nec illi malo, cui anima uoluntate consentit; non enim potestis dicere naturale malum esse gentis tenebrarum, quod ibi aliena uoluntate instituitur, hoc est animae uoluntate. Cui ergo naturae deputabitur ista natura, id est ista consensio, si natura est, quae ñeque animae ñeque tenebrarum genti naturalis est, nisi, ut contra Manichaeum disputes, non duas, sed tres esse naturas?

Quia et si aliquando fuerunt duae, nunc tamen iam, posteaquam exorta est ista consensio, tres utique factae sunt. Quam sane tertiam, quae nata est ex anima consentiente et ex malo, cui consentit, quasi utriusque filiam cogeris dicere; sed cum ex duabus naturis nata sit, quarum altera bona est, altera mala, quaero, cur non aliquid neutrum natum sit. But you confess that consent is evil; You affirm that when the soul consents to evil it sins of its own will. Do you perhaps think that good nature and bad nature are like two sexes, one male and the other female, and thus, just as something neutral does not come from the male and the female, but rather a male or a female, do you claim that a third reality does not originate from good and evil, which is neither good nor bad, but another bad one? If this is so, where is the victorious nature of the soul? Is it so far from victory that precisely another good is not born? Also, don't you realize that you are already talking about different sexes, not natures? For, if there were diversity of natures in good and evil, from one and the other only a third reality would be born, which would be neither good nor bad; or it could also be that it was a sterile union and that third substance did not originate from it. If from the union of the animals mentioned above, only a mule or mule is born, which is neither horse nor donkey, how much more appropriate was it that this should be the case in such a great and supreme diversity between good and evil? Or again, if no new nature resulted from their union, it would not be bad, although it could not be good. The only thing left, then, is the impossibility of avoiding such incredible absurdities, unless we recognize that it is not a substance, and affirm that enim ex equo et asino quod nascitur, nec equus [926] nec asinus est, ita, quod de bona et mala natura natum est, si et ipsa natura est, nec bona nec mala esse debenbat. movement from what is in the maximum degree to what is less, so that it too is less. And the less it is, the closer it comes to nothing, since what becomes less tends not to be at all. Although the arrival does not happen, perishing, unless it is absolutely nothing, it is clear that every decrease is the beginning of perishing. Now open the eyes of your heart and see, if you can, that any substance is a certain good and that, therefore, evil is a lack of substance, since being a substance is a good. But not every decrease is guilty, but only the voluntary affection by which the rational soul, abandoning its creator, slides towards created things that are inferior to it. This is what we call sin. All other decreases, those that are not voluntary, are either penalties for the punishment of sins under the moderation and ordering of the supreme justice, or they have to do with the hierarchization of the lowest realities, by virtue of which the things that precede give way to those that follow, and thus all temporal beauty is realized in its moment and in its kind. It's just like a speech. This develops thanks to a certain dying of some and being born of other syllables that extend over a certain interval and a certain duration and, after filling their own space, they disappear and are succeeded by those that follow them, according to an order, until the discourse as a whole comes to an end. And it does not depend on the transient sounds themselves, but on the regulation of the speaker, to what extent a syllable must be lengthened or shortened, or with what type of letters each one must keep the time it contains.
EVIL, NOT SUBSTANTIAL, IN A GOOD SUBSTANCE

15. Let us continue and investigate with the utmost diligence what substance it is in. Although to whom is it not evident that as persuasion does not exist except in the nature that persuades, so consent does not exist except in the nature that consents? Therefore, when the soul consents to evil, it itself is a substance, but its consent is not. You see, as I believe, what substance it is in; That is to say, you see that consent actually resides in the soul; consent that you do not doubt is a sin and, therefore, an evil. From here you already understand that it can happen that in a good substance, such as the soul, there is some evil that is not a substance, which is this consent, and by virtue of that evil the soul is also called bad. The sinful soul is evil without a doubt; Now, she sins when she consents to evil. Thus, then, the same and identical reality, that is, the soul, as a substance, is good; but insofar as it has some evil that is not a substance, that is, this consent, to that same extent it is evil. That consent does not mean perfection for her, but rather a decline. In truth, when he consents to evil, he diminishes, he has less being and, consequently, he begins to have less power than he can when he maintains virtue without consenting to any evil. It becomes all the worse, the greater the deslinisi illam consensionem, quam constat malam esse atque culpabilem, fateamur non esse substantiam, sed in aliqua substantia esse dicamus. 15. rresponds to its place. For the very art that originates discourse does not consist either in emitting sounds or in repeating or varying temporal spaces. In the same way, temporal beauty is a fabric resulting from birth and death, from the disappearance and appearance of temporary things in fixed and defined spaces until reaching the pre-established term. This beauty is not bad because we can understand and contemplate better things in spiritual creatures; On the contrary, within its way of being, it has its own harmony and intimates to those who live well the supreme wisdom of God, deeply secret beyond all temporal limits, who has created it and governs it 21.

Then we will see how much this helps my cause. But to show what I have promised, which should I prefer among so much abundance of data? What should I choose, I repeat, but this: What we praise as a celestial creature, you worship as a portion of the creator himself? 22. What is more resplendent than this sun, among all visible creatures? However, if anyone desires its light without due moderation, he will carry on his side the war for his enjoyment, in case he obtains some power by which he can carry out what he desires; He will demolish the neighbors' houses, located in front of the windows of his, so that, under the open sky, the sun can spread its rays through the interior of it. Is it perhaps a fault of the sun that that subject loved this light so much that he dared to put it before the light of justice and, wanting to receive with greater abundance the light of the carnal eyes in the abode of the body, he also dared to close the door of the heart and the gaze of the mind to the light of equity? You see, then, that you can love a good thing with a bad love. Therefore, although you call that evil, consenting to which the soul sins, I maintain that it is a good in its kind, but a good such that the soul, as superior, should not grant its assent. The soul is superior to the body and has God as superior to itself; Therefore, although the nature of the body is good in its order, the soul sins—and with sin becomes evil—if it grants the body, which is inferior to it, the consent of the love it owes to God, who is superior to it.
LOVING A GOOD THING WITH A NOT GOOD LOVE

16. The soul sins by voluntarily consenting to evil. If so, there is no logic in saying that something is evil because it is not loved rightly. 17. And if you affirm that you do not call consent guilty, when one loves a reality that does not act so that consent is granted, but rather the soul consents when it persuades or forces something to the one to whom it consents23, and for that reason it is an evil, because it persuades and urges the commission of some evil, this is a second question that must also be dealt with in due time. What then? If the soul, already made sinful and vicious by such love, persuades others of the same sin, does not the one who gives her consent to the one who persuades her remain depraved by a vice such as the one that had depraved the one she follows? The first sin is, therefore, to put the creature, although good, before the creator in love; The second consists of also tempting another to do the same, either by persuading him or by forcing him to do so. For no one wants to lead another to evil if he has not depraved himself first. Those who sin want to drag others into sin, either out of foolish benevolence or out of malicious ill will. Do they want the most money in any way? It is true that he does not hate them and yet he instills harmful persuasion in them. That father is already corrupted by the love of such things, although gold and silver are not an evil, nor is the sun that I spoke of previously; However, he who loves a good thing inordinately becomes guilty. Malice, on the other hand, by which one wants another to sin, loves honor with immoderate pride and desires to stand out and excel in it above others. Since he sees that this honor is granted more widely and truly to the virtues, so that they may not surpass him in it, he wishes that others should be cast down from the fortress of equity to the abyss of iniquity. It is not evil, then, insofar as it is a substance, but insofar as, being a created substance, it loved itself more than its creator. And it is bad because it is less than what it would be if he had loved the supreme being. The decrease, then, is bad. 18. I think that it will be easy for you to understand, from the words of your own letter, in which you said: "The soul, when it consents to evil, sins voluntarily" Z4, that no evil is a bad nature or love of a bad nature, but, since all natures are good in their kind, evil is the sin that is committed by virtue of the will of the soul, when it loves the creature instead of the creator himself, whether by its own whim, if it is already bad, or by suggestion of another, when he gives his consent to someone who is bad. And yet, it becomes evil in such a way that punishments accompany it so that the extremely good creator arranges everything according to his own merits in the good creature, but not extremely good, because he did not generate it from himself, but made it from nothing. You, on the contrary, established two natures, of which you want one to be good and the other bad, or better, one of good and the other of evil. In fact, the bad nature also originates from the good through sin. You recognize, however, pe summus, qualem pietas divinorum exhibitat, utique deo debentur. Qui ergo amat honorem, deum ímitatur. Sed humiles animae in illo se honorari uolunt, superbi prae illo. Iam, ut arbitror, facile est tibi intellegere ex ipsius uerbis epistulae tuae, quibus dixisti: «Animam, cum consentit malo, uoluntate peccare», nullum malura esse naturam malam uel dilectionem naturae malae, sed, cum omnes naturae in suo genere bonae sint, malum esse peccatum, quod fit uoluntate animae, cum diligit pro ipso creatore creaturam, siue suo nutu, cum sit mala, siue alterius persuasu, cum consentit malo. Et nihilominus sic quoque fit mala consequentibus subpliciis, ut pro meritis omnia disponantur a creatore summe bono in creatura bona, sed non summe bona, quia non eam genuit de se ipso, sed fecit ex nihilo. Tu autem constituisti duas naturas, quarum unam uis bonam esse, alteram malam, uel potius unam boni, alteram mali; nam mala natura ex bona etiam sin fit. that the nature that you call good works evil by consenting to evil, that is, it sins by its will. But I affirm that both are good, and that one of them does evil by suggesting it, and the other by giving its consent. As the consent of the latter is not a nature, so neither is the suggestion of the former. And as the one remains good and maintains the integrity of its nature, if it does not consent, so also the other, if it does not suggest evil it will do better, and it does not even commit the sin that it does not suggest that another commit it, they will be equally upright and worthy of praise in their kind. Even if she sins twice if she herself commits the sin and also invites it to be committed, and once if she only gives her consent to do evil, they become bad because of the sin, but they are not bad by nature. Or if one nature is evil for suggesting sin, the other is evil for giving its consent. If it seems to you that it is worse to suggest it than to consent to evil, let it be one bad and the other worse. But let there not be such a respect for persons and an iniquitous judgment so gratuitous that, with both sinning, although one more seriously and the other more lightly, one is called the nature of evil and the other the nature of good, instead of considering that either both are good but the one that sins less is better, or both bad, but the one that sins more is worse. But regardless of the name you give it, I ask you, sharp and capable man and your Roman ingenuity of which you boast 25, where does this nature of good come from being able to suffer what it suffers in order to consent to evil. The false argument of the small number will chatter that shameful fable mentioned above, which sows execrable and clumsy blasphemies in the ears that feel the itch of fornication, to join the flock of those of whom it is predicted that a time will come, when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, to satisfy their desires, they will give themselves a multitude of teachers for the itch of hearing and, turning their ears away from the truth, They will return to fables. If, on the contrary, you wisely accept this recommendation and convert yourself to the immutable God, by virtue of this praiseworthy change, you will become one of those of whom the Apostle says: Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. This cannot be said either of the nature of God, which was never evil and deserving of this name of darkness, nor of the nature of evil, which, if it existed, could never change or become light. But it is rightly and truthfully affirmed that that nature is not immutable, but by abandoning the immutable light by whom it was made, it becomes darkness in itself, but converted to it it becomes light not in itself, but in the Lord. It shines not by itself, since it is not the true light, but as illuminated by him of whom it has been said: He was the true light that illuminates every man who comes into this world. This is what you must believe, what you must understand, what you must retain, if you want to be good by participation in the immutable good, which you cannot be by yourself.
